- **Abstraction levels:** The diagrams can be explored at different levels of abstraction. An LLM agent groups modules into conceptual modules, abstractions, and summaries, so you start with a high-level view. Component-level Markdown documentation is stored in a .codeboarding/ folder, which covers the lower levels. (The layered-view claim comes from the everydev.ai listing, which also lists a "Multilayered architecture visualization" feature.)
- **Method:** Static analysis comes first. It extracts modules and their relationships from control flow, not just import graphs. The LLM layer then builds the higher-level abstractions on top of that output. One source describes the pipeline as an orchestration workflow that invokes a static code analyzer to extract raw graph data, which an AI analysis engine then processes into high-level models.
- **Output:** Diagrams are rendered as Mermaid.js, so they can be embedded in docs, IDEs, and CI. Other listed features include PNG export, incremental re-analysis of changed parts, and a GitHub Action for updating diagrams in CI.
- **Access:** It is available as a CLI, a VS Code extension, and a GitHub Action. The project is MIT-licensed.
- **Languages and models:** Supported languages include Python, TypeScript, JavaScript, Java, Go, PHP, Rust, and C#. It works with several LLM providers.

Caveats: Several results are unreliable. The succubuns.com pages contain garbled details (such as nonexistent Python versions), so I would not rely on them. The braindetox.kr post is a secondhand write-up. The everydev.ai listing has pricing and version details that may be stale. The official sources are the GitHub repo (github.com/CodeBoarding/CodeBoarding) and the demo at codeboarding.org/demo. ```text
**Summary**

The page describes the repo map as a concise overview of a git repository that lists files and their key symbols, such as classes, methods, and function signatures, with the critical lines for each definition. Aider sends it to the LLM with each change request so the model can understand how the code fits together and reuse existing abstractions.

For large repos, Aider selects only the most relevant parts. It ranks files with a graph-based algorithm, where files are nodes and dependencies are edges, then fits the highest-ranked identifiers into a token budget. The budget is set by `--map-tokens`, which defaults to 1k tokens, and Aider resizes the map as the chat changes. It can expand the map well beyond that budget when no files have been added and the model needs a broader view.

**Key quotes**

- "Aider uses a **concise map of your whole git repository**"
- "computed on a graph where each source file is a node and edges connect files which have dependencies"
- "The token budget is influenced by the `--map-tokens` switch, which defaults to 1k tokens."
- "It only includes the most important identifiers, the ones which are most often referenced by other portions of the code."

**Not covered by the page**

The page doesn't mention tree-sitter, tags.scm query files, explicit definition/reference extraction, PageRank by name, or caching. It only says "graph ranking algorithm," so I can't confirm those details from this source.

The search turned up enough to answer, though the sources are mostly API reference pages rather than a full explanation of the easing behavior.

- **Which functions accept animation options:** The v12 docs say the `duration` option works across the viewport functions, including `fitView`, `setCenter`, `setViewport`, `zoomTo`, and `fitBounds`. You can pass a duration option parameter to define the animation duration for every function that alters the viewport.
- **`ease` and `interpolate`:** The v12 API reference lists `ease` as a function of type `(t: number) => number` and `interpolate` as `"smooth" | "linear"` on the viewport helpers, and the `FitViewOptions` page lists them too. The `setCenter` signature takes `ViewportHelperFunctionOptions` plus an optional `zoom`. The v12 `general.d.ts` source describes `ease` as an optional ease function on `setViewport` and `setCenter`. (setCenter(x: number, y: number, options?: ViewportHelperFunctionOptions & { zoom?: number; }) => Promise<boolean>.)
- **v11 vs. v12:** The v11 docs list only `{ duration: number }` for these helpers, so `ease` and `interpolate` appear to be v12-era additions. The v11 page also shows `fitView` returning a boolean with no animation fields.
- **Vue Flow differs:** Vue Flow's docs describe `duration` in milliseconds, with `ease` and `interpolate` options. Don't assume React Flow uses the same units or defaults.
- **Unclear points:** The sources I found don't state the default `interpolate` value for React Flow v12 or give a worked example of a custom `ease`. Check the v12 docs or source for those details.

 `https://reactflow.dev/learn/layouting/sub-flows`

```text
## Sub Flows in React Flow v12

- **`parentId`**: Set this on a child node to make it a sub flow member. The page says the older `parentNode` option was renamed in 11.11.0 and "will be removed in version 12," so use `parentId`.
- **Relative positioning**: A child's position is relative to its parent, so `{ x: 0, y: 0 }` is the parent's top-left corner.
- **`extent: 'parent'`**: Keeps a child from being dragged outside its parent.
- **Moving parents**: Without `extent: 'parent'`, a child can be dragged outside its parent, but moving the parent still moves the child with it.
- **Parent types**: Any node type can be a parent. The `group` type is a convenience type with no handles.
- **Edges between nested nodes**: Children in the same group can connect to each other, and they can also connect to nodes outside the parent.
- **Edge z-index**: Edges render below nodes by default, including edges attached to group nodes. Edges connected to a node with a parent render above nodes. Use the `zIndex` option, such as in `defaultEdgeOptions`, to change stacking.
- **Child-level options**: A child can set `draggable: false` to prevent dragging.

## Gotchas

- **Array order matters**: Parent nodes must come before their children in the `nodes`/`defaultNodes` array, or they won't be processed correctly.
- **Deprecated property**: Code still using `parentNode` needs migrating before v12.
- **Edge stacking**: Edges attached to child nodes appear above nodes, which can surprise you if you expect the default stacking.
- **Not covered here**: This page doesn't mention `expandParent` or `elevateEdgesOnSelect`, so check the node and edge API reference for those.
```

```text
**Tree-sitter:** The article says that "Tree-sitter parses source code into an Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) based on the syntax of the programming language." It uses the py-tree-sitter-languages Python module, which provides pip-installable binary wheels for many languages.

**Definitions and references:** Using the AST, the tool can find where definitions occur: "functions, classes, variables, types and other definitions occur in the source code." It can also locate where those symbols are used or referenced elsewhere in the code.

**Tags queries:** The article doesn't explain how tags queries work. It only credits "modified versions of the tags.scm files" from several open source tree-sitter language implementations, such as those for C, Python, Go, and Rust. It doesn't say exactly how these queries feed into the map.

**Graph ranking (PageRank?):** The article doesn't name PageRank. It describes "a graph ranking algorithm, computed on a graph where each source file is a node and edges connect files which have dependencies." It also says the ranking selects the most important identifiers, "the ones which are most often referenced by other portions of the code," and doesn't name the specific algorithm.

**How the map is built:** Aider uses the definitions and references to find the most important identifiers in the repo. The map lists the repo's files and their key symbols, and it includes the critical lines for each definition. The map is trimmed to fit a token budget set by `--map-tokens`, which defaults to 1k tokens. The tree-sitter map replaces the earlier ctags-based map.

 `https://reactflow.dev/examples/layout/elkjs-multiple-handles`

```text
**Elkjs usage in this example**

- **Layout options:** The layered algorithm with direction `RIGHT`. Spacing is 40 for `elk.layered.spacing.edgeNodeBetweenLayers` and `elk.spacing.nodeNode`, and node placement uses the `SIMPLE` strategy.
- **Ports/handles mapping:** Each node's target handles become elk ports on the `WEST` (left) side, and its source handles become ports on the `EAST` (right) side. Each node also gets a port using its own node id, so edges without a specific handle still connect. Nodes use `FIXED_ORDER` port constraints to reduce edge crossings. Edges point to `sourceHandle` or `source` and `targetHandle` or `target`.
- **Nested/subflow layout:** Not shown. The graph is flat, with one root and node children, and no nested children or subflow handling.
- **Web worker:** The page doesn't mention one. It imports `elkjs/lib/elk.bundled.js` and awaits `elk.layout(graph)`, with no worker setup shown.
- **Hook behavior:** `useLayoutNodes` runs the layout once nodes are initialized, writes the new positions with `setNodes`, and calls `fitView`.

**Other layout-related examples linked on the page**

- Elkjs Tree (`/examples/layout/elkjs`), the previous example
- Horizontal Flow (`/examples/layout/horizontal`), the next example
- Dagre Tree (`/examples/layout/dagre`)
- Expand and Collapse (`/examples/layout/expand-collapse`)
- Auto Layout (`/examples/layout/auto-layout`). The page doesn't label it as Pro.
- Force Layout (`/examples/layout/force-layout`)
- Dynamic Layouting (`/examples/layout/dynamic-layouting`)
- Node Collisions (`/examples/layout/node-collisions`)

The Sub Flow example (`/examples/grouping/sub-flows`) is listed under Subflows & Grouping, not Layout.

 `https://docs.structurizr.com/dsl/cookbook/implied-relationships/`

```text
**How implied relationships work**

By default, the Structurizr DSL creates implied relationships automatically. In the main example, a user relates only to a container inside a software system. The DSL never declares a link between the user and the system, but it infers one. The source says this relationship is implied "because of the relationship between the person and the container" (about 95 characters).

**Caveats**

- **Disabling:** You can turn this off with `!impliedRelationships false`. The docs note that "With the implied relationships functionality disabled, you will need to explicitly define every relationship" (about 107 characters), so every relationship you want on a diagram must be declared.
- **One per pair:** The DSL uses the Java library's `CreateImpliedRelationshipsUnlessAnyRelationshipExistsStrategy`, which "prevents multiple implied relationships from being created" (about 66 characters). If a user has two relationships to the same container ("Uses 1" and "Uses 2"), only one implied relationship to the software system is created, namely the first one defined.
- **Showing all relationships:** To display every relationship, define each one explicitly, including the link to the software system.
- **Preferred approach:** Rather than listing many near-identical relationships, the docs recommend consolidating them into one relationship with a summarising description, which yields less cluttered diagrams.
```
</details></tool-use>

The search didn't turn up a specific recommended number of elements per diagram. The notation guidance it did find covers the basic elements, labelling, and keys.

- **Basic elements:** For levels 1 to 3, the C4 model uses 5 basic diagramming elements: persons, software systems, containers, components and relationships.
- **Styling:** The official site says all diagrams should have a key/legend to make the notation explicit, and this also applies to UML, ArchiMate and SysML diagrams.
- **Titles:** Its notation page recommends that every diagram should have a title describing the diagram type and scope.
- **Element labels:** One commentary suggests that every element includes a name, the element type, a technology choice (if appropriate), and some descriptive text.
- **Layout:** The model is not prescriptive about appearance, and it recommends using simple diagrams based on nested boxes in order to facilitate interactive collaborative drawing.

Simon Brown's notation page (c4model.com/diagrams/notation) is the primary source and is where any per-diagram element guidance would be. I didn't reach its full text, so I can't confirm whether it sets a number. The "number of elements" point is still open.

```text
**Model vs. diagrams:** IcePanel stores each object once in a shared model, and diagrams are views onto it. Objects can be reused, and edits sync everywhere. "In IcePanel, changing an object will update it everywhere it exists." Removing an object from a diagram only hides it there. "Removing an object from your diagram does not delete it from the model." Deleting from the model is permanent and removes the object from all diagrams, flows, and connections.

**Connections across levels:** The page describes what each C4 level's diagrams include, but not how lower-level connections roll up to higher-level diagrams. Level 2 (App) diagrams show apps and stores within the zoomed-in system, plus other systems and actors. Level 3 (Component) diagrams show components within an app, plus nearby apps, stores, systems, and actors. Whether deeper connections appear as implied links on higher-level views isn't covered.

**Flows:** The page only lists flows as an attribute of model objects and links to a dedicated guide. It doesn't explain how flows work.

**Tags and overlays:** The page lists tags as a model object detail and links to a guide. It doesn't mention overlays.

- Flows: /visual-storytelling/flows.md

- Domains: /core-features/domains.md
- Ownership teams: /collaboration/ownership-teams.md
- Linking to code: /integrations/linking-to-reality.md

For the connection roll-up behaviour, flows, and overlays, check those pages or query the documentation with the `ask` parameter described at the end of the page.

The search turned up the original paper's context and several implementations, but not the paper's own text on rho or the optimal-path duration formula.

- **The method:** The d3 documentation describes an interpolator for smoothly zooming between two 2D views, based on the van Wijk and Nuij paper. The returned interpolator exposes an interpolate.duration property which encodes the recommended transition duration in milliseconds. This duration is based on the path length of the curved trajectory through xy space.
- **Scaling duration:** If you want a slower or faster transition, multiply this by an arbitrary scale factor (V as described in the original paper).
- **Rho:** d3 exposes an interpolateZoom.rho(rho) method, and the d4_interpolate docs describe it as returning a new zoom interpolator using the specified curvature rho. Tulip's animator constructor takes an optimal-path flag, a velocity of 1.1 and p = sqrt(1.6) as defaults, which appear to correspond to rho. I could not confirm that mapping from a primary source.
- **Original paper:** A Polymaps implementation notes that You only need to understand section 3 (equations 1 through 5) of the paper, which is the derivation the implementation follows. The paper itself is linked from Tulip's docs as www.win.tue.nl/~vanwijk/zoompan.pdf, but I did not retrieve its contents.
- **Later work:** Reach and North describe the van Wijk and Nuij method as the current state-of-the art technique for automatic zooming and panning, and note that it minimizes perceptual cost, quantified via optical flow.

For the exact rho and duration formulas, the original PDF at the Tulip-linked URL is the place to check.

const i = d3.interpolateZoom([30, 30, 40], [135, 85, 60]);

const slower = i.duration * 2;      // scale factor V = 2 (illustrative)

## elkjs Summary (from the GitHub README)

**Current version:** The page doesn't state a specific version number. Install the latest release with `npm install elkjs`, or the development build based on ELK's `master` branch with `npm install elkjs@next`. Release minor versions match ELK's, but revision numbers may differ.

**Web workers:**
- Pass `workerUrl` to the `ELK` constructor to run layout in a Web Worker. In Node, the example path is `./node_modules/elkjs/lib/elk-worker.min.js`. In the browser, use `elk-api.js` with `workerUrl: './elk-worker.js'`.
- For debugging, `workerFactory(url)` can return a Worker built from the non-minified `elk-worker.js`.
- Node 10.x and later uses worker threads through the `web-worker` package, which is not installed automatically. Without it, a warning is raised and elkjs falls back to the non-worker version.

**Bundle files:**
- `elk-api.js` provides the API, and `elk-worker.js` contains the layout engine generated from ELK's Java code with GWT.
- `elk.bundled.js` is a browserify bundle that exposes a global `ELK` for `<script>` tags.
- `main.js` is the Node entry point for `require('elkjs')`.
- The page does not mention file sizes.

**License:** The page links to a LICENSE.md file but does not name the license in the text provided, so I can't confirm EPL-2.0 from this content.

**Performance notes:**
- The page says laying out diagrams "can be a time-consuming job," which is why Web Workers are supported.
- Logging reports times in seconds, but elkjs measures in milliseconds, and "For small graphs this may often result in execution times being reported as `0`."
- The sample log output shows `"executionTime": 0.000096` for the whole layout.
- A link to an execution time comparison against Java ELK is provided, but the page gives no numbers from it.

**Node vs. browser usage:**
- **Node:** `const ELK = require('elkjs')`, then `new ELK()`.
- **Browser:** Include `elk.bundled.js` in a script tag and use the global `ELK`, or use `elk-api.js` with a worker URL.
- **TypeScript:** Import from `elkjs/lib/elk.bundled.js` or `elkjs/lib/elk-api`.

**Sync vs. async:** Layout is asynchronous. `layout(graph, options)` returns a Promise that resolves to the laid-out graph or rejects with an error.
```

The search turned up documentation for both options and the related research, but nothing that describes a "sketch-driven" layout mode by name.

- **Option behavior:** The layer constraint is evaluated only by the InteractiveLayeredGraphVisitor and is not in ELK Layered's default configurations. If set to i, it expresses that the node should be placed in i-th layer. The position constraint works the same way within a layer, expressing that the node should be placed at the i-th position.
- **How they're used:** Domrös's ELK blog describes an interactive workflow built on the INTERACTIVE cycle-breaking and layering strategies. KLighD configures a second layout run with the interactive strategies mentioned above if the interactiveLayout property is set on the root. For the second final run the layerChoiceConstraints and positionsChoiceConstraints are evaluated. The same post says ELK only specifies the constraints, and this solution requires more than ELK can deliver, so enforcing them is left to the surrounding tooling.
- **Research paper:** Petzold, Domrös, Schönberner and von Hanxleden (VISIGRAPP 2023) present an interactive constraint framework for the layered algorithm. Its focus is on reevaluating existing constraints based on the intended movement of the constrained node so that conflicts between constraints are prevented. The paper says the framework is independent of the actual layout implementation.
- **Stability:** The blog post frames constraints as a way to increase layout stability. I didn't find a source that measures stability for these specific options.

<summary>Tool use: **WebFetch**</summary>
 `https://eclipse.dev/elk/blog/posts/2023/23-01-09-constraining-the-model.html`

```text
# Keeping ELK Layered Layouts Stable

The post describes several ways to constrain node order and layer placement. Most options are in ELK 0.8.1, and some are planned for 0.9.0.

## 1. Interactive Strategies (Reuse Existing Positions)

Set these options together. They apply to cycle breaking, layer assignment, and crossing minimization:

- `cycleBreaking.strategy: INTERACTIVE`
- `layering.strategy: INTERACTIVE`
- `crossingMinimization.semiInteractive: true`
- `separateConnectedComponents: false`

The post writes the last option without the "s" in another section.

The strategies read positions from each node. The simplest source is a pseudo position, such as `layout [position: 100, 0]`.

**Constraint-based positions:** KLighD can run a second layout pass when the `interactiveLayout` property is set on the root. It evaluates `layerChoiceConstraint` and `positionsChoiceConstraint` (the post's spelling) and converts them into pseudo positions. ELK only defines these constraints. Evaluating and enforcing them happens outside ELK. The post also notes that its example does not apply them correctly because no second run is configured.

## 2. Layer Constraints (`layerConstraint: FIRST / LAST`)

- Pins a node to the first or last layer.
- Works with Partition and model order cycle breaking.
- Other approaches may behave unexpectedly when combined with it.

## 3. Partition (Layer Assignment)

- Set `partitioning.activate: true` to enable partition-based cycle breaking and layer assignment.
- Set `partitioning.partition` on nodes to define the layers.

## 4. Model Order Cycle Breaking (`cycleBreaking.strategy`, ELK 0.8.1)

- `GREEDY_MODEL_ORDER`: Minimizes backward edges and uses textual node order as a tie-breaker.
- `MODEL_ORDER`: Uses only textual order and reverses every edge that goes against it.
- Both honor `layerConstraint` FIRST and LAST.

## 5. Model Order Layer Assignment (ELK 0.9.0, planned)

- Set `nodePromotion` to `MODEL_ORDER_LEFT_TO_RIGHT`.
- Combine it with `LONGEST_PATH_SOURCE` and model order cycle breaking.
- Nodes are promoted to layers in breadth-first model order, so the layer of each node can be specified.

## 6. Model Order in Crossing Minimization

**Pre-crossing-minimization sorting (`considerModelOrder.strategy`):**

- `PREFER_EDGES` (0.8.1): Keeps edge order. Node order only applies to nodes without incoming edges.
- `NODES_AND_EDGES` (0.8.1): Keeps both orders. This can add crossings when the two conflict.
- `PREFER_NODES` (0.9.0): Keeps node order. Edge order follows the node order of their targets.

Sorting happens before crossing minimization, which may reorder the graph again.

**Weighting order violations:**

- `crossingCounterNodeInfluence` and `crossingCounterPortInfluence` weigh ordering violations against edge crossings.
- Use values below zero so crossings stay more important. The post suggests 0.1 as an example, meaning ten order violations equal one crossing.
- `thoroughness` limits how many random tries are made. Increase it if the best ordered solution is missed.

**Enforcing order:**

- `crossingMinimization.forceNodeModelOrder` constrains only the node order.
- To enforce the full model order, set the crossing minimization strategy to `NONE` and `greedySwitch.type` to `OFF`. The sorted order is then kept as is.

## 7. Component Ordering

Set `separateConnectedComponent` to `true`. Components can then be ordered by:

- Size (default)
- The sum of their `priority` values
- Model order, using `considerModelOrder.components` (the preferred `MODEL_ORDER` option arrives in 0.9.0)

## Limits

- **Relative constraints are not yet supported.** `crossingMinimization.inLayerPredOf` and `inLayerSuccOf` are planned for future releases.
- **Choice constraints need external evaluation.** `layerChoiceConstraint` and `positionsChoiceConstraint` only take effect when a tool such as KLighD evaluates them.
- **Hierarchical layouts are not covered.** The post does not discuss compatibility with `INCLUDE_CHILDREN` hierarchy handling.
- **Some options depend on version.** `PREFER_NODES`, `MODEL_ORDER` for components, and model order layer assignment are planned for 0.9.0.
```

The paths derived here and in the previous section can easily
be translated into an implementation of a smooth animation. The
simplest and also most flexible approach is to calculate for each new
frame everything anew. We take advantage here of the property that
geodesics are unique: if C is a point on the geodesic from A to B,
then the geodesic from C to B is a subset of the original one. We
typically use a procedure which takes as input the current view (c0
and w0 ), the target view (c1 and w1 ), the animation parameters (V

average value of the last five to ten frames.
Another implementation is to recalculate the path only when one
of the parameters changes. This requires two separate procedures
(one for making a step and one for changing the path), where care
has to be taken that the latter one is always called when a parameter is changed. The suggested state-less implementation takes care
of this automatically, simplifying the change of parameters during
the flight, at the expense of some additional computing cost. But
typically, this cost is neglectable when compared to the rendering
of the frame.

  url?: unknown;
  title?: unknown;
  published?: unknown;
  summary?: unknown;
}

/** The last JSON array in the reply, or [] if there isn't a valid one. */
function picksFrom(text: string): Pick[] {
  const match = /\\[[\\s\\S]*\\]/.exec(text.slice(text.lastIndexOf("[\\n") >= 0 ? text.lastIndexOf("[\\n") : 0));
  for (const candidate of [match?.[0], /\\[[\\s\\S]*\\]/.exec(text)?.[0]]) {
    if (!candidate) continue;
    try {
      const parsed: unknown = JSON.parse(candidate);
      if (Array.isArray(parsed)) return parsed as Pick[];
    } catch {
      // try the next candidate
    }
  }
  return [];
}

/**
 * Asks Claude to search the web and pick the most useful pages. Claude replies
 * with a JSON list (url, title, date, one-sentence summary); only URLs its
 * searches actually returned are kept, so nothing is invented.
 */
export async function searchWeb(query: string, options: { limit: number; instructions?: string }): Promise<WebPage[]> {
  const client = liveClient();
  const today = new Date().toISOString().slice(0, 10);
  const messages: AnthropicSDK.Beta.BetaMessageParam[] = [
    {
      role: "user",
      content: [
        `Today is ${today}. Search the web for: ${query}`,
        options.instructions ?? "Find the most relevant, recent pages.",
        `Then reply with only a JSON array of the ${options.limit} most useful results, best first:`,
        '[{"url": "...", "title": "...", "published": "YYYY-MM-DD or null", "summary": "one factual sentence from the page"}]',
      ].join("\\n\\n"),
    },
  ];

  const found = new Map<string, WebPage>();
  let reply = "";
  for (let turn = 0; turn <= MAX_CONTINUATIONS; turn++) {
    const response = await client.beta.messages.create({
      model: loadConfig().anthropicModel,
      max_tokens: 6000,
      output_config: { effort: "low" },
      tools: [{ type: "web_search_20260209", name: "web_search", max_uses: 3 }],
      messages,
      betas: ["server-side-fallback-2026-07-01"],
      fallbacks: "default",
    });
    for (const block of response.content) {
      if (block.type === "web_search_tool_result" && Array.isArray(block.content)) {
        for (const page of block.content) {
          if (!found.has(page.url)) found.set(page.url, { title: page.title, url: page.url, snippet: "", pageAge: page.page_age ?? null });
        }
      } else if (block.type === "text") {
        reply += block.text;
      }
    }
    if (response.stop_reason !== "pause_turn") break;
    messages.push({ role: "assistant", content: response.content });
  }

  const pages: WebPage[] = [];
  for (const pick of picksFrom(reply)) {
    if (typeof pick.url !== "string") continue;
    const seen = found.get(pick.url);
    if (found.size > 0 && !seen) continue;
    pages.push({
      url: pick.url,
      title: typeof pick.title === "string" && pick.title ? pick.title : (seen?.title ?? pick.url),
      snippet: typeof pick.summary === "string" ? pick.summary : "",
      pageAge: typeof pick.published === "string" ? pick.published : (seen?.pageAge ?? null),
    });
  }
  // If the reply couldn't be parsed, fall back to the raw search results.
  return (pages.length ? pages : [...found.values()]).slice(0, options.limit);
}

 `https://eclipse.dev/elk/reference/options/org-eclipse-elk-hierarchyHandling.html`

```text
**Values** (the default is `INHERIT`):

- **INHERIT**: The node takes its hierarchy handling from its parent. If the root is `INHERIT` or unset, the behavior is the same as `SEPARATE_CHILDREN`.
- **INCLUDE_CHILDREN**: The node and all of its descendants are laid out in one run, until a descendant set to `SEPARATE_CHILDREN` is reached.
- **SEPARATE_CHILDREN**: The node triggers its own separate layout run.

**Supporting algorithms:** The page doesn't say which algorithms support `INCLUDE_CHILDREN`. It only lists the available algorithms, with no support details. It does list a separate "Hierarchy Handling (Graphviz Dot)" option, but doesn't explain how it differs. Check each algorithm's reference page to confirm support.

**Caveats:**

- The option controls how layout runs are split. It doesn't change the layout itself.
- The page notes that "Including multiple levels of hierarchy in a single layout run may allow cross-hierarchical edges to be laid out properly."
- An unset or `INHERIT` root behaves as `SEPARATE_CHILDREN`, so hierarchy grouping only changes if you set it explicitly.
- The page doesn't cover performance tradeoffs or other limitations of `INCLUDE_CHILDREN`.
```

tour around ten different locations was shown. We asked the users
to set the parameters such that the perceived animation was smooth,
fluent, and suitable for a daily use application. The task was done at
a notebook computer, and took about 5 minutes to complete. Users
could set the values via sliders, no feedback on numerical values
was given to prevent bias. The 26 users were colleagues and students from our department, and all had (much) experience with using computers.
Many users commented on the importance of cognitive aspects.

They pointed out that familiarity of the image shown, the amount
of detail in the image, and the exact task would influence their preferences. Also, we found that some users set ρ to get a zoom-out
level which they liked, where the aspect of smooth motion was of
lesser importance. On the positive side, the users found the final
paths (given their preferences) smooth, pleasant, and natural.
Figure 7 shows the parameter settings that were selected by our
users. It shows that preference for ρ and V were uncorrelated,
hence these seem to be independent dimensions, and that the conditions (two vs. ten locations) did not strongly influence the result.
The average value for V is 0.90, the standard deviation 0.43. For
ρ the average value is 1.42 and the standard deviation is 0.47. The
value of 1.42 is (statistically significant) smaller than 1.565, the
value which we derived from using the root mean squared
average
√
velocity. The average value found suggests that ρ = 2 is possibly
an optimal value, but we have not found yet a model to explain this.
Furthermore, the variation in the results was large, much larger than
we expected. Nevertheless, we think that these average values will
yield reasonable results for a variety of users and use cases. For an
optimal result, the setting has to be customizable to the preference
of the user.

7 CONCLUSIONS
We have shown how to generate a smooth animation from one view
on a 2D model to another. The problem turned out to be more complex than it seems at first sight, we needed differential geometry
and had to solve a system of three differential equations to find an
optimal path. Was this worth it? We think it was. The end result
is a set of closed equations, which can easily be used to implement
smooth and efficient zooming and panning. The visual result, as
we observed from user tests is pleasing and smooth. The original
impetus for this work was the visualization of call graphs via a hierarchical matrix visualization [van Ham 2003]. The use of a smooth
zoom-pan strategy to maintain a good overview was vital here, because the information shown is abstract and varies per level. The
method described here has been integrated, and gives very good results, visually. Finally, there are many other applications that can
take advantage of this method, i.e. any application where a user
observes some 2D object and is enabled to zoom and pan.
Besides from practical use, the approach described here is also
interesting from a more theoretical point of view. We used measurement of average perceived velocity as our starting point, and
have presented a model to relate zooming and panning. In the future we will explore if the approach described here also can deal
with more general image transforms, especially anisotropic scaling
and rotation. Another possible variation is to use a varying velocity,

such as acceleration at the beginning and deceleration at the end of
the animation. Furthermore, we focussed here on animations where
the start and end are given. The metric introduced here can possibly
also be used to optimize free navigation, where the user is free to
control the path himself.
We aimed at perceptually pleasing results, however, cognitive aspects also play an important role for this kind of animations. More
research can be done to study the role of perception versus cognition. Specifically, it is interesting to study what the average value
and variation of ρ is when perceptual effects are isolated in some
way. A more precise analysis of the various cognitive aspects as
well as guidelines for good values for ρ given a variety of tasks,
image contents, etc. would be useful. An extended model, in which
the user can additionally specify that he for instance wants to zoom
out more than the optimal paths defined here could also be useful
to tackle the cognitive aspects. Meanwhile however, the model presented here is already useful for a variety of cases, especially if the
user can tune the two parameters to his preferences.

----
Apprehension
Group similar transitions. The Gestalt principle of Common Fate
[17] states that objects that undergo similar visual changes are more
likely to be perceptually grouped, helping viewers to understand that
elements are simultaneously undergoing the same operation.
Minimize occlusion. If objects occlude each other during a transition,
they will be more difficult to track, potentially harming perception.
Maximize predictability. If the target state of a transitioning item is
predictable after viewing a fraction of its trajectory, this will reduce
cognitive load and improve tracking. This suggests slow-in slow-out
timing—not only are starting and ending states emphasized, the use
of acceleration should improve spatial and temporal predictability.
Use simple transitions. Complicated transforms with unpredictable
motion paths or multiple simultaneous changes result in increased
cognitive load. Simple, direct transitions alleviate confusion, impose
less memory burden, and improve predictability. Perceptual research
provides evidence that translation and divergence (expand/contract)
motions are easier to understand than rotation [4].
Use staging for complex transitions. Some transitions are inherently
complex and do not lend themselves to simple transitions. In such
cases, one can break up the transition into a set of simple subtransitions, allowing multiple changes to be easily observed. For
example, separating axis rescaling from value changes may help.
Make transitions as long as needed, but no longer. Transition stages
and dwells between them must be long enough for accurate change
tracking, but when too slow can result in longer task times and
diminished engagement [2, 21]. The results of Robertson et al [21]
recommend transition times around 1 second, though transitions with
minimal movement can likely be performed faster. Empirical testing
may be needed to determine optimal parameters.

The search returned yFiles documentation covering the folding edge mechanism, though not a dedicated guide to aggregating edges.

- **Folding basics:** It adds the functionality of collapsing (closing) and expanding (opening) group nodes. In the setup, a masterGraph which is the fully expanded graph and the so-called view graph which supports collapsing and expanding.
- **Folding edges:** Edges that touch content inside a collapsed group can be shown as folding edges in the view. The process of converting one or more true edges from the MasterGraph to zero or more folding edges can be customized. This conversion is handled by an edge converter.
- **Converter interface:** IFoldingEdgeFactory.addAsSeparateEdge(com.yworks.yfiles.graph.IPort, com.yworks.yfiles.graph.IPort), or IFoldingEdgeFactory.addToExistingFoldingEdge(IEdge), or null if the edge will be excluded from the view. That is, a converter can add a separate edge, merge into an existing folding edge, or exclude the edge.
- **Merging converter:** The `MergingFoldingEdgeConverter` class has an option that indicates whether edge direction should be ignored for the determination of the folding edges that are currently part of the graph. Its `addFoldingEdge` method tries to add the folding edge to an existing folding edge, considering the ignoreEdgeDirection property. This is the class that aggregates parallel edges into one folding edge.
- **Excluding converter:** The `ExcludingFoldingEdgeConverter` prevents folding edges from appearing in the view.

For your query, the aggregation behavior is in `MergingFoldingEdgeConverter`. I did not find the default converter's behavior or a conceptual guide to aggregated edges in these results, so check the yFiles folding guide for that. Note that the results mix versions: some pages are for yFiles for HTML 2.6 and others are unversioned.

The search turned up the paper's abstract and a secondary source that lists its guidelines. I did not find the full text of the guidelines section, so the entity budget details below come from one secondary summary.

- **The paper:** Elmqvist and Fekete's TVCG 2010 article (pp. 439–454) is available as a preprint from the authors' site. Its abstract presents a model for building, visualizing, and interacting with multiscale representations of information visualization techniques using hierarchical aggregation. The abstract also says the model yields a set of design guidelines for aggregated visualizations.

- **Entity budget:** A 2.5D treemap patent document that summarizes this work lists six guidelines, G1 through G6. The first is the entity budget, which it describes as a maximum of displayed entities should be maintained. The other five are visual summary, visual simplicity, discriminability, fidelity, and interpretability.

- **Related concept:** A separate UNH page on hierarchical aggregation is not the same work, but it describes a similar idea. It notes that a screen budget combined with the number of data objects can be used to calculate the degree of aggregation necessary.

The search turned up the core SHriMP papers, but nothing that directly addresses composite arcs.

- **Layout method:** A 1995 Graph Drawing paper by Storey and Müller describes a layout adjustment algorithm for fisheye views of nested graphs. It keeps lines straight and resizes nodes uniformly when more screen space is requested, and it has variants that preserve other graph properties ([source](https://rigi.cs.uvic.ca/downloads/papers/pdf/glas_abs.html)).
- **Purpose and setting:** SHriMP was built into the Rigi reverse engineering system as a fisheye-view alternative to multiple windows. A 1996 chapter presents it as a way to limit context loss when exploring large legacy software ([source](https://rigi.cs.uvic.ca/downloads/papers/pdf/mdss_abs.html)).
- **Evaluation:** A 1996 experiment compared SHriMP against the multi-window approach. A retrospective slide deck says the early fisheye views were "not so useful," and efficiency was a concern ([source](https://www.slideshare.net/slideshow/icpc-2011-storey-8471063/8471063)).
- **Related idea:** A Jambalaya course note says nested nodes can stand in for arcs for any kind of relation. This is the closest hit to composite arcs, but it's a teaching summary, not a treatment of the technique ([source](https://webhome.cs.uvic.ca/~mstorey/teaching/infovis/course_notes/trees-6up.pdf)).

For composite arcs specifically, the Storey and Müller papers or the SHriMP chapter in *Software Visualization* (World Scientific, 1996) would be the next places to look. I only ran one search, so I haven't checked those directly.

The search turned up the official 3.31.0 announcement and the WebGL preview post, but nothing specific about WebGL and compound nodes.

- **Release:** Cytoscape.js 3.31.0 added initial, experimental WebGL rendering support, and the release notes say it does not support all styles (e.g. segments edges are not supported).
- **Motivation:** The blog post says the default Canvas renderer is single-threaded, so the more elements there are the longer it takes to draw them all. WebGL is meant to take better advantage of hardware graphics acceleration.
- **Compound nodes:** None of the results address whether compound (parent/child) nodes work in the WebGL renderer or how they perform. The 3.31.0 notes and preview post are silent on it. A later docs snippet describes the WebGL renderer as structured around a modular design to handle high-performance graph rendering, but it is an unstable, indexed doc page and doesn't cover compound nodes.

For compound-node support, check the WebGL preview post in full or the GitHub issues for the 3.31.0 milestone.

```text
**Summary of cytoscape.js-expand-collapse**

**Node collapse/expand**
- Collapses and expands compound nodes, individually, recursively, or all at once (`collapse`, `collapseRecursively`, `collapseAll`, and their expand counterparts).
- Provides query helpers such as `isExpandable`, `isCollapsible`, and `getCollapsedChildren`.
- Clickable cues (plus/minus icons) can be enabled or disabled, positioned, resized, or replaced with custom images.

**Edge aggregation**
- `collapseEdges` merges edges only when all of them connect the same two nodes and there are at least two.
- `collapseEdgesBetweenNodes` and `collapseAllEdges` handle larger sets.
- The `groupEdgesOfSameTypeOnCollapse` and `edgeTypeInfo` options control how edges are grouped by type.
- Collapsed edges carry a `directionType` field, marked as unidirectional or bidirectional.

**Meta-edges**
- Edges connected to collapsed nodes are marked with the `cy-expand-collapse-meta-edge` class.
- `allowNestedEdgeCollapse` controls whether a compound edge can be collapsed without expanding it first.

**Animation and view options**
- `animate` toggles animation and can also take a function.
- `animationDuration` defaults to 1000 ms.
- `fisheye` (default true) applies a fisheye view after each operation and can also take a function.

**Layout**
- `layoutBy` runs a layout after expand/collapse, accepting either layout options or a function.
- The README recommends cose-bilkent with `randomize: false` to preserve the user's mental map.

**Other features**
- Optional undo/redo through cytoscape-undo-redo.
- Events for before and after each node and edge collapse or expand.
- `loadJson` and `saveJson` for elements.

**Known limitations**
- The README states that the repository "this repositoy is no longer being maintained," so it's unlikely to receive fixes.
- The page doesn't explain how node positions are restored on expand. The only related guidance is the layout recommendation above.
- Only compound nodes can be collapsed, and the README notes that compounds are nodes.
- Layout runs after the events fire, so layout-dependent logic must account for that ordering.
- Layout and undo/redo are optional dependencies, and the library requires Cytoscape.js ^3.3.0.
```
</details></tool-use>

// Per-file parse/extract benchmark: Harness regex vs oxc-parser vs swc vs web-tree-sitter (+tags query) vs ast-grep.
import fs from 'node:fs';
import path from 'node:path';
import { performance } from 'node:perf_hooks';
import { parseSync as oxcParse, Visitor } from 'oxc-parser';
import swc from '@swc/core';
import { Parser, Language, Query } from 'web-tree-sitter';
import { parse as sgParse, Lang } from '@ast-grep/napi';
import { parseImports } from './harness-imports.mjs';
import { scanWrites } from './harness-writes.mjs';

const HERE = path.dirname(new URL(import.meta.url).pathname);
const corpora = {
  scout: ['/Users/johnzhang/Documents/GitHub/scout-agent', ['src', 'vendor', 'web/src', 'scripts', 'test']],
  hono: [`${HERE}/corpus/hono`, ['src']],
  excalidraw: [`${HERE}/corpus/excalidraw`, ['packages']],
};

function walk(root, dir, out) {
  const abs = path.join(root, dir);
  if (!fs.existsSync(abs)) return;
  for (const e of fs.readdirSync(abs, { withFileTypes: true })) {
    if (e.name === 'node_modules' || e.name.startsWith('.')) continue;
    const rel = path.join(dir, e.name);
    if (e.isDirectory()) walk(root, rel, out);
    else if (/\.(ts|tsx|mts|js|jsx|mjs)$/.test(e.name) && !e.name.endsWith('.d.ts')) out.push(rel);
  }
}

const stats = (xs) => {
  const s = [...xs].sort((a, b) => a - b);
  const q = (p) => s[Math.min(s.length - 1, Math.floor(p * s.length))];
  return { mean: xs.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0) / xs.length, p50: q(0.5), p95: q(0.95), max: s[s.length - 1] };
};
const fmt = (n) => (n < 1 ? n.toFixed(3) : n.toFixed(2));

// ---- tree-sitter setup
await Parser.init();
const wasmDir = `${HERE}/node_modules/tree-sitter-wasms/out`;
const tsLang = await Language.load(`${wasmDir}/tree-sitter-typescript.wasm`);
const tsxLang = await Language.load(`${wasmDir}/tree-sitter-tsx.wasm`);
const tagSrc = fs.readFileSync(`${HERE}/queries/javascript.tags.scm`, 'utf8') + '\n' + fs.readFileSync(`${HERE}/queries/typescript.tags.scm`, 'utf8');
// Extra query: imports + call sites with enclosing function, the facts Harness needs.
const extra = `
(import_statement source: (string (string_fragment) @import))
(export_statement source: (string (string_fragment) @import))
(call_expression function: (import) arguments: (arguments (string (string_fragment) @import)))
`;
const mkQ = (lang) => new Query(lang, tagSrc + extra);
const tsQ = mkQ(tsLang), tsxQ = mkQ(tsxLang);
const tsParser = new Parser(); tsParser.setLanguage(tsLang);
const tsxParser = new Parser(); tsxParser.setLanguage(tsxLang);

// ---- extractors (each returns a small summary so work isn't optimized away)
const extractors = {
  'regex (Harness today)': (file, src) => {
    const imps = parseImports(src); const w = scanWrites(src);
    return { imports: imps.length, writes: w.length };
  },
  'oxc: parse + module record': (file, src) => {
    const r = oxcParse(file, src);
    const m = r.module;
    return { imports: m.staticImports.length + m.dynamicImports.length, exports: m.staticExports.length };
  },
  'oxc: parse + AST walk (defs, calls)': (file, src) => {
    const r = oxcParse(file, src);
    const m = r.module;
    let defs = 0, calls = 0;
    new Visitor({
      FunctionDeclaration() { defs++; },
      ClassDeclaration() { defs++; },
      MethodDefinition() { defs++; },
      VariableDeclarator(n) { if (n.init && /Function/.test(n.init.type)) defs++; },
      CallExpression() { calls++; },
      NewExpression() { calls++; },
    }).visit(r.program);
    return { imports: m.staticImports.length + m.dynamicImports.length, defs, calls };
  },
  'swc: parseSync (AST only)': (file, src) => {
    const ast = swc.parseSync(src, { syntax: 'typescript', tsx: file.endsWith('x'), comments: false });
    return { items: ast.body.length };
  },
  'tree-sitter: parse only': (file, src) => {
    const p = file.endsWith('x') ? tsxParser : tsParser;
    const t = p.parse(src); const n = t.rootNode.childCount; t.delete();
    return { top: n };
  },
  'tree-sitter: parse + tags query': (file, src) => {
    const tsx = file.endsWith('x');
    const t = (tsx ? tsxParser : tsParser).parse(src);
    const caps = (tsx ? tsxQ : tsQ).captures(t.rootNode);
    let defs = 0, refs = 0, imports = 0;
    for (const c of caps) {
      if (c.name.startsWith('definition.')) defs++;
      else if (c.name.startsWith('reference.')) refs++;
      else if (c.name === 'import') imports++;
    }
    t.delete();
    return { defs, refs, imports };
  },
  'ast-grep napi: parse + find calls': (file, src) => {
    const root = sgParse(file.endsWith('x') ? Lang.Tsx : Lang.TypeScript, src).root();
    const calls = root.findAll({ rule: { kind: 'call_expression' } }).length;
    return { calls };
  },
};

const results = {};
for (const [name, [root, dirs]] of Object.entries(corpora)) {
  const files = [];
  for (const d of dirs) walk(root, d, files);
  const srcs = files.map((f) => [f, fs.readFileSync(path.join(root, f), 'utf8')]);
  const lines = srcs.reduce((a, [, s]) => a + s.split('\n').length, 0);
  results[name] = { files: files.length, lines, by: {} };
  console.log(`\n## ${name}: ${files.length} files, ${lines} lines`);
  for (const [ename, fn] of Object.entries(extractors)) {
    // warmup
    for (const [f, s] of srcs) fn(f, s);
    const totals = [];
    let per = [];
    let agg = {};
    for (let run = 0; run < 3; run++) {
      per = [];
      agg = {};
      const t0 = performance.now();
      for (const [f, s] of srcs) {
        const a = performance.now();
        let out;
        try { out = fn(f, s); } catch (e) { out = { error: 1 }; }
        per.push(performance.now() - a);
        for (const [k, v] of Object.entries(out)) agg[k] = (agg[k] ?? 0) + v;
      }
      totals.push(performance.now() - t0);
    }
    const st = stats(per);
    const total = Math.min(...totals);
    results[name].by[ename] = { total, ...st, agg };
    console.log(`${ename.padEnd(38)} total ${fmt(total).padStart(8)} ms | per-file mean ${fmt(st.mean)} p50 ${fmt(st.p50)} p95 ${fmt(st.p95)} max ${fmt(st.max)} ms | ${JSON.stringify(agg)}`);
  }
}

// ---- incremental reparse in tree-sitter: single-character edit in the largest excalidraw file
{
  const root = corpora.excalidraw[0];
  const files = []; walk(root, 'packages', files);
  const biggest = files.map((f) => [f, fs.statSync(path.join(root, f)).size]).sort((a, b) => b[1] - a[1])[0][0];
  const src = fs.readFileSync(path.join(root, biggest), 'utf8');
  const p = biggest.endsWith('x') ? tsxParser : tsParser;
  let t0 = performance.now();
  const tree = p.parse(src);
  const full = performance.now() - t0;
  const at = src.indexOf('function ') + 9;
  const edited = src.slice(0, at) + 'x' + src.slice(at);
  const pt = (i) => { let row = 0, col = 0; for (let k = 0; k < i; k++) { if (src[k] === '\n') { row++; col = 0; } else col++; } return { row, column: col }; };
  const startPosition = pt(at);
  tree.edit({ startIndex: at, oldEndIndex: at, newEndIndex: at + 1, startPosition, oldEndPosition: startPosition, newEndPosition: { row: startPosition.row, column: startPosition.column + 1 } });
  t0 = performance.now();
  const tree2 = p.parse(edited, tree);
  const inc = performance.now() - t0;
  const changed = tree.getChangedRanges(tree2);
  t0 = performance.now();
  oxcParse(biggest, edited);
  const oxcFull = performance.now() - t0;
  console.log(`\n## incremental: ${biggest} (${src.length} bytes, ${src.split('\n').length} lines)`);
  console.log(`tree-sitter full parse ${fmt(full)} ms, incremental reparse after 1-char edit ${fmt(inc)} ms, changed ranges ${changed.length}; oxc full parse ${fmt(oxcFull)} ms`);
  results.incremental = { file: biggest, bytes: src.length, full, inc, oxcFull };
}

fs.writeFileSync(`${HERE}/results-parse.json`, JSON.stringify(results, null, 2));

```text
## WebGL Renderer Summary (Cytoscape.js 3.31 Preview)

**Enabling it:** Keep `name: 'canvas'` and add `webgl: true` to the `renderer` options. Optional settings include `showFps` (shows FPS at the top-left) and `webglDebug` (logs debug info to the console). Provisional tuning options are `webglTexSize`, `webglTexRows`, `webglBatchSize`, and `webglTexPerBatch`, which can usually be left at their defaults. The article notes these may change in future releases.

**Performance:** Tests on an M1 MacBook Pro using Chrome showed:
- A network of about 1,200 nodes and 16,000 edges improved from roughly 20 FPS (canvas) to over 100 FPS (WebGL).
- A network of about 3,200 nodes and 68,000 edges improved from about 3 FPS to 10 FPS. The author says 10 FPS still isn't truly smooth.

The author stresses that results depend on styles, network size, browser, and hardware.

**Limitations:**
- **Nodes and labels:** All node and label styles are fully supported, and nodes should look the same as in the canvas renderer.
- **Edges:** Only straight, haystack, and bezier edges are supported. Other types (such as taxi or segmented) render as bezier. Dashed lines, overlays, and underlays are unsupported. Edges can have one centre label, with no source or target labels. Only triangle arrows are supported, with no hollow arrows. Colours must be solid (no gradients), though opacity is supported.
- **Compound nodes:** The article doesn't mention them.
- **Load time:** Sprite sheets take time to build on initial load, and there is no progress bar.

**Labels and text rendering:** Nodes are drawn off-screen onto a sprite sheet (texture atlas) using the existing canvas renderer, then used as textures by WebGL. Each node is drawn to the sheet once and then repeatedly rendered by the GPU. Because the canvas code that draws node labels is reused, labels are most likely baked into these textures. The article doesn't explicitly say how edge labels are rendered.
```

individual visual data items do not occlude each other. Representative techniques include treemaps, most 2D and 3D geometric
visualizations, and adjacency matrices.
In the following text, we will also use the term aggregate hierarchy
(or aggregate tree) to mean a grouping of the original data items into a
hierarchical structure of data aggregates, each representing their children. Visual aggregates are the graphical depictions of data aggregates, whereas visual items are graphical representations of data items.
As a common term for both aggregates and items, we use visual entity.
Finally, given the above terms, we define visual entity budget as an
upper limit of the number of visual entities to render for a particular hierarchically aggregated visualization. By controlling this limit,
we can either use it to ensure a minimum frame rate by capping the
amount of visual entities to draw, or to control the amount of visual
clutter for the purposes of efficiently perceiving the visualized data.
3.2

---
Entity Budget (G1)

Principle: Maintain a visual entity budget when rendering hierarchical aggregated visualizations.

Discussion: Aggregated visualizations automatically support the
use of a budget of the number of visual entities to draw. If for no
other reason than technical, it makes sense to cut off rendering for
entities smaller than a pixel. In addition, it makes even more sense
to control the amount of data rendered on the screen to avoid visually
overloading the viewer.
The added benefit of a visual item budget is that it limits time spent on
rendering and guarantees a lower bound on the framerate.
5.2

Visual Summary (G2)

Principle: Visual aggregates should convey information about the
underlying data.
Discussion: We should design our visual aggregates to convey information about the underlying data that is currently not visible. This
is one of the most basic features of a hierarchically aggregated visualization: the viewer can gain a reasonably detailed overview of a dataset
while not being overloaded by the full data.
In some cases, it may even be useful for visual summary reasons to
adopt an adaptive rendering scheme as described in Section 3.4 so that
areas of the visualization with interesting features are automatically
rendered at higher detail level than those with less variance.
5.3

Visual Simplicity (G3)

Principle: Design visual aggregates to have a clean and simple
visual appearance.
Discussion: The purpose of aggregated visualizations is to reduce clutter in order to improve overview. Remember that even visual
aggregates may be rendered in large quantities, so choosing a visual
representation that is too complex or attempts to convey too much information may cause clutter in the visualization all over again.

Fig. 17. Slice-and-dice treemap visualization showing a typical Cygwin
distribution for Windows (648 directories, 6552 files, 181 MB).

Discussion: Data abstraction operations simplify datasets, but inherent in this process is also a loss of fidelity—the visualization may,
in effect, lie about the size of the effect [61, 72]. This should be made
clear to viewers using a visualization, either explicitly as done by Cui
et al. [22], or by indications in the visual aggregates (i.e. deliberately
choosing rough or imprecise visual indications of the aggregated data).
The use of averaging for data aggregation can be particularly problematic; Hans Rosling’s TED 2006 talk about global health highlights
how misleading averages can be when aggregating groups of countries
together. Or, as Andrienko and Andrienko remark, “the mean surface
temperature on the Moon may seem quite comfortable, but the actual
temperature ranges from −230◦ C to +130◦ C, and this should be taken
into account in designing clothes for astronauts.” [4]
Fortunately, the very tools provided by this article—interactive aggregation control—are exactly what is needed to counteract this problem.
Drilling down into the dataset, if only a few levels down, will invariably uncover inconsistencies compared to higher-level aggregations.
5.6

The simplest possible choice of visual representation for the visual
aggregate may often be the one used for visual data items. However,
as argued by G4, this is often a bad idea, so a more complex (or at least
different) representation may be necessary.

Interpretability (G6)

Principle: Aggregate items only so much so that the aggregation
is still correctly interpretable within the visual mapping.

Principle: Design visual aggregates to be easily distinguishable
from visual data items.

Discussion: Related to guideline G5, this guideline reinforces the
basic message of this article: aggregates convey meaning to the viewer,
and if an aggregate is degenerate, it will cause the viewer to easily
become misinformed. Items should not be aggregated merely for the
sake of reducing visual complexity, but the aggregation should also be
interpretable to the viewer in visual space.

Discussion: Visual aggregates and visual data items must be easy
to differentiate in order to not convey the wrong information to the
viewer. While using the same visual representation for both aggregates
as for items is often easiest, it may give the viewer the wrong idea
about the data.

For example, aggregates in a space-filling visualization based on containment, such as treemaps [63] or pivot graphs [78], carry high interpretability. However, an overlapping visualization such as a scatterplot, for example, will have low interpretability if the items are aggregated using dimensions not mapped to the visual attributes (i.e., the
vertical and horizontal axes for a 2D scatterplot).

5.4

Discriminability (G4)

For example, the aggregate of two points in a scatterplot might be a
single point, or the aggregate of two polylines in a parallel coordinate display might be a single polyline on their average [75]. A better
choice is to introduce a novel representation for the visual aggregate,
or to decorate the aggregate with some extra graphical feature, like the
shadows for the growing polygons technique [32] (Figure 13).

Also relevant in the interpretability discussion is the fact that visual
aggregates should be designed so that they communicate to the viewer
that there is more to see by expanding aggregated nodes (this goes
hand in hand with guideline G4, which states that visual aggregates
and visual data items should be distinguishable from each other).
6

5.5

Fidelity (G5)

Principle: Counteract fidelity problems in visual aggregates.

- **Layout factors:** Global layout features such as network size or crossing count mattered more than features of the shortest path itself, such as its length or straightness. (The authors found that global features generally had a greater impact than those of the shortest path.)

The search confirmed the headline finding of the 2004/2005 work but didn't return the detailed per-task numbers.

- **Main finding:** The study was published in Information Visualization in 2005 and compared matrix-based views with node-link diagrams across seven generic graph tasks. When graphs were bigger than twenty vertices, the matrix-based visualization outperformed node-link diagrams on most tasks.
- **Exception:** Only path finding was consistently in favor of node-link diagrams.
- **Size and density:** The authors tied their recommendations to graph size and density. The French version of the paper adds that for graphs larger than 20 nodes or sufficiently dense, most tasks are performed more efficiently on the matrix-based representation.
- **Conference version:** The 2004 InfoVis paper appeared at the 10th IEEE Symposium on Information Visualization, Oct 2004, Austin, and its abstract states the same 20-vertex threshold (when graphs are bigger than twenty vertices, the matrix-based visualization performs better than node-link diagrams on most tasks).
- **Later replication:** A later study with a much larger sample (N = 600, on 20- and 50-node social networks) partially replicated the Ghoniem et al. work. It found participant understanding was best for the node-link visualization, with higher accuracy and faster task times than the two matrix visualizations. It also noted that this performance advantage for node-link over matrix was attenuated in the larger (50-node) networks. So the replication does not fully line up with the original 2004/2005 conclusion, and I'd check its details before relying on it.

**sigma v4.0.0** was released on **8 October** (the page doesn't show the year). It is marked as the latest release.

- **Overall:** The release is a "complete rewrite of the programs system," aimed at depth and opacity problems and extended to styles, primitives, node shapes, and edge paths.
- **Rendering:** Node and edge labels now render in WebGL using signed distance fields. All WebGL layers merge into one, and WebGL 1 support is dropped in favor of WebGL 2.
- **Programs and styles:** Multi-program support is replaced by primitives compiled into a single program. A declarative styles API links graph data and state to those primitives. Depth layers let any item render at any depth. New built-in edge paths include curved, step, and loop variants. Dashed edge layers and node and edge opacity are added. The `@sigma/edge-curve` and `@sigma/node-square` packages are removed.
- **Label features:** New label attachments, backdrops, and backgrounds are included, along with node and edge label events.
- **Other features:** Internal state for nodes, edges, and the graph; native handling of parallel edges and self-loops; built-in node dragging; right-click drag camera rotation; larger picking hit areas via padding settings.
- **Layers:** `@sigma/layer-leaflet` and `@sigma/layer-maplibre` now sync one way from sigma to the map. `@sigma/layer-webgl` adds a simple color layer and a heatmap layer.
- **Breaking changes:** `hidden` and `forceLabel` are replaced by `visibility` and `labelVisibility`. The default `itemSizesReference` changes from `screen` to `positions`.
- **Documentation:** The site and examples move to Astro Starlight with a generated API reference, and Storybook is dropped.

The page does not mention HTML support, so I can't confirm anything about it in this release.

The most recent 3.x release is **sigma@3.0.3**, released on **30 April** (year not shown).

The paper is "The Not-so-Staggering Effect of Staggered Animated Transitions on Visual Tracking," published in IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics in 2014. Its main finding is negative: staggering did not help tracking.

- **Main result:** The authors found that adding staggering had a negligible or even negative effect on multiple object tracking performance. They found that introducing staggering has a negligible, or even negative, impact on multiple object tracking performance.
- **Why:** They suggest the costs outweigh the benefits. Staggering removes common-motion grouping cues and makes it harder to predict when a given object will start moving. The potential benefits of staggering may be outweighed by strong costs: a loss of common-motion grouping information about which objects travel in similar paths, and less predictability about when any specific object would begin to move.
- **Simulations and design:** They ran simulations showing staggering can reduce crowding in some dot-cloud transitions, then tested two staggering techniques on tracking tasks chosen to favor staggering. They confirmed through simulation that staggering can in some cases reduce crowding in animated transitions involving dot clouds. They empirically evaluated the effect of two staggering techniques on tracking tasks, focusing on cases that should most favour staggering.
- **Conclusion:** The authors say staggering may still help in some conditions, but that has not yet been shown.

The search confirmed the Furnas 1986 paper but returned nothing on Card and Nation (2002) or "degree-of-interest trees."

**Furnas (1986), "Generalized Fisheye Views," CHI '86:**
- The paper is a CHI '86 conference paper by George W. Furnas of Bell Communications Research, with pages 16–23. Furnas, George W. is listed as the author, and the DOI is 10.1145/22339.22342.
- The core idea is a Degree of Interest (DOI) function. It assigns to each point in the structure a number telling how interested the user is in seeing that point, given the current task. A display of a given size then shows the most interesting points.
- The formalism splits the DOI into two parts. Generalized fisheye views arise by decomposing the DOI into two components: a priori importance and distance. The simplest additive form is DOI = API(x) − D(x,y).
- Later secondary sources describe the same framework. One says the DOI takes into account both factors of A Priori Importance (API) and Distance (D), with distance measured from the user's current focus.
- The paper's motivating analogy is that people represent their own surroundings in more detail than distant things. Furnas used a calendar example that shows the current day in more detail, which is reflected in later work.

**Card and Nation (2002), "degree-of-interest trees":** No results were found. The search returned no source for this paper, so I can't confirm its details, and I'd suggest searching the title directly in the ACM Digital Library or Google Scholar.

The search turned up the original Holten paper and several implementations that document beta.

**The method:** Holten's 2006 paper (IEEE TVCG 12(5)) addresses visually bundling the adjacency edges, i.e., non-hierarchical edges, together. Each edge is modeled as a B-spline and drawn toward the hierarchy path between its endpoints. This hierarchical bundling reduces visual clutter and also visualizes implicit adjacency edges between parent nodes.

**Beta:** The bundling strength is controlled by a parameter, beta [0,1], that effectively controls the amount of bundling by straightening the spline curve. Lower values reduce ambiguity problems: If this approach is used directly for bundling adjacency edges, ambiguity problems may arise. These problems can be reduced by diminishing the bundling strength.

**Call graph example:** The paper's software-system figure is a call graph with callers in green and callees in red. It shows the system with bundling strength β = 0.85 using a balloon layout (node labels disabled) and a radial layout. The authors note that bundling reduces visual clutter, making it easier to perceive the actual connections compared with non-bundled versions.

**Effect of beta across values:** Per the paper's figure on the trade-off, low values mainly provide low-level, node-to-node connectivity information, whereas high values provide high-level information as well.

**Implementation defaults:** In graph-tool, the default is 0.8, and for beta == 0 the edges are straight lines, and for beta == 1 they strictly follow the hierarchy. A PureScript implementation cites 0.85 as D3's default, describing it as good balance of bundling and readability. That is a secondary library doc, so treat it as a convention rather than a value from the paper.

Note that the search returned no details on the exact call-graph dataset or the paper's full evaluation, so I can't confirm more specifics from these results.

The paper is findable, and its bibliographic details are consistent across sources. It appeared at Advanced Visual Interfaces (AVI) 2004, pages 421–424, with DOI 10.1145/989863.989941. Its authors are Jeffrey Heer and Stuart K. Card, and the UW Interactive Data Lab hosts a copy of it.

**Main contribution:** The paper presents a space-constrained, multi-focal tree layout algorithm called "TreeBlock," along with system- and interaction-level techniques for handling large data. These are implemented in a new version of the Degree-Of-Interest Tree browser, which can handle data sets with around a million nodes in real time (index 3-1, 3-2).

**Context:** The authors build on focus+context visualization of tree data. A related system, SpaceTree, uses filtering and aggregation with animation, but large trees often require a lot of manual panning (index 1-7, 1-9). The paper's goal is a computationally efficient layout that supports multiple foci within a limited display area (index 1-11).

**Example:** The paper's figure shows the Open Directory Project tree, with over 600,000 nodes, where expanded branches receive as much space as the display allows (index 5-4, 5-5).

Wallinger, M., Archambault, D., Auber, D., Nöllenburg, M., & Peltonen, J. (2022). Edge-Path Bundling: A Less Ambiguous Edge Bundling Approach. IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics, 28(1), 313–323. https://doi.org/10.1109/tvcg.2021.3114795

**The problem:** Existing bundling methods group edges by direction and proximity, which can produce connections that aren't in the data. Confluent drawings avoid these false connections but require the layout to be computed during bundling (All edge bundling techniques to date implicitly or explicitly cluster groups of individual edges, or parts of them, together based on these attributes. These clusters can result in ambiguous connections that do not exist in the data. Confluent drawings of networks do not have these ambiguities, but require the layout to be computed as part of the bundling process.).

**The method:** The approach takes a layout as input and routes each edge along a weighted shortest path, which keeps it close to a straight line (Edge-path bundling takes a layout as input and clusters each edge along a weighted, shortest path to limit its deviation from a straight line.). Bundling strength can be tuned using shortest-path distances, Euclidean distances, or a mix of both, and directed bundling falls out of the model naturally.

**Evidence:** In the paper's Migrations dataset comparison, force-directed bundling over-aggregates at the center of the drawing, while Edge-Path bundling distinguishes several flows that match paths in the underlying graph (per the figure caption at index 4-5 and 4-8).

Note that this is the arXiv/IEEE version details I found; I did not check the published full text for any changes from the 2021 preprint.

The paper is Gustafson, Baudisch, Gutwin, and Irani's CHI 2008 work. Its abstract reports that Wedge was more accurate than Halo on three off-screen tasks.

- **Problem and approach:** Halo shows direction and distance but can clutter when halos overlap. Wedge draws each off-screen target as an acute isosceles triangle whose tip marks the location, and it avoids overlap by rotating wedges that collide. (Halo conveys direction and distance, but is susceptible to clutter resulting from overlapping halos. We present Wedge, a visualization technique that conveys direction and distance, yet avoids overlap and clutter.)
- **Accuracy result:** The abstract's key finding is that participants were significantly more accurate when using Wedge than when using Halo.
- **Study details:** A course slide deck summarizing the study lists 18 subjects, with 2 removed for high error rates, and three tasks: locating a target, avoiding traffic-jam-adjacent targets, and identifying the closest off-screen location. These details come from lecture slides, not the paper itself, so I'd check the full paper before citing the sample size.
- **Related work:** A 2006 comparison by Burigat et al. found a different trade-off. Arrows helped users order objects by distance, while Halo helped them identify exact locations better. (Arrows allowed users to order off-screen objects faster and more accurately according to their distance, while Halo allowed users to better identify the correct location of off-screen objects.)

The full paper is available via the ACM DOI 10.1145/1357054.1357179, and Gustafson's 2009 master's thesis at the University of Manitoba covers the Wedge work in more depth.

The search didn't turn up Tempo-specific service graph documentation, but it did cover the node graph panel fields you asked about.

- **mainStat and secondaryStat** are the two stat lines shown inside a node, with the second sitting below the first. The mainstat field is the first stat shown inside the node itself. Secondarystat works like mainStat but appears under it inside the node.
- **Arc colors** use fields with an `arc__` prefix. Each field so named forms part of the colored ring around the node, and the values should total 1. A matching `_color` field sets each segment's color, such as arc__cpu paired with arc__cpu_color. Per the Infinity datasource docs, values must fall between 0 and 1, and all arc values for one node should sum to 1.
- **Single-color alternative:** a `color` field can replace arc segments with one color, and it can be a string such as an HTML color, or a number whose behavior depends on the field's color mode setting.
- **Edges** can carry mainStat and secondaryStat too, but edges do not support arc fields.

A Grafana community thread from 2021 reports users struggling to find how to set arc colors and stat formatting through the UI, and one commenter guessed the setup was for Tempo. That thread doesn't confirm how Tempo's service graph data maps to these fields, so verify the field names against the Tempo service graph output in your own environment.

// plus "which symbols did this edit change" via symbol-span hashing on oxc.
import fs from 'node:fs';
import path from 'node:path';
import crypto from 'node:crypto';
import { performance } from 'node:perf_hooks';
import { parseSync as oxcParse } from 'oxc-parser';
import { Parser, Language } from 'web-tree-sitter';

const HERE = path.dirname(new URL(import.meta.url).pathname);
await Parser.init();
const wasmDir = `${HERE}/node_modules/tree-sitter-wasms/out`;
const langs = { ts: await Language.load(`${wasmDir}/tree-sitter-typescript.wasm`), tsx: await Language.load(`${wasmDir}/tree-sitter-tsx.wasm`) };

const targets = [
  `${HERE}/corpus/excalidraw/packages/excalidraw/components/App.tsx`,

const ptAt = (s, i) => { const pre = s.slice(0, i); const row = (pre.match(/\n/g) || []).length; return { row, column: i - (pre.lastIndexOf('\n') + 1) }; };
const best = (f, n = 7) => { const xs = []; for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) { const a = performance.now(); f(); xs.push(performance.now() - a); } return Math.min(...xs); };

// Top-level + class-member symbols with a content hash of their span (whitespace-insensitive).
function symbols(file, src) {
  const r = oxcParse(file, src);
  const out = new Map();
  const add = (name, kind, node) => {
    const text = src.slice(node.start, node.end).replace(/\s+/g, ' ');
    out.set(name, { kind, start: node.start, end: node.end, hash: crypto.createHash('sha1').update(text).digest('hex').slice(0, 12) });
  };
  for (let st of r.program.body) {
    if (st.type === 'ExportNamedDeclaration' || st.type === 'ExportDefaultDeclaration') st = st.declaration ?? st;
    if (!st) continue;
    if (st.type === 'FunctionDeclaration' && st.id) add(st.id.name, 'function', st);
    else if (st.type === 'ClassDeclaration' && st.id) {
      add(st.id.name, 'class', st);
      for (const m of st.body.body) if (m.key?.name) add(`${st.id.name}.${m.key.name}`, 'method', m);
    } else if (st.type === 'VariableDeclaration') for (const d of st.declarations) { if (d.id.type === 'Identifier') add(d.id.name, 'const', d); }
    else if ((st.type === 'TSInterfaceDeclaration' || st.type === 'TSTypeAliasDeclaration') && st.id) add(st.id.name, 'type', st);
  }
  return out;
}

for (const file of targets) {
  const src = fs.readFileSync(file, 'utf8');
  const lang = file.endsWith('x') ? langs.tsx : langs.ts;
  const p = new Parser(); p.setLanguage(lang);
  // Edit: insert a statement into the body of the middle function-ish thing.
  const fnAt = (() => { const all = [...src.matchAll(/\)\s*(?::[^{=]+)?\{\n/g)]; return all[Math.floor(all.length / 2)].index; })();
  const at = src.indexOf('{\n', fnAt) + 2;
  const ins = '    console.log("harness");\n';
  const edited = src.slice(0, at) + ins + src.slice(at);

  const full = best(() => p.parse(src).delete());
  const base = p.parse(src);
  const sp = ptAt(src, at), ep = ptAt(edited, at + ins.length);
  const inc = best(() => {
    const t = base.copy();
    t.edit({ startIndex: at, oldEndIndex: at, newEndIndex: at + ins.length, startPosition: sp, oldEndPosition: sp, newEndPosition: ep });
    const t2 = p.parse(edited, t); t2.delete(); t.delete();
  });
  const oxcFull = best(() => oxcParse(file, edited).module);
  const oxcAst = best(() => oxcParse(file, edited).program);
  let changed;
  const diffT = best(() => {
    const a = symbols(file, src), b = symbols(file, edited);
    changed = [];
    for (const [k, v] of b) { const o = a.get(k); if (!o) changed.push(`+${k}`); else if (o.hash !== v.hash) changed.push(`~${k}`); }
    for (const k of a.keys()) if (!b.has(k)) changed.push(`-${k}`);
  }, 3);
  console.log(`${path.basename(file)}: ${src.split('\n').length} lines, ${src.length} bytes`);
  console.log(`  tree-sitter full ${full.toFixed(2)} ms | incremental (copy+edit+reparse) ${inc.toFixed(2)} ms`);
  console.log(`  oxc full parse (module only) ${oxcFull.toFixed(2)} ms | with JS AST ${oxcAst.toFixed(2)} ms`);
  console.log(`  symbol-diff old vs new (2 oxc parses + hash spans) ${diffT.toFixed(2)} ms -> changed: ${changed.join(', ')}`);
}
