The official Figma help article covers the Spotlight feature, which is the documented way to follow a collaborator. Observation mode itself has no official off switch in these results.

- **Spotlight:** Spotlight lets you share your view of a Figma Design file or prototype. This allows others to follow along with you and track each movement you make on the canvas. Anyone with can view or can edit access to a file or prototype can follow.
- **Following someone:** Once you follow a person, you will see their actions and cursor as they move through the prototype. To leave, you click Stop following at the top of the canvas (8-12).
- **Your own visibility:** The article notes that Figma still shows your cursor's location when you're following a presenter, and collaborators with Multiplayer Cursors enabled can see your cursor in their viewport.
- **Turning off cursors:** A Figma forum moderator suggested that if you are distracted by cursors moving around the file, you can disable them: View → Multiplayer cursors. This hides cursors, not observers.
- **Observation complaints:** Users have asked for a way to disable observe mode for years. A forum thread on the topic is still open, and one suggestion is to disable observe mode for an hour or set who can observe us. I found no evidence that Figma has shipped that.

The help article is written for Figma's older interface and says some steps may differ in the newer UI, so check the menu names in your version.

The search turned up documentation on Jaeger's deep dependency graph (DDG), mostly from third-party docs that quote the Jaeger documentation.

- **What it is:** The graph is built from the traces returned by your search and is also called a transitive dependency graph. A single graph requires a "focal" service (shown in pink) and only displays the paths passing through that service.
- **Use for large systems:** It gives a partial graph relevant to the service you care about, which helps when a full architecture graph is unreadable, such as with hundreds of services. The full architecture only shows up if a hub such as an API gateway is chosen as the focal service. Typically, this type of graph does not represent the full architecture of the system, unless there is a service that is connected to everything, e.g. an API gateway, and it is selected as a focal service.
- **Hop controls:** The graph lets you focus on the up and downstream hops of a service call and define the aggregation and graph density for the layout. In the UI, you open it from the search results and can set which service to focus on as origin (in pink) and expand and collapse the levels in the diagram.
- **Highlighting:** Entering a service or operation in the search box highlights it in the deep dependency graph.

A Harbor task description also says the DDG component lives under the Jaeger UI's DeepDependencies package and is reachable at a /deep-dependencies route with service and operation parameters. That source is a benchmark task rather than official docs, so treat it as less authoritative. It also notes that the server-side code for this view was never migrated out of Uber's internal codebase, which may mean the backend isn't fully supported in open-source Jaeger.

For comparison, the separate service-level Dependencies page, which Jaeger's FAQ describes, is a different feature and is not the focal-service hop view.

The Datadog Service Map docs cover most of your question, but the results don't say how nodes are colored.

- **Environment scoping:** Services are scoped by `env`, and you can also add a second primary tag. Choosing a different scope from the dropdowns draws a separate map made up of the services in that scope. Services in one environment can't call or be called by services in other environments.
- **Cross-environment dependencies:** The map still shows connections outside the selected environment. For example, a service deployed only in prod still shows its connections to services in staging.
- **Filtering:** You can filter with facets or a fuzzy match on service names. Facets include service type, last deploy time, or monitor status. Filtering matters most in microservice setups with hundreds or thousands of nodes.
- **Monitors:** The snippets are cut off, but one result suggests monitors can be tagged and used in the map. I couldn't confirm how monitor status is shown visually.
- **Edges and requests:** Hovering over a service highlights it and shows its request traffic as animated lines that indicate direction. Services on the left tend to be closer to customers, and those on the right are more likely root causes.
- **Node colors:** None of the results describe node coloring. The Network Map docs mention a "Map clusters" feature for grouping, but that's a separate product, so I'd check the Service Map page directly for color meanings.

The search didn't turn up anything on `transformPagePoint` or a layout-animation fix for a zoomed canvas. The results cover a related case, layout animation inside a scaled parent, and that's the useful part for you.

- **Scale correction is built in.** The official Motion docs say layout animations run on the `transform` property, and that this can visually distort children. The fix is to give the element's first child elements the `layout` prop as well. The motion component will automatically correct distortion on borderRadius and boxShadow, as long as they're set as motion values.
- **Three.js canvases need special cameras.** Motion's docs describe LayoutCamera and LayoutOrthographicCamera components to pre-distort a 3D scene so that when the CSS transform is applied to the host canvas element, it looks correct throughout the animation.
- **Scaled parents are a known pain point.** One older Stack Overflow question asks how to scale a parent without scaling its children. The answerer notes that the old `useInvertedScale()` was deprecated in favor of the `layout` prop, which didn't produce the same effect for that user. (The source is an offline mirror of a 2021 post, so its details may be dated.)
- **Nothing on `layoutId` inside a zoomed canvas.** A third-party guide describes assigning the same layoutId to two different components, and Framer will morph between them when one unmounts and the other mounts. It says nothing about pan/zoom canvases.

For a zoomed canvas, the results suggest that a `layout` element inside a scaled parent may need its children marked `layout` too, and that the built-in correction may not handle a canvas-wide `scale` the way it handles element-level transforms. I couldn't confirm that from these sources. Searching the Motion GitHub issues for "transform scale layout" or your canvas library's name plus "framer-motion" would be the next step.

```text
**Node color:** Node borders are colored red or yellow based on Service Health: "Service node borders are colored with red or yellow depending on their respective Service Health state." Service Health combines Watchdog anomalies, paging monitors, and incidents. Monitor status is shown separately, since "The status of monitors is exposed directly on the Service Map." The doc doesn't say monitor status sets the color itself.

**Edges and traffic:** Edges represent aggregate calls between services. Traffic is animated to show direction, as the map "shows its request traffic as animated lines to better emphasize directionality."

**Hover:** Hovering over a service highlights it and shows its traffic lines.

**Click:** Clicking a service offers an inspect option, which isolates that service, shows the services sending it requests, and shows the requests it sends. Each node can be inspected in turn to move through dependencies. Clicking also opens filtering options that pivot to related Datadog views scoped to that service.

**Layout direction:** The doc doesn't describe a formal left-to-right layout. It gives a general ordering: "the services on the left are closer to your customers, and the ones on the right are more likely root causes."

**Grouping and clustering:** You can group the map "by team or application" to show service ownership and application dependencies. Nodes can also collapse: "A node is collapsed when there are two services in the filter" connected through services that are not in the filter.

**Filtering:** You can filter by facets (such as service type, last deploy time, or monitor status), by fuzzy match on service names, and by incident status. You can also scope by time range. Maps are scoped by `env` and optionally a Second Primary Tag, and "These services cannot call or be called by services in other environments."

The thread has no official maintainer recipe for animating node position changes. The maintainers said the feature shouldn't be built into the core library. chrtze (Member) wrote: "i think there will not be a built-in solution for this." justrhysism (Contributor) agreed.

The workarounds discussed are:

- **Custom edges:** chrtze suggested building custom edge types, or hiding edges while nodes animate and showing them afterward.
- **CSS transition on the node:** wdfinch (the issue author) reported that a short `transform` transition on the node's translate styling "helped a lot." Edges don't get this, since they are SVG and don't use the same transform logic.
- **Framer Motion shared layout:** lee175 (community user) said wrapping the custom node in `motion.div` with the shared `layout` property works. keyserj shared a sandbox and noted that nodes also animate on initial render, so they added a state flag to animate only after that.
- **requestAnimationFrame edge syncing:** vogelsgesang proposed syncing edge positions with the node's rendered position during `transition` events. This was untested in the thread.

Known limitations:

- **Edge lag:** ClementHoang noted that longer durations cause a visible lag when dragging nodes.
- **Edges:** Edges are SVG, so animating them requires custom edge components or a simple fade.

d3-timer isn't mentioned anywhere in the thread.

 `https://github.com/motiondivision/motion/issues/3132`

```text
**Bug:** Drag misbehaves when a parent has a `transform: scale`. At a 0.5 scale, the reporter saw the drag delta come out at half the expected value, so the element lagged behind the cursor. The reporter also saw the element's internal position jump during layout animations.

**Resolution:** The thread doesn't say whether Motion now compensates for parent scale by default. Commits referencing the issue (in PR #3624, closed March 9, 2026) are titled "Fix drag offset when parent has scale transform" and add a test for `correctParentTransform`. The maintainer's suggested fix is to pass `correctParentTransform(ref)` to `transformPagePoint` on `MotionConfig`, with a ref to the scaled container. The maintainer's comment says: "You can use `correctParentTransform` to fix this."

**Other points:**
- A commenter reported that setting `initial={{ scale: 0.5 }}` on the element reduced the problem, though the wrong position still flickered occasionally.
- The thread doesn't mention `getBoundingClientRect` or how layout animations measure elements under scaled parents, so I can't answer that from this content.
```

Gource is an open-source tool that turns a repository's history into an animated, time-lapse view. The official documentation describes it as an OpenGL-based 3D visualisation tool for source control repositories.

**How the tree works:** Gource draws the project's directory structure as a tree. The repository is displayed as a tree where the root of the repository is the centre, directories are branches and files are leaves. Contributors appear as they work: contributors to the source code appear and disappear as they contribute to specific files and directories. Avatars can use Gravatar images or custom pictures.

**Inputs:** You point it at a repository directory or at a pre-generated log file. Either a supported version control directory, a pre-generated log file (see log commands or the custom log format), a Gource conf file or '-' to read STDIN. Supported systems include Git, Mercurial, Bazaar, and SVN (via custom log formats).

**Requirements and export:** It needs graphics hardware. Gource's display is rendered using OpenGL and requires a 3D accelerated video card to run. For video output, combined with FFmpeg, it can export high-quality MP4 or WebM videos.

**Caveat:** One secondary source describes the visuals differently, saying each file and directory is represented by a node, and their interactions are displayed as lines connecting them. The official man page's branch-and-leaf description is the more authoritative account.

The Krzywinski, Birol, Jones and Marra paper "Hive plots: rational approach to visualizing networks" is a 2012 journal issue entry, with online publication in December 2011 (doi:10.1093/bib/bbr069). The search results support these main points:

- **Critique of existing layouts:** Force-based and spectral layouts lack reproducibility and perceptual uniformity because they do not use a node coordinate system. Their output is hard to read and unsuitable for assessing differences in networks.
- **Hairballs:** The author's project is tagged "Rational Network Visualization – Farewell to Hairballs". A related page calls hairballs irrational network visualizations.
- **Method:** Hive plots place nodes on radially distributed linear axes, with placement based on network structural properties. The rules typically are a function of local network structure around the node (connectivity, density, centrality, etc).
- **Interpretability:** Because the layout depends only on structural properties, the plot is rational and predictable. The mapping can be tuned to the user's domain, as the HiveR documentation notes.
- **Abstract claims:** The paper says hive plots generate informative, quantitative and comparable network layouts, and that the method is computationally straightforward, scales well and is amenable to a plugin for existing tools.
- **Implementations:** The HiveR R package is a fresh R implementation of Krzywinski's Perl program, and a d3.js version also exists.

The search returned the abstract and project pages, not the full paper text, so details beyond these points are unverified.

The results do cover the core CodeCity study. The ICSE 2011 paper by Wettel, Lanza, and Robbes ran a controlled experiment with 41 participants from both academia and industry across four locations across three countries. It reported that CodeCity leads to a statistically significant increase in terms of task correctness and decrease in task completion time. The USI technical report says the study compared completion time of CodeCity and of a baseline toolset, in providing support in solving the task set. None of the snippets name Eclipse or Excel as that baseline, so I can't verify that detail.

A later study, by Moreno-Lumbreras et al. (VISSOFT 2021), compared on-screen and VR versions of CodeCity. It found that people using the VR version performed the assigned tasks in much less time, while still maintaining a comparable level of correctness.

To check the specific percentages, the next step would be to open the full ICSE 2011 PDF (https://www.inf.unibz.it/~rrobbes/p/ICSE2011-codecity.pdf) or the USI technical report (https://www.inf.usi.ch/faculty/lanza/PUBS/M/Wett2010a.pdf) and look at the results section.

The search turned up tldraw's documented level-of-detail (LOD) behavior, mostly from its SDK docs, release notes, and an example page.

- **Shape simplification at low zoom:** The "many shapes" example says sticky-note shadows disappear when zoomed out far enough, "draw" dash strokes become solid, and pattern fills flatten to solid colors. Every 7th shape is a sticky note, which has box shadow LOD behavior. Geo shapes with "draw" dash style will also simplify to solid strokes at low zoom levels, and "pattern" fills will flatten to solid colors.
- **Image LOD:** Tldraw added an image level-of-detail system in June 2024. On shared tldraw rooms, it optimizes images by loading smaller versions when resized or zoomed out.
- **Camera-driven rendering:** The camera system's rendering pipeline culls shapes outside the viewport, scales level of detail based on zoom, synchronizes updates with the browser's refresh cycles.
- **Zoom-debouncing for performance:** On large documents, the editor provides getEfficientZoomLevel(), which returns a stable value during camera movement when the document has more than 500 shapes. The threshold is configurable via debouncedZoomThreshold, the number of shapes that must be on the page for the debounced zoom level to be used. Defaults to 500 shapes.
- **Custom shapes:** The SDK docs suggest shape components read the efficient zoom level for rendering properties rather than the raw zoom, so stroke widths stay stable while the camera moves.
- **Related work:** The v4.4.0 release added R-tree spatial indexing and skipped hover hit-testing during panning, along with 2D canvas rendering for selection indicators. It said indicator rendering can be up to 25x faster in some scenarios. This significantly improves performance when selecting or hovering over many shapes.
- **Custom shape tip:** One third-party skills page advises that custom shapes always implement indicator(), which renders when zoomed out instead of the full component. That source is a secondary site, so verify it against the official docs.

Tldraw's documented limit is up to 4,000 shapes on a page at a time as of the June 2024 release notes. I didn't find a dedicated official page describing the full LOD API, so the specifics above come from the docs and examples rather than a single reference.

The search turned up Mapbox's documentation for `symbol-sort-key`, but nothing on zoom-based label fading.

- **Sort order sets placement priority:** Mapbox's docs say features are sorted in ascending order by this value, and those with lower sort keys are drawn and placed first. The iOS SDK reference says the same thing.
- **Effect depends on overlap settings:** Priority only applies when overlap is disallowed. When icon-allow-overlap or text-allow-overlap is false, features with a lower sort key will have priority during placement. When overlap is allowed, the ordering flips in terms of what sits on top: features with a higher sort key will overlap over features with a lower sort key.
- **Ordering without a sort key:** The docs note that overlapping symbols in the same layer may be rendered in data-source order or by y-position, and to control prioritization otherwise, symbol-sort-key should be used.
- **Tile edges:** Global collision detection in GL JS 0.42.0 and later means enabling symbol-avoid-edges is not needed to prevent clipped labels at tile boundaries.
- **Gaps:** None of the results covered zoom-based fading, opacity transitions, or how collision priority interacts with zoom. The results were also almost entirely duplicate iOS and Android reference pages, so a search aimed at the style spec or GL JS docs on symbol fading would be a good follow-up.

```mjs
// Semantic call graph with ts-morph (bundles TypeScript 6.0): program cost, call resolution, incremental edit.
import fs from 'node:fs';
import path from 'node:path';
import { performance } from 'node:perf_hooks';
import { Project, ts } from 'ts-morph';

const HERE = path.dirname(new URL(import.meta.url).pathname);
const which = process.argv[2] ?? 'scout';
const cfg = {
  scout: { root: '/Users/johnzhang/Documents/GitHub/scout-agent', tsconfig: 'tsconfig.json', edit: 'src/tools/news-summarize.ts' },
  hono: { root: `${HERE}/corpus/hono`, tsconfig: 'tsconfig.build.json', edit: 'src/hono-base.ts' },
  excalidraw: { root: `${HERE}/corpus/excalidraw`, tsconfig: 'tsconfig.json', edit: 'packages/element/src/mutateElement.ts' },
}[which];

const mem = () => `${(process.memoryUsage().heapUsed / 1e6).toFixed(0)} MB heap`;
let t = performance.now();
const lap = (label) => { const n = performance.now(); console.log(`  ${label}: ${(n - t).toFixed(0)} ms (${mem()})`); t = n; };

console.log(`## ts-morph ${which}`);
const project = new Project({ tsConfigFilePath: path.join(cfg.root, cfg.tsconfig), skipLoadingLibFiles: false });
lap(`load tsconfig + parse ${project.getSourceFiles().length} source files`);
const program = project.getProgram().compilerObject;
lap('create Program (module resolution, incl. tsconfig paths)');
const checker = program.getTypeChecker();
lap('create TypeChecker (binder)');

const inRepo = (sf) => sf.fileName.startsWith(cfg.root) && !sf.fileName.includes('/node_modules/') && !sf.isDeclarationFile;
const rel = (f) => path.relative(cfg.root, f);

function declName(decl) {
  const parts = [];
  for (let n = decl; n && !ts.isSourceFile(n); n = n.parent) {
    const nm = n.name && ts.isIdentifier(n.name) ? n.name.text : (n.name && ts.isPrivateIdentifier?.(n.name) ? n.name.text : null);
    if (nm && (ts.isFunctionDeclaration(n) || ts.isClassDeclaration(n) || ts.isMethodDeclaration(n) || ts.isVariableDeclaration(n) || ts.isPropertyDeclaration(n) || ts.isPropertyAssignment(n) || ts.isInterfaceDeclaration(n) || ts.isMethodSignature(n) || ts.isPropertySignature(n))) parts.unshift(nm);
  }
  return parts.join('.') || '<anon>';
}
function enclosing(node) {
  for (let n = node.parent; n; n = n.parent) {
    if (ts.isFunctionDeclaration(n) || ts.isMethodDeclaration(n) || ((ts.isArrowFunction(n) || ts.isFunctionExpression(n)) && n.parent && (ts.isVariableDeclaration(n.parent) || ts.isPropertyAssignment(n.parent)))) {
      return declName(ts.isArrowFunction(n) || ts.isFunctionExpression(n) ? n.parent : n);
    }
  }
  return '<module>';
}

function callsIn(sf) {
  const edges = [];
  let total = 0, resolved = 0;
  const visit = (node) => {
    if (ts.isCallExpression(node) || ts.isNewExpression(node)) {
      total++;
      let sym = checker.getSymbolAtLocation(ts.isPropertyAccessExpression(node.expression) ? node.expression.name : node.expression);
      if (sym && sym.flags & ts.SymbolFlags.Alias) sym = checker.getAliasedSymbol(sym);
      const decl = sym?.declarations?.[0];
      if (decl) {
        resolved++;
        const tsf = decl.getSourceFile();
        if (inRepo(tsf)) edges.push({ from: `${rel(sf.fileName)}#${enclosing(node)}`, to: `${rel(tsf.fileName)}#${declName(decl)}` });
      }
    }
    ts.forEachChild(node, visit);
  };
  visit(sf);
  return { edges, total, resolved };
}

const files = program.getSourceFiles().filter(inRepo);
let all = [], total = 0, resolved = 0;
for (const sf of files) { const r = callsIn(sf); all.push(...r.edges); total += r.total; resolved += r.resolved; }
lap(`resolve ${total} call/new sites in ${files.length} repo files -> ${resolved} resolved, ${all.length} in-repo call edges`);
const crossFile = all.filter((e) => e.from.split('#')[0] !== e.to.split('#')[0]);
console.log(`  cross-file call edges: ${crossFile.length}; sample:`, crossFile.slice(0, 4).map((e) => `${e.from} -> ${e.to}`));

// Incremental: append a function that calls something, then re-resolve that one file.
const target = project.getSourceFileOrThrow(path.join(cfg.root, cfg.edit));
const text = target.getFullText();
const times = [];
for (let i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
  const a = performance.now();
  target.replaceWithText(text + `\nexport function __harnessProbe${i}() { return ${i}; }\n`);
  const p2 = project.getProgram().compilerObject;
  const c2 = p2.getTypeChecker();
  const sf2 = p2.getSourceFile(target.getFilePath());
  // re-resolve with the new checker
  let n = 0;
  const v = (node) => { if (ts.isCallExpression(node)) { c2.getSymbolAtLocation(node.expression); n++; } ts.forEachChild(node, v); };
  v(sf2);
  times.push(performance.now() - a);
}
console.log(`  incremental edit of ${cfg.edit}: new Program+checker+re-resolve one file: ${times.map((x) => x.toFixed(0)).join(', ')} ms`);

// Built-in call hierarchy from the LanguageService (what an LSP would give).
const ls = project.getLanguageService().compilerObject;
const fn = target.getFunctions()[0] ?? target.getClasses()[0]?.getMethods()[0];
if (fn) {
  const pos = fn.getNameNode().getStart();
  let a = performance.now();
  const items = ls.prepareCallHierarchy(target.getFilePath(), pos);
  const item = Array.isArray(items) ? items[0] : items;
  const inc = item ? ls.provideCallHierarchyIncomingCalls(target.getFilePath(), pos) : [];
  const out = item ? ls.provideCallHierarchyOutgoingCalls(target.getFilePath(), pos) : [];
  console.log(`  LanguageService call hierarchy for ${fn.getName()}: ${inc.length} incoming, ${out.length} outgoing in ${(performance.now() - a).toFixed(0)} ms`);
}

````text
## `d3.interpolateZoom`

`d3.interpolateZoom` creates an interpolator for smoothly zooming between two views of a 2D plane. It is based on ["Smooth and efficient zooming and panning"](http://www.win.tue.nl/~vanwijk/zoompan.pdf) by Jarke J. van Wijk and Wim A.A. Nuij.

### Input and output format

Each view is an array of three numbers, `[cx, cy, width]`:

- **`cx`, `cy`**: the center of the viewport.
- **`width`**: the size of the viewport.

`interpolateZoom(a, b)` returns an interpolator between views `a` and `b`. Calling it with a parameter `t` in [0, 1] returns an intermediate view in the same `[cx, cy, width]` format:

```js
d3.interpolateZoom([30, 30, 40], [135, 85, 60])(0.5)
// [72, 52, 126.04761005270991]
```

### Duration

The interpolator exposes a `duration` property, which is the recommended transition time in milliseconds. It is derived from the length of the curved path through xy space. To make a transition slower or faster, multiply it by a scale factor (called *V* in the paper):

```js
const interp = d3.interpolateZoom(from, to);
const ms = interp.duration * 1.5; // 50% slower
```

### Curvature: `rho`

`d3.interpolateZoom.rho(rho)` returns a new zoom interpolator with the given curvature.

- The default is `sqrt(2)`.
- As `rho` approaches 0, the path becomes nearly linear.

```js
d3.interpolateZoom.rho(0.5)([30, 30, 40], [135, 85, 60])(0.5)
// [72, 52, 51.09549882328188]
```

### Use with d3-zoom transitions

The page does not cover d3-zoom integration directly. The common pattern is to tween from the current view to a target view during a transition, then apply each intermediate view to the zoom transform. A typical sketch (not taken from the page; check the d3-zoom docs for the exact transform mapping) looks like this:

```js
const current = [width / 2, height / 2, width]; // current [cx, cy, width]
const target  = [200, 150, 80];                 // target  [cx, cy, width]

const interp = d3.interpolateZoom(current, target);

svg.transition()
    .duration(interp.duration)
    .tween("zoom", () => t => {
      const [cx, cy, w] = interp(t);
      // Convert the view to a zoom transform and apply it, e.g. via zoom.transform
    });
```

For live examples, see the [interpolateZoom examples on Observable](https://observablehq.com/@d3/d3-interpolatezoom).
````

The official Linear post is confirmed, and secondary sources say the redesign moved theme generation from HSL to LCH. The excerpts I got don't include Linear's own LCH passage, so that detail rests on summaries.

- **Redesign scope:** Linear's post describes adjusting the sidebar, tabs, headers, and panels to cut visual noise and improve navigation hierarchy (linear.app/blog/how-we-redesigned-the-linear-ui).
- **LCH theming:** A third-party summary of the post says the redesign adopted a more uniform and adaptable theme generation system, shifting from HSL to LCH color space for better consistency in appearance. A second summary repeats this (plushcap, March 2024 summaries).
- **Contrast:** Linear's changelog says the default dark and light themes have increased contrast. It also says the Inbox got increased density and better contrast.
- **Rationale for LCH:** A design blog says LCH keeps perceived lightness steady across hues, so colors at the same lightness value look equally bright (buildmvpfast.com). This is a general explanation, not a quote from Linear.
- **Caveat on contrast:** The same blog reports that Linear's faintest gray, #62666d, measures about 3.6:1 against the near-black background, below the WCAG AA 4.5:1 minimum for body text (buildmvpfast.com). This is an outside measurement, not an official Linear figure.

- **Focus:** Kumu's focus feature temporarily hides everything except chosen elements, and it's aimed at simplifying a map while you present it. You can activate it by clicking and holding an element, connection or loop, or by selecting one and clicking the focus icon. Degree expansion is adjustable with the in/out controls, and the keyboard shortcuts let you expand or contract focus, or press a number to set exactly how many degrees the focus should extend.
- **Pre-set focus:** In the Advanced Editor, you can define focus in `@settings` for any view. The docs give an example that loads a hub element plus everything within 2 degrees (focus: #jack out 2;), and you can add multiple hubs separated by commas.
- **Clustering:** The view editor's Connect by option allows you to activate clustering on your map. The docs say it's particularly useful on stakeholder and network maps. Clustering creates new elements for each value of a chosen field and connects them to the elements that have that value (Kumu will create new elements to represent each possible value for a field of your choice).
- **Showcase:** The docs have a Showcase control guide, but the search only returned its navigation menu, so I can't summarize its behavior. Its page is at docs.kumu.io/guides/showcase.

// TypeScript 7 (Go) "unstable" sync API: oxc finds call sites, tsgo resolves them in batches.
import fs from 'node:fs';
import path from 'node:path';
import { performance } from 'node:perf_hooks';
import { API, SymbolFlags } from 'typescript/unstable/sync';
import { parseSync, Visitor } from 'oxc-parser';

const HERE = path.dirname(new URL(import.meta.url).pathname);
const which = process.argv[2] ?? 'scout';
const cfg = {
  scout: { root: '/Users/johnzhang/Documents/GitHub/scout-agent', tsconfig: 'tsconfig.json', edit: 'src/tools/news-summarize.ts' },
  hono: { root: `${HERE}/corpus/hono`, tsconfig: 'tsconfig.build.json', edit: 'src/hono-base.ts' },
  excalidraw: { root: `${HERE}/corpus/excalidraw`, tsconfig: 'tsconfig.json', edit: 'packages/element/src/mutateElement.ts' },
}[which];

let t = performance.now();
const lap = (label) => { const n = performance.now(); console.log(`  ${label}: ${(n - t).toFixed(0)} ms`); t = n; };
console.log(`## typescript@7 unstable/sync API: ${which}`);
const api = new API({ cwd: cfg.root });
lap('spawn tsgo');
const tsconfig = path.join(cfg.root, cfg.tsconfig);
let snap = api.updateSnapshot({ openProjects: [tsconfig] });
const project = snap.getProject(tsconfig) ?? snap.getProjects()[0];
lap(`open project (${project.program.getSourceFileNames().length} files incl. libs)`);

const repoFiles = project.program.getSourceFileNames().filter((f) => f.startsWith(cfg.root) && !f.includes('/node_modules/') && !f.endsWith('.d.ts'));
function callSites(file, src) {
  const pos = [];
  const r = parseSync(file, src);
  new Visitor({
    CallExpression(n) { const c = n.callee; pos.push(c.type === 'MemberExpression' ? c.property.start : c.start); },
    NewExpression(n) { pos.push(n.callee.start); },
  }).visit(r.program);
  return pos;
}
function resolveFile(proj, file) {
  const src = fs.readFileSync(file, 'utf8');
  const positions = callSites(file, src);
  if (!positions.length) return { total: 0, resolved: 0, inRepo: 0 };
  const syms = proj.checker.getSymbolAtPosition(file, positions);
  let resolved = 0, inRepo = 0;
  for (let s of syms) {
    if (!s) continue;
    if (s.flags & SymbolFlags.Alias) s = proj.checker.getAliasedSymbol(s);
    const d = s.declarations?.[0];
    if (!d) continue;
    resolved++;
    if (String(d.path).startsWith(cfg.root.toLowerCase()) || String(d.path).startsWith(cfg.root)) if (!String(d.path).includes('node_modules')) inRepo++;
  }
  return { total: positions.length, resolved, inRepo };
}
let total = 0, resolved = 0, inRepo = 0;
for (const f of repoFiles) { const r = resolveFile(project, f); total += r.total; resolved += r.resolved; inRepo += r.inRepo; }
lap(`resolve ${total} call sites in ${repoFiles.length} files -> ${resolved} resolved, ${inRepo} to in-repo declarations`);

// Incremental: write a modified copy? We must not modify the corpus for scout (read-only), so use the
// virtual-change path only for corpora we own; for scout just re-snapshot with "changed" (no content change).
const editFile = path.join(cfg.root, cfg.edit);
const times = [];
const original = fs.readFileSync(editFile, 'utf8');
const canWrite = which !== 'scout';
for (let i = 0; i < 4; i++) {
  if (canWrite) fs.writeFileSync(editFile, original + `\nexport function __probe${i}() { return ${i}; }\n`);
  const a = performance.now();
  const s2 = api.updateSnapshot({ fileChanges: { changed: [editFile] } });
  const p2 = s2.getProject(tsconfig) ?? s2.getProjects()[0];
  resolveFile(p2, editFile);
  times.push(performance.now() - a);
  snap.dispose(); snap = s2;
}
if (canWrite) fs.writeFileSync(editFile, original);
console.log(`  incremental: updateSnapshot(changed: 1 file) + re-resolve that file: ${times.map((x) => x.toFixed(0)).join(', ')} ms${canWrite ? '' : ' (content unchanged; scout is read-only)'}`);
api.close();

```

```mjs
// Benchmark elkjs (layered, hierarchical) and dagre on synthetic repo-shaped graphs.
// Usage: node bench.mjs <pkgsDir>
import { createRequire } from 'node:module';
import { performance } from 'node:perf_hooks';
const pkgs = process.argv[2];
const require = createRequire(pkgs + '/package.json');
const ELK = require('elkjs/lib/elk.bundled.js');
const dagre = require('@dagrejs/dagre');

// deterministic PRNG
function rng(seed) { let s = seed >>> 0; return () => ((s = (s * 1664525 + 1013904223) >>> 0) / 2 ** 32); }

const DOMAINS = 6, LAYERS = 4;
function makeGraph(nFiles, seed = 1) {
  const r = rng(seed);
  const files = [];
  for (let i = 0; i < nFiles; i++) {
    const d = Math.floor(r() * DOMAINS), l = Math.floor(r() * LAYERS);
    files.push({ id: `f${i}`, d, l });
  }
  const edges = [];
  const nEdges = Math.round(nFiles * 1.5);
  for (let k = 0; k < nEdges; k++) {
    const a = files[Math.floor(r() * nFiles)];
    // prefer targets in same domain, lower layer
    let b;
    for (let t = 0; t < 10; t++) {
      b = files[Math.floor(r() * nFiles)];
      if (b !== a && (r() < 0.7 ? b.d === a.d : true) && b.l >= a.l) break;
    }
    if (b && b !== a) edges.push({ id: `e${k}`, s: a.id, t: b.id, a, b });
  }
  return { files, edges };
}

const W = 140, H = 36;
function elkHier(g, routing = 'ORTHOGONAL') {
  const domains = [];
  for (let d = 0; d < DOMAINS; d++) {
    const cells = [];
    for (let l = 0; l < LAYERS; l++) {
      cells.push({ id: `c${d}_${l}`, layoutOptions: {}, children: g.files.filter((f) => f.d === d && f.l === l).map((f) => ({ id: f.id, width: W, height: H })) });
    }
    domains.push({ id: `d${d}`, children: cells.filter((c) => c.children.length) });
  }
  return {
    id: 'root',
    layoutOptions: {
      'elk.algorithm': 'layered', 'elk.direction': 'DOWN', 'elk.hierarchyHandling': 'INCLUDE_CHILDREN',
      'elk.edgeRouting': routing, 'elk.layered.spacing.nodeNodeBetweenLayers': '30', 'elk.spacing.nodeNode': '20',
    },
    children: domains,
    edges: g.edges.map((e) => ({ id: e.id, sources: [e.s], targets: [e.t] })),
  };
}

// Per-cell independent layout: each cell's files + intra-cell edges only (top grid fixed).
function elkPerCell(g) {
  const out = [];
  for (let d = 0; d < DOMAINS; d++) for (let l = 0; l < LAYERS; l++) {
    const fs = g.files.filter((f) => f.d === d && f.l === l);
    if (!fs.length) continue;
    const ids = new Set(fs.map((f) => f.id));
    out.push({
      id: `c${d}_${l}`,
      layoutOptions: { 'elk.algorithm': 'layered', 'elk.direction': 'DOWN', 'elk.edgeRouting': 'ORTHOGONAL' },
      children: fs.map((f) => ({ id: f.id, width: W, height: H })),
      edges: g.edges.filter((e) => ids.has(e.s) && ids.has(e.t)).map((e) => ({ id: e.id, sources: [e.s], targets: [e.t] })),
    });
  }
  return out;
}

function elkFlat(g) {
  return {
    id: 'root',
    layoutOptions: { 'elk.algorithm': 'layered', 'elk.direction': 'DOWN', 'elk.edgeRouting': 'ORTHOGONAL' },
    children: g.files.map((f) => ({ id: f.id, width: W, height: H })),
    edges: g.edges.map((e) => ({ id: e.id, sources: [e.s], targets: [e.t] })),
  };
}

function elkStressFlat(g) {
  return {
    id: 'root',
    layoutOptions: { 'elk.algorithm': 'stress' },
    children: g.files.map((f) => ({ id: f.id, width: W, height: H })),
    edges: g.edges.map((e) => ({ id: e.id, sources: [e.s], targets: [e.t] })),
  };
}

function dagreCompound(g) {
  const G = new dagre.graphlib.Graph({ compound: true, multigraph: true });
  G.setGraph({ rankdir: 'TB', nodesep: 20, ranksep: 30 });
  G.setDefaultEdgeLabel(() => ({}));
  for (let d = 0; d < DOMAINS; d++) { G.setNode(`d${d}`, {}); for (let l = 0; l < LAYERS; l++) { G.setNode(`c${d}_${l}`, {}); G.setParent(`c${d}_${l}`, `d${d}`); } }
  for (const f of g.files) { G.setNode(f.id, { width: W, height: H }); G.setParent(f.id, `c${f.d}_${f.l}`); }
  for (const e of g.edges) G.setEdge(e.s, e.t, {}, e.id);
  // remove empty cells
  for (let d = 0; d < DOMAINS; d++) for (let l = 0; l < LAYERS; l++) if (!G.children(`c${d}_${l}`).length) G.removeNode(`c${d}_${l}`);
  return G;
}

async function time(label, fn, reps = 3) {
  await fn(); // warm-up
  const ts = [];
  for (let i = 0; i < reps; i++) { const t0 = performance.now(); await fn(); ts.push(performance.now() - t0); }
  ts.sort((a, b) => a - b);
  console.log(`${label.padEnd(48)} median ${ts[Math.floor(ts.length / 2)].toFixed(0).padStart(6)} ms  (min ${ts[0].toFixed(0)}, max ${ts[ts.length - 1].toFixed(0)})`);
}

const elk = new ELK();
for (const n of [100, 500, 2000]) {
  const g = makeGraph(n);
  console.log(`\n== ${n} files, ${g.edges.length} edges, ${DOMAINS}x${LAYERS} cells`);
  await time(`elk layered INCLUDE_CHILDREN orthogonal`, () => elk.layout(elkHier(g)), n >= 2000 ? 1 : 3);
  await time(`elk layered INCLUDE_CHILDREN splines`, () => elk.layout(elkHier(g, 'SPLINES')), n >= 2000 ? 1 : 3);
  await time(`elk layered per-cell (sum of ${elkPerCell(g).length} runs)`, () => Promise.all(elkPerCell(g).map((c) => elk.layout(c))));
  await time(`elk layered flat (no hierarchy)`, () => elk.layout(elkFlat(g)), n >= 2000 ? 1 : 3);
  await time(`elk stress flat`, () => elk.layout(elkStressFlat(g)), n >= 2000 ? 1 : 3);
  await time(`dagre compound (domain>cell>file)`, () => dagre.layout(dagreCompound(g)), n >= 2000 ? 1 : 3);
}

```

**LCH color space:** The team rebuilt theme generation on LCH instead of HSL. They describe it as "perpetually uniform," so colors at the same lightness look about equally light to the eye, which helps produce consistently good-looking themes.

**Theme generation:** The new system reduced theme inputs to three values. Rather than defining 98 variables per theme, they now set a base color, an accent color, and a contrast level. **Typography:** Headings use Inter Display for more personality while staying readable. The rest of the text stays in regular Inter.

**Density:** The redesign aimed to increase the hierarchy and density of navigation elements, making room for Linear to grow beyond a basic issue tracker.

Semantic zoom is a Pad++ concept from Bederson and Hollan's CHI '95 demo. Objects can change how they look depending on factors such as their on-screen size, so zooming changes the level of detail. Such changes in view we call semantic zooming. The usual example is that zooming out shows a simplified version of an object, and zooming in reveals more detail (When you zoom out, you see a simplified rendering of the object, and when you zoom in, you see more details.).

The lineage runs from Perlin and Fox's 1993 Pad system, which kicked off the ZUI era in 1993 with a paper titled "Pad—An Alternative Approach to the Computer Interface." Pad used an infinite, two-dimensional information plane that is shared among users, with users peering into virtual magnifying glasses called portals. Pad++ was developed later by Bederson and Hollan with collaboration with Prof. Ben Bederson and Prof. James Hollan at the University of New Mexico.

Caveat: these results don't show that Perlin and Fox's 1993 paper itself used the term "semantic zoom." The explicit definition comes from the Pad++ work, so the term's origin is best checked against the original papers.

# Code Canvas | Microsoft Learn

I’ve been working in Microsoft Research on a project called Code Canvas for a while now, and we finally got through enough of the patent process so that I’m able to release some details publically.

Code Canvas is a research prototype focused on spatial orientation of code as the foundation of an integrated development environment. It is a spatial (2.5D) representation of source code, visual designers, and project-related artifacts that utilizes infinite panning and smooth semantic zoom for navigation. It is also extensible to allow analysis overlays and graph-based relationship visualizations.

Whenever a developer draws their code on a whiteboard, they are applying a sense of space to their software that includes directional relationships and architectural boundaries. Code Canvas lets developers write their code on a two-dimensional infinite canvas instead of in tabbed editors, so all of their source code is arranged in the same way as it would be on the whiteboard. They can still write code as they do today, in C# or C++ or whatever, but the directional relationships and architectural boundaries are part of the same canvas, and they can easily navigate and zoom smoothly in and out to understand everything at once.

In addition to utilizing spatial memory, the ability to overlay visualizations among multiple files at once is proving to be extremely valuable, especially when the visualizations are drawn directly on top of the same source code that you have already been working with. This essentially takes the canvas from a simple code editing surface and turns it into a full-blown diagramming surface, but I’ll have to go more into that later…

In the mean time, here is a somewhat old video of Code Canvas that shows some of the first features I implemented when getting started on this project.

The search turned up the ICSE 2010 poster/NIER paper and several related sources, but not the full text, so I couldn't confirm details about stable layout.

- **Publication:** Microsoft Research lists "Code Canvas: Zooming towards Better Development Environments" by Robert DeLine and Kael Rowan as a New Ideas and Emerging Results paper at ICSE. Proceedings of the International Conference on Software Engineering (New Ideas and Emerging Results)
- **Core idea:** The paper argues that the "bento box" layout of current IDEs makes it hard to stay oriented, and proposes an infinite zoomable surface for software development.
- **Spatial memory and layers:** A canvas both houses editable forms of all of a project's documents and allows multiple layers of visualization over those documents. The stated goal is to leverage spatial memory to keep developers oriented and to make it easy to synthesize information.
- **Semantic zoom:** Rowan's blog describes the prototype as a spatial (2.5D) representation of source code, visual designers, and project-related artifacts that utilizes infinite panning and smooth semantic zoom for navigation. A third-party summary says zooming out drops levels of details as you zoom out, up to the level of a UML diagram.
- **Execution traces:** A related paper says the prototype features two thematic maps, an interactive visualization of debug traces and spatial search results. The ICSE 2010 demo coverage says it demonstrates the debugger experience and how call stacks can be shown on the canvas.
- **Layout:** A related paper says CodeCanvas allows developers to rearrange the layout, to tear classes apart into smaller parts, and to filter by working sets and stack traces. I found no source that specifically describes layout stability.
- **Patent:** A Microsoft patent, US8561015, titled "Source code semantic zoom and spatial layout," lists Rowan and DeLine as inventors. Its listed status is expired for non-payment of fees.

**Abstract:** The authors state they examined "whether clustering by topic offers a sound base layout, and how developers interact with maps."

// Path-alias resolution on the excalidraw monorepo: Harness relative-only resolver vs get-tsconfig paths matcher vs oxc-resolver.
import fs from 'node:fs';
import path from 'node:path';
import { performance } from 'node:perf_hooks';
import { parseSync } from 'oxc-parser';
import { ResolverFactory } from 'oxc-resolver';
import { getTsconfig, createPathsMatcher } from 'get-tsconfig';
import { resolveImport, resolvePath } from './harness-imports.mjs';

const HERE = path.dirname(new URL(import.meta.url).pathname);
const root = `${HERE}/corpus/excalidraw`;
const files = [];
(function walk(d) { for (const e of fs.readdirSync(path.join(root, d), { withFileTypes: true })) { const r = path.join(d, e.name); if (e.isDirectory()) walk(r); else if (/\.(tsx?|mts)$/.test(e.name) && !e.name.endsWith('.d.ts')) files.push(r); } })('packages');
const exists = (p) => { try { return fs.statSync(path.join(root, p)).isFile(); } catch { return false; } };

const specs = [];
for (const f of files) {
  const m = parseSync(f, fs.readFileSync(path.join(root, f), 'utf8')).module;
  for (const i of m.staticImports) specs.push([f, i.moduleRequest.value]);
  for (const e of m.staticExports) for (const en of e.entries) if (en.moduleRequest) specs.push([f, en.moduleRequest.value]);
}
const uniq = [...new Map(specs.map((s) => [s.join('\0'), s])).values()];
const bare = uniq.filter(([, s]) => !s.startsWith('.'));
console.log(`${files.length} files, ${uniq.length} unique (file, specifier) pairs, ${bare.length} non-relative`);

const run = (label, fn) => {
  let ok = 0, inRepo = 0; const a = performance.now();
  for (const [f, s] of uniq) { const r = fn(f, s); if (r) { ok++; if (!r.includes('node_modules')) inRepo++; } }
  const ms = performance.now() - a;
  console.log(`${label.padEnd(44)} ${ok} resolved (${inRepo} in repo) in ${ms.toFixed(1)} ms = ${(ms * 1000 / uniq.length).toFixed(1)} µs/import`);
};

run('Harness resolveImport (relative only)', (f, s) => resolveImport(f, s, exists));

const tsc = getTsconfig(root);
const matcher = createPathsMatcher(tsc);
run('get-tsconfig paths matcher + Harness resolvePath', (f, s) => {
  const rel = resolveImport(f, s, exists);
  if (rel) return rel;
  for (const cand of matcher?.(s) ?? []) { const r = resolvePath(path.relative(root, cand), exists); if (r) return r; }
  return null;
});

const resolver = new ResolverFactory({
  tsconfig: { configFile: path.join(root, 'tsconfig.json'), references: 'auto' },
  extensions: ['.ts', '.tsx', '.mts', '.js', '.jsx', '.mjs', '.json'],
  extensionAlias: { '.js': ['.ts', '.tsx', '.js'] },
  conditionNames: ['types', 'import', 'module', 'default'],
  mainFields: ['types', 'module', 'main'],
});
run('oxc-resolver (tsconfig paths, cold cache)', (f, s) => resolver.sync(path.dirname(path.join(root, f)), s).path ?? null);
run('oxc-resolver (warm cache)', (f, s) => resolver.sync(path.dirname(path.join(root, f)), s).path ?? null);
const unresolved = bare.filter(([f, s]) => !resolver.sync(path.dirname(path.join(root, f)), s).path).map(([, s]) => s);
console.log('unresolved non-relative (no node_modules in this checkout):', [...new Set(unresolved)].slice(0, 8).join(', '), '…');

```text
**Meta edges:** The README defines them as "edges from/to collapsed nodes," and says they have the class "cy-expand-collapse-meta-edge."

**Edge rerouting:** The README doesn't explicitly describe rerouting edges to a collapsed node.

**groupEdgesOfSameTypeOnCollapse:** The default is `false`. When enabled, "the edges to be collapsed will be grouped according to their types," and the collapsed edges take that type. When disabled, the collapsed edge's type is "unknown."

**Cue images:** `expandCueImage` and `collapseCueImage` default to undefined. In that case, the library draws its standard expand and collapse cues.

**Animation:** `animate` defaults to `true`. `animationDuration` defaults to 1000 ms and applies only when animation is on.

**Fisheye:** `fisheye` defaults to `true`, which applies a fisheye view after expand or collapse. It can also be set to a function.

**New framework:** The README says the maintainers are "developing a new unified framework for complexity management of graphs." It gives no name or link for that framework, and it notes that this repository is no longer maintained.

(it all boils down to the same idea: recording the whole browser session so that you can back in time to see the application's entire state and debug retroactively.)
- **Breakpoints vs. print statements:** Early on, the team found that nobody uses breakpoints. A 2021 changelog says breakpoints were reworked to behave more like print statements, with an in-line action added for them (breakpoints function more like print statements).

Honeycomb's Service Map shows how traffic moves through your system. The docs say it displays known services, service dependencies, and communication between services. It is an Enterprise feature, and it is built with distributed tracing data that you send to Honeycomb.

On the "highlight path" part of your query, the docs describe hover highlighting rather than a dedicated path-tracing feature. Hovering over a service also highlights that service's dependencies within the Service Map. Selecting a service shows its service name and p95 duration information, and Isolate mode narrows the view to a smaller set of services.

To move from the map to actual requests, selecting a service or edge updates the side panel to display a list of five traces that contain the selected service(s). The See More button opens a Query Builder view. For a service, it creates a query with a filter where = <service>. For an edge between two services, it filters for traces where one service calls the other. Any filter applied to the map also carries into that query.

I found no source describing a feature that highlights a full request path from start to finish. The search did not reach the full docs page on isolate mode or the edge-specific UI, so those details are unverified.

```text
**Design lessons from the Honeycomb Service Map**

**Start with real data, not idealized graphs.** The team couldn't wait for the streaming pipeline, so they wrote a one-off script that pulled edge data from early access teams' traces. They describe the outcome as "Using the intended data schema and storage location early on made for a seamless switchover" once the streaming service was ready. Real graph data also let them test assumptions, such as whether service graphs are mostly hierarchical and how often cycles appear.

**Hairballs were the first failure.** Early renderings were rough: "Early versions of the map looked more like a tangle of spaghetti than anything else!" The fix was to make complex maps readable and navigable, which the post treats as the core design problem.

**Prototype outside the main app.** A separate playground let them compare graphing algorithms and rendering libraries without adding dependencies to the product.

**Measure layouts.** They later logged layer counts and node density. These metrics informed decisions such as zoom thresholds for showing labels and how to bucket edge weights.

**Numbers:**
- Honeycomb's internal system had fewer than 10 connected instrumented services.
- The median Honeycomb team had about 30 services, and the largest customers had hundreds.
- The map launched to all users in October 2022.

**Iterate with users early.** Early access users validated the focus on layout and readability and suggested use cases the team hadn't considered. The post's conclusion is that iterating on code and getting users involved early led to faster progress and better design decisions.

**Not covered:** The post doesn't discuss hover or isolate interactions, or specific edge rendering choices beyond edge-weight bucketing.
```
</details></tool-use>

```text
## @ast-grep/napi JavaScript API Summary

**Overview:** The API is built on napi.rs. "ast-grep's JavaScript API enables you to write JavaScript to programmatically inspect and change syntax trees." Install it with `npm install --save @ast-grep/napi`.

**Parsing:** Call `parse(Lang.JavaScript, source)` to get an `SgRoot`, then call `.root()` to get the root `SgNode`. The `SgNode` API works like jQuery for traversing the tree.

**Searching with patterns and rules:**
- `find` returns the first matching node. The docs say "`find` returns `null` if no node is found."
- `findAll` returns every match as an array. If nothing matches, it returns an empty array.
- A matcher can be a string pattern, a numeric kind ID (from `kind(Lang, name)`), or a config object with `rule` and `constraints`.
- `getMatch` and `getMultipleMatches` retrieve meta variable captures.

**Built-in languages:** The page says "`@ast-grep/napi` ships JavaScript ecosystem languages by default." It does not list them.

**Extra languages with `registerDynamicLanguage`:** Install a parser package such as `@ast-grep/lang-python`, then register it before calling `parse`. The docs say "`registerDynamicLanguage` should be called once per process." Calling it repeatedly "is not supported," so register all dynamic languages in a single call. pnpm 10+ needs an explicit build allowance for these packages.

**parseFiles / findInFiles (multi-threaded):** The page does not cover these functions.

**Performance notes:** The page links to a "Performance Tip" section, but that content is not included in the text provided, so I can't summarize it.

**Other capabilities:** The API also covers refinement (`matches`, `inside`, `has`, etc.), inspection (`range`, `kind`, `text`), and editing. Editing works through `replace` to create an `Edit` and `commitEdits` to apply it. Metavariables are not substituted automatically in `replace`, so you must build the replacement string in JavaScript.
```
</details></tool-use>

```text
**Step-by-step playback:** You can present a flow by pressing play, or move through it with the Back and Next buttons, the arrow keys, the step dropdown, or by clicking a step on a connection in the diagram. The docs recommend that you "hide details until they're needed."

**Highlighting on the diagram:** Each step's title is added to the diagram with its step number, and the step is highlighted while it's in focus. By default, the diagram shows only "the descriptions of the previous and next steps." You can turn on an option to show all step titles, and another to show all connection names.

**Subflows across levels:** A "Go to another flow" step links flows in the same or another diagram. The docs suggest using "high-level flows that have more detail lower down" to tell a story across multiple C4 levels. When you jump to another flow, you can return to the original step during or at the end of that flow.

**Paths and branches:**
- **Alternate paths** (OR logic) show different options, such as success or failure. By default, the diagram highlights "the first path created," and the ⇥ button moves between paths.
- **Parallel paths** (AND logic) show simultaneous or asynchronous steps. "the first step of each path" is highlighted by default, and the flow then continues through the first path.
- **Go to flow** steps change the Next button to "Go to flow" by default. You can use the "Skip flow" button to bypass the jump.

**Tags:** You can pin tags alongside a flow to layer attributes like risk or cost onto the diagram during a presentation.

The page describes highlighting and navigation behavior but doesn't detail specific animation effects or transitions.

**Node graph:** Agent execution appears as an interactive graph. The README says Agent Flow lets you "Watch agent execution as an interactive node graph with real-time tool calls, branching, and return flows." You can pan and zoom the canvas and click agents or tool calls to inspect them.

**File attention heatmap:** The page only names this. The Timeline & transcript panels include a file attention heatmap, along with the full execution timeline and message transcript. It gives no detail on how the heatmap is computed or displayed.

**Timeline and replay:** The timeline panel shows the full execution sequence. The README doesn't describe a scrubbing or replay control. Replay is mentioned in the JSONL section, which says you can "Point at any JSONL event log to replay or watch agent activity."

**Tool calls:** Tool calls are nodes in the graph. The Codex integration surfaces tool calls and reasoning from Codex's event stream. Clicking a tool call opens its details. The page doesn't say how tool inputs or outputs are rendered.

**Hooks and data sources:**
- **Claude Code hooks:** A "Lightweight HTTP hook server receives events directly from Claude Code for zero-latency streaming." The extension configures these hooks automatically the first time you open the panel.
- **Event relay:** In development, `pnpm run dev` runs an event relay that "receives Claude Code events and streams them to the browser via SSE."
- **Codex:** Agent Flow tails `~/.codex/sessions/**/rollout-*.jsonl` files, which respects `CODEX_HOME`.
- **JSONL logs:** Any JSONL event log can be watched as a source.
```

The paper is Hornbæk, Bederson, and Plaisant, published in *ACM Transactions on Computer-Human Interaction* vol. 9, no. 4 (2002), pp. 362–389. The abstract reports a split result: preference went to the overview interface, while speed went to the interface without one.

- **Design:** The authors compared zoomable user interfaces with and without an overview to understand their navigation patterns and usability. Thirty-two subjects solved navigation and browsing tasks on two maps.
- **Accuracy:** No difference was found between the interfaces in subjects' ability to solve tasks correctly.
- **Preference:** Eighty percent of subjects preferred the interface with an overview, saying it supported navigation and helped them track their position on the map.
- **Speed:** Subjects were faster with the interface without an overview when using one of the two maps. The abstract's wording is that the speed advantage held only for one of the two maps, so it is not a general finding.

The abstract's opening also notes that results for zoomable user interfaces are mixed, though the literature establishes the usability of interfaces with an overview.

- **Taxonomy:** The review sorts interfaces by how they separate and blend focused and contextual views. It covers four families: overview+detail (spatial separation), zooming (temporal separation), focus+context (a single continuous view), and cue-based techniques that highlight or suppress items. The four approaches are overview+detail, which uses a spatial separation between focused and contextual views; zooming, which uses a temporal separation; focus+context, which minimizes the seam between views by displaying the focus within the context; and cue-based techniques which selectively highlight or suppress items within the information space.
- **Evaluation:** The abstract says the authors discuss the critical features of each category and the empirical evidence for how well each works (Critical features of these categories, and empirical evidence of their success, are discussed.).
- **Stated aim:** The full text says the goal is to give a succinct summary of the state-of-the-art.
- **Citation details:** The paper appears in ACM Computing Surveys, vol. 41, no. 1, 2008, pp. 1–31.

```text
## Confidence tagging

Every relationship is tagged with one of three labels:

| Tag | Meaning |
|-----|---------|
| `EXTRACTED` | Found directly in the source (e.g. a function call, an import) |
| `INFERRED` | A reasonable inference Claude made, with a `confidence_score` (0.0–1.0) |
| `AMBIGUOUS` | Uncertain — flagged in the report for manual review |

EXTRACTED edges always have confidence 1.0. INFERRED edges use a discrete rubric:
- **0.95** — near-certain (explicit cross-file reference, one plausible target)
- **0.85** — strong evidence (naming + context align)
- **0.75** — reasonable (contextual but not explicit)
- **0.65** — weak (naming similarity only)
- **0.55** — speculative

---

## Token benchmark

The first run extracts and builds the graph — this costs tokens. Every subsequent query reads the compact graph instead of raw files. That's where the savings compound.

On a mixed corpus (Karpathy repos + 5 papers + 4 images, 52 files): **71.5x fewer tokens per query** vs reading the raw files directly.

| Corpus | Files | Reduction |
|--------|-------|-----------|
| Karpathy repos + papers + images | 52 | **71.5x** |
| graphify source + Transformer paper | 4 | **5.4x** |
| httpx (synthetic Python library) | 6 | ~1x |

Token reduction scales with corpus size. Six files already fits in a context window — the graph value there is structural clarity, not compression. At 52 files the savings compound quickly.

Each `worked/` folder in the repo has the raw input files and actual output (`GRAPH_REPORT.md`, `graph.json`) so you can run it yourself and verify.

---

## Parallel extraction

Code files are extracted in parallel using `ProcessPoolExecutor` — bypasses Python's GIL for genuine multiprocessing. Doc/paper/image batches are dispatched as parallel Claude subagents. On a corpus of 84 code files, parallel AST extraction runs in about 1.66x less time than sequential.

---

## SHA256 cache

Every extracted file is fingerprinted by content hash. Re-runs skip unchanged files entirely — only new or modified files go through extraction again. The cache lives in `graphify-out/cache/`.

---

## The graph format

The output `graph.json` uses NetworkX's node-link format. Each node has:
- `id` — stable identifier
- `label` — human-readable name
- `file_type` — `code`, `document`, `paper`, `image`, `rationale`
- `source_file` — where it came from

See [RFC: file-level node summaries](node-summaries-rfc.md) for two proposed
ways to add compact optional summaries for AI navigation.

Each edge has:
- `source`, `target` — node IDs
- `relation` — verb phrase (e.g. `calls`, `imports`, `implements`, `semantically_similar_to`)
- `confidence` — `EXTRACTED`, `INFERRED`, or `AMBIGUOUS`
- `confidence_score` — float (INFERRED only)
- `source_file` — where the relationship was found

Hyperedges (group relationships connecting 3+ nodes) live in `G.graph["hyperedges"]`.
```

```typescript
import { Fragment, type ReactNode } from "react";
import { Redacted } from "./Redacted";

/**
 * Model output rendered as light Markdown: headings, paragraphs, bullet and
 * numbered lists, **bold**, *italic* and `code`. Redaction tokens inside the
 * text still show as markers.
 */

const INLINE = /(\*\*[^*]+\*\*|__[^_]+__|\*[^*\s][^*]*\*|`[^`]+`)/g;

function inline(text: string): ReactNode[] {
  return text.split(INLINE).map((part, i) => {
    if (/^(\*\*|__)/.test(part)) return <strong key={i}>{inline(part.slice(2, -2))}</strong>;
    if (/^\*[^*]/.test(part) && part.endsWith("*")) return <em key={i}>{inline(part.slice(1, -1))}</em>;
    if (/^`.+`$/.test(part)) return <code key={i}>{part.slice(1, -1)}</code>;
    return <Redacted key={i} text={part} />;
  });
}

type Block =
  | { kind: "heading"; text: string }
  | { kind: "paragraph"; lines: string[] }
  | { kind: "list"; ordered: boolean; items: string[] };

function blocks(text: string): Block[] {
  const out: Block[] = [];
  for (const raw of text.replace(/\r/g, "").split("\n")) {
    const line = raw.trim();
    const last = out[out.length - 1];
    const bullet = /^[-*•]\s+(.*)$/.exec(line);
    const numbered = /^\d+[.)]\s+(.*)$/.exec(line);
    if (!line) {
      out.push({ kind: "paragraph", lines: [] });
    } else if (/^#{1,6}\s+/.test(line)) {
      out.push({ kind: "heading", text: line.replace(/^#{1,6}\s+/, "") });
    } else if (bullet || numbered) {
      const ordered = Boolean(numbered);
      const item = (bullet ?? numbered)?.[1] ?? "";
      if (last?.kind === "list" && last.ordered === ordered) last.items.push(item);
      else out.push({ kind: "list", ordered, items: [item] });
    } else if (last?.kind === "paragraph") {
      last.lines.push(line);
    } else {
      out.push({ kind: "paragraph", lines: [line] });
    }
  }
  return out.filter((b) => b.kind !== "paragraph" || b.lines.length > 0);
}

export function Prose({ text, className }: { text: string; className?: string }) {
  return (
    <div className={className ? `prose ${className}` : "prose"}>
      {blocks(text).map((block, i) => {
        if (block.kind === "heading") return <p key={i} className="prose-heading">{inline(block.text)}</p>;
        if (block.kind === "list") {
          const items = block.items.map((item, j) => <li key={j}>{inline(item)}</li>);
          return block.ordered ? <ol key={i}>{items}</ol> : <ul key={i}>{items}</ul>;
        }
        return (
          <p key={i}>
            {block.lines.map((line, j) => (
              <Fragment key={j}>
                {j > 0 && " "}
                {inline(line)}
              </Fragment>
            ))}
          </p>
        );
      })}
    </div>
  );
}

```

```text
8. SUMMARY
We have presented four interface approaches that allow users to attain both focused and
contextual views of their information spaces. Overview+detail systems allow concurrent
focus and context views that are spatially segregated in the x, y, or z dimensions.
Zooming systems allow the entire display space to be dedicated to either focused or
contextual views by temporally segregating their display. Focus+context systems present
both focus and context within a single display. This is achieved through a variety of
techniques, including selectively removing, diminishing or magnifying items, and various
displays supporting a wide field of view. Finally, cue-based systems modify the display
of items to highlight or suppress them, dependent on context or search criteria. Many
systems support combinations of these techniques.
None of these approaches is ideal. Spatial separation demands that users assimilate
the relationship between the concurrent displays of focus and context. Evidence that this
assimilation process hinders interaction is apparent in the experiments of Hornbaek et al
(2002), who note that “switching between the detail and the overview window required
mental effort and time”. Baudisch et al (2002) made similar observations of costs
associated with split attention with overview+detail interfaces. The temporal separation
of zooming also demands assimilation between pre- and post-zoom states. This difficulty
was observed by Cockburn and Savage (2003) in their evaluations, who note that “the
abrupt transitions between discrete zooming levels… meant that the participants had to
reorient themselves with each zoom action”. Animation can ease this problem (Bederson
and Boltman 1999), but it cannot be removed completely. Baudisch et al (2002) describe
how some users rapidly completed tasks using a zooming interface by first zooming out
and memorizing all target locations, but the burden of memorization is likely to be
ineffective for many tasks. Finally, many focus+context systems distort the information
space, which is likely to damage the user’s ability to correctly assess spatial properties
such as directions, distances and scales. Even in non-spatial domains, evaluations of
distortion-based techniques have largely failed to provide evidence of performance
enhancements, and several studies have shown that fisheye views can damage
fundamental components of interaction such as target acquisition.
Regardless of the usability challenges raised by each of the techniques,
overview+detail and zooming interfaces are now standard components of many desktop
graphical user interfaces. The usability benefits they can provide often outweigh their

32

costs, as demonstrated by several evaluations. For example Hornbaek and Frokjaer
(2003) showed that when reading electronic documents, both overview+detail and
fisheye interfaces offer performance advantages over traditional ‘flat’ text interfaces.
Although rare, fisheye views are starting to appear in desktop components such as the
Mac OS X Dock. In this case the usability benefits are purely cosmetic, yet many users
are happy to trade off efficiency for fashion and design lustre, which is not surprising,
since aesthetics and enjoyment are essential aspects of the computer experience (Norman
2004).
It therefore seems clear that supporting both focused and contextual views can
improve interaction over constrained single view software. The question then becomes
which style of interface, or which combination of styles, offers the greatest performance
advantages, for what tasks, and under what conditions? The current state of research fails
to provide clear guidelines, despite a recent surge in empirical analysis of the techniques’
effectiveness. Results to date have revealed that the efficiency of different techniques is
dependent on many factors, particularly the nature of the users’ task. For example,
Hornbaek et al. (2002) showed that fisheye text views allowed documents to be read
faster than overview+detail, but that participants understood documents better with
overview+detail; Schaffer et al. (1996) showed that hierarchical fisheye views
outperformed full-zoom techniques, but it remains unclear whether an alternative
implementation of zooming (continuous rather than full) would have defeated fisheye
views; Bederson et al. (2004) showed that a table-based fisheye interface for calendars on
PDAs outperformed a standard interface for complex tasks, but for simpler tasks, the
normal interface was more efficient and preferred.
We offer the following concluding comments and recommendations, with the
cautionary note that it is important for designers to use their own judgment as to which
approach to pursue. We also encourage researchers to continue to empirically analyze
these techniques to solidify our understanding of the trade-offs inherent in the different
approaches.
Overview+Detail. Several studies have found that overview+detail interfaces are
preferred to other techniques. For particular tasks, such as document comprehension, no
alternative has been found to be more effective. Notable disadvantages of
overview+detail are the additional use of screen real estate (which may be more
effectively used for details) and the mental effort and time required to integrate the
distinct views. The real estate issue can often be addressed by offering users control over
whether or not to display the overview. Even so, the time costs of this technique may

33

make it sub-optimal for dynamic activities, as shown by Baudisch et al’s (2002) driving
simulation. For consistency with state of the art interfaces, users should be able to browse
the overview without influencing the detail view, but changes in the detail view should be
immediately reflected in the overview.
Zooming. Temporal separation of views can easily create substantial cognitive load for
users in assimilating the relationship between pre- and post-zoom states—zooming is
easy to do badly, as indicated by many studies in which it has performed poorly.
Animating the transition between zoom levels can dramatically reduce the cognitive load
(but fine-tuning the duration of the animation is important). There is also evidence that
users can optimize their performance with zooming interfaces when concurrent,
unimanual controls for pan and zoom are supported.
Focus+Context. There are several distinct strategies for displaying the focal region
within its surrounding context: removal of non-focal items from the display, distortion to
alter the scale of items according to a calculated interest value, and specialized wide field
of view displays. Most of the empirical research on focus+context interfaces has
investigated distortion-oriented visualizations. Results in favour of these techniques have
been produced for tasks that involve gaining a rapid overview of the data-space or
quickly following graph structures that have clear categories. However, distortionoriented displays are likely to impair the user’s ability to make relative spatial judgments,
and they can cause target acquisition problems. Other empirical work on wide-screen
displays suggests that large high resolution displays will help users employ their natural
capabilities for focused visual attention and peripheral vision.
ACKNOWLEDGEMENTS
Many thanks to the anonymous reviewers for their extremely detailed and constructive
comments. This work was partially funded by New Zealand Royal Society Marsden
Grant 07-UOC-013.

Paul Lewis is the originator of the FLIP technique, and the results describe it consistently. The original post on aerotwist.com (Lewis's blog) explains the four steps and includes code examples. FLIP stands for First, Last, Invert, Play. In brief, you record the element's starting and ending geometry, apply inverse transforms so it visually appears to remain in its starting spot, then remove those transforms so a CSS transition eases it into place.

Other sources add context:
- **Why it matters:** FLIP lets you animate layout changes that would otherwise be costly. One source notes that FLIP converts expensive-to-animate properties (like top, left, width or height) to cheaper compositor-centric properties.
- **Origin:** A Frontend Masters lesson says the technique was first introduced by Paul Lewis at Google, and this is all the way back in 2015.
- **Tooling:** GSAP's Flip plugin automates the technique, and as of the 3.9 release (Dec 2021), it's no longer a members-only plugin.

The search did not return the Google Developers video transcript, so I can't confirm its details beyond the description that Paul steps through how to FLIP animations.

The search turned up a forum thread on performance, a forum rebuttal, and a few plugins that address the hairball problem.

- **Performance on huge vaults:** In a forum thread about a 130k-note vault, the poster reported slow indexing and a local graph that froze even at depth 1. A moderator replied that there is not a hard limit but the performance of graph view degrades with the number of notes. They also said this is not a bug but a current limitation.
- **Defenders of the graph:** A forum post titled "You All Say the Graph Is Useless" argues that the problem is lack of real information density, and that color-coding by category makes the same graph informative. This is an opinion piece, not a measurement.
- **Hairball explanation:** A blog post argues that the core issue is that Obsidian's graph view treats all connections equally by default.
- **Plugins:** Advanced Graph View is described as an advanced replacement for Obsidian's Graph View, built for large vaults (5,000–50,000 notes) where the default graph turns into a hairball. It is desktop-only and installed via BRAT, since it is not yet in the Community Plugins directory. For the depth problem, Local Graph Depth opens local graph views at a configurable default depth, since local graphs otherwise always open at depth 1. It was tested against Obsidian 1.8.

Caveat: the "useless" framing comes mostly from blog and forum opinion. The only hard data points are the forum user's own report and a moderator's general statement about degradation, with no official benchmarks in these results.

IcePanel's "implied connections" feature is documented in its blog and tips content, but I found no result using the term "lower connections."

IcePanel describes implied connections as a way to reuse existing connections created at lower levels of the C4 model. The workflow, roughly, is to create a connection between apps or components at a lower level, then draw a connection between their parent objects at a higher level, and finally pick the lower-level connection from the "implied" heading in the right-hand panel (zoom into the 2nd or 3rd level, create the connection, zoom upwards and draw a connection between the parent objects, then select the existing connection under the implied heading). IcePanel also advises against putting technical connection labels on the top context level, since that level is meant for non-technical audiences (don't reuse connections with technical labels at that level).

Nothing in these results describes a diagram-rendering style or visual notation for implied connections, so if you were looking for how they appear visually, the IcePanel docs or product UI would be the place to confirm.

Boyer","url":"https://researchweb.draco.res.ibm.com/publications/search-show-context-expand-on-demand-supporting-large-graph-exploration-with-degree-of-interest"},{"title":"Managing cloned variants: A framework and experience","url":"https://researcher.ibm.com/publications/search-show-context-expand-on-demand-supporting-large-graph-exploration-with-degree-of-interest"},{"title":"Anonymous and revocable fingerprint recognition","url":"https://researcher.draco.res.ibm.com/publications/search-show-context-expand-on-demand-supporting-large-graph-exploration-with-degree-of-interest"},{"title":"Real-time Intelligent Clustering for Graph Visualization","url":"https://www.scitepress.org/PublishedPapers/2013/43055/pdf/index.html"}]

The paper is van Ham and Perer's 2009 work, published at IEEE InfoVis and in IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics (vol. 15, no. 6, pp. 953–960). It appeared at IEEE InfoVis in Atlantic City, New Jersey, in 2009. The journal record is in IEEE transactions on visualization and computer graphics. 1996. 15(2009), 6, 20 Nov., pp. 953-60.

The core idea is to stop chasing a full overview of a huge graph. The authors argue that overviews are often unnecessary for users with semi-specific information needs, and that remote or low-powered users often can't compute them. Instead, they propose letting users browse the immediate context around a node of interest. Their method adapts Furnas' degree-of-interest function from trees to graphs, which lets them extract contextual subgraphs, limit visual complexity, and point users to interesting nodes. They test it on a database of over 3 million legal citations.

Some of the search results are unreliable. Several IBM research pages list the abstract with unrelated author names, so I'd rely on the CMU, AVIZ, and DHI records for attribution. A 2014 slide deck from the University of Vienna course (Markovic) also summarizes the paper's expand-on-demand step, which highlights a limited number of the most interesting directions.

- **Networking:** Services in the same project share a private network. Services within a project are automatically joined to a private network scoped to that project.
- **Staged changes:** Edits to services are collected as staged changes that must be reviewed and deployed before they take effect. As you create and manage your services, your changes will be collected in a set of staged changes that you must review and deploy, in order to apply them.
