```text
The paper is confirmed: Ka-Ping Yee, Danyel Fisher, Rachna Dhamija, and Marti Hearst, all at UC Berkeley, presented it at IEEE InfoVis 2001. The main results:

- **Core idea:** The layout is a radial tree, and selecting a focus node determines the view. The paper's main contribution is animating the transition when the focus changes.
- **Interpolation:** The authors interpolate node positions in polar coordinates, with ordering and orientation constraints, so the motion stays easy to follow. The animation linearly interpolates the polar coordinates of the nodes, while enforcing ordering and orientation constraints.
- **Applications:** The technique was applied to social networks and the Gnutella file-sharing network, with informal usability tests. We apply this technique to visualizations of social networks and of the Gnutella file-sharing network, and discuss the results from our informal usability tests.

Full-text copies are hosted at the Berkeley and University of Washington course pages. Citation details: Yee, K., Fisher, D., Dhamija, R., and Hearst, M., InfoVis 2001, pp. 43–50.
```

```text
7:This document is the official documentation of Sourcetrail and explains everything you need to know about working with the software.
11:Sourcetrail is an interactive source explorer that simplifies navigation in existing source code by indexing your code and gathering data about its structure. Sourcetrail then provides a simple interface consisting of three interactive views, each playing a key role in helping you obtain the information you need:
13:<img src="docs/documentation/concept.png" height="400" alt="Sourcetrail Concept">
19:Note: Sourcetrail currently supports the languages C/C++, Java and Python. Much of the UI design is therefore based on these languages and might change as soon as other languages are supported. For more information have a look at [supported languages](#supported-languages).
25:C support is powered by [Clang 11.0.0](https://clang.llvm.org/). For issues loading C code, please have a look at [Clang language compatibility](https://clang.llvm.org/compatibility.html) or report a bug in our [bug tracker](https://github.com/CoatiSoftware/SourcetrailBugTracker).
29:C++ support is powered by [Clang 11.0.0](https://clang.llvm.org/). For more Information please visit [Clang C++ Status](https://clang.llvm.org/cxx_status.html). 33:Sourcetrail includes support for Java 12 and lower which is powered by [Eclipse JDT](https://github.com/eclipse/eclipse.jdt.core). If you encounter any issues while using Sourcetrail on a Java project, please let us know by providing a minimal example in our [bug tracker](https://github.com/CoatiSoftware/SourcetrailBugTracker).
37:Sourcetrail includes support for Python 2 and Python 3 which is powered by our open-source [SourcetrailPythonIndexer](https://github.com/CoatiSoftware/SourcetrailPythonIndexer). If you encounter any issues while using Sourcetrail on a Python project, please let us know by providing a minimal example in our [bug tracker](https://github.com/CoatiSoftware/SourcetrailPythonIndexer/issues).
42:This short introduction will briefly guide you through the project setup and the user interface of Sourcetrail. The bullet point lists will provide you with the next steps to take:
44:## Starting Up Sourcetrail
46:Once you've [downloaded](https://github.com/CoatiSoftware/Sourcetrail/releases) Sourcetrail successfully you are ready to run the application. For assistance wth installation, visit the [installation](#installation) section.
49:> * Launch Sourcetrail.
51:After launching Sourcetrail you will see the [Start Window](#start-window). From here you can create your own project or choose a pre-indexed one.
61:When creating a new Sourcetrail project you will use the [Project Setup Wizard](#project-setup-wizard). This wizard splits the setup process into several subsequent steps. Depending on your project's structure and the used build system, there are different types for project setup. Choosing the correct setup method is important and can make the setup process a lot easier.
64:> * Give your project a **Name** and select a **Location** for your Sourcetrail project to live.
71:Sourcetrail projects consist of multiple *Source Groups*. Each Source Group uses a certain language, a set of files, and all configurations to index these files. There are different types of Source Groups for each supported programming language. In addition, creating a single Source Group is sufficient for most projects.
86:If you are using [CMake](https://cmake.org/) or [Make](https://www.gnu.org/software/make/) as build environment you can export a [clang JSON Compilation Database](https://clang.llvm.org/docs/JSONCompilationDatabase.html) as `compile_commands.json` file. A Compilation Database holds all information necessary for building the project, such as source files, include paths and compiler flags. Having a Compilation Database makes project setup within Sourcetrail a lot easier. We recommend using this approach if possible.
133:If you want to browse your Python source code with Sourcetrail, please continue at [Create an Empty Python Source Group](#create-an-empty-python-project) and come back here as soon as the project is created.
139:After the project is created, Sourcetrail will ask you whether you want to start indexing. Click **Start** and wait for the indexing to complete. This may take a bit of time. The [Indexing Dialog](#indexing-dialogs) and the [Status Bar](#status-bar) will give you information about the progress. Otherwise the UI will be empty. Sourcetrail indexes all named symbols and their relationships throughout the provided source files.
144:> * or Click **Stop** or press ESC to stop indexing (Sourcetrail will provide all information gathered so far and the indexing can be continued later by [refreshing](#refresh)).
148:After indexing is completed, Sourcetrail will show an overview of all indexed symbols in the [graph view](#graph-view) and some statistics in the [code view](#code-view).
155:> * Fix your errors and [refresh](#refresh) to re-index the files with errors (Open Issue: As long as there was no change in the specific file, Sourcetrail won't reindex it, use the **Force Refresh** option from the [Edit Menu](#edit)).
162:As mentioned earlier, Sourcetrail's user interface is split into three main views. Their arrangement can be adjusted as preferred and can also be detached from the main window and split into different screens (see [Window Widgets](#widget-windows)).
174:When entering a search query, the [autocompletion popup](#autocompletion-popup) will provide you with a concise list of all matching symbols. Note that Sourcetrail uses a fuzzy matching algorithm, that allows you to skip characters while entering a query.
182:* **Nodes:** All named symbols in your source code will be displayed as different [nodes](#nodes), such as `functions`, `classes` or `files`. Nodes with members (like `classes`) can be expanded to show all their contents, the number at the expansion arrow shows how many members are hidden. Clicking a node will activate it and update all the views to the new selection. Dragging a node can be used to change its position.
183:* **Edges:** The relationships between the symbols are displayed as different [edges](#edges), such as `type use`, `function call` or `file include`. Sometimes edges get bundled together and are displayed as `bundled edges` that show a number of how many edges are contained. Clicking an edge will highlight its source location in the code view.
207:The [code view](#code-view) displays all locations of the currently active symbol within the indexed source files. It does not allow for editing the source code. Syntax highlighting is used to increase readability. Source locations that are surrounded by a box when hovered can be clicked to activate the respective symbol. Active source locations are highlighted.
211:The source locations are displayed as code snippets, containing the line of interest and extra lines added to the top and bottom to give information about its context. Code snippets are then bundled together into files.
213:**Note:** A file can be selected as active symbol by clicking its name in the title bar. By clicking the title bar or the icon on the right hand side of the title bar, the file can switch between 3 different states:
231:At this point, you should have an understanding of the basics of Sourcetrail's user interface and can begin exploring your codebase. Sourcetrail will allow you to see your source code from a whole new perspective, by giving you a concise overview of its parts and a faster way of drilling down to its internals, while always maintaining the connection to the implementation details of the actual source code.
235:The Sourcetrail team wishes you a good start with our product, lots of saved time, increased productivity and much cleaner code.
245:Download and open the zip file and extract its contents into a temporary folder of your choice. Run the `setup.exe` and go through the wizard. You can now launch Sourcetrail from your start menu.
248:Download and open the Sourcetrail.dmg file and drag Sourcetrail.app into the applications folder. You can now launch Sourcetrail from your Applications.
256:Download the `.tar.gz` file and extract it. To start Sourcetrail run the `Sourcetrail.sh` script. Sourcetrail creates a folder `~/.config/sourcetrail` at the first run, this is the folder for Sourcetrail settings.
259:To install Sourcetrail run the `install.sh` script with `sudo`. It will install Sourcetrail to `/opt/sourcetrail` and create the `/usr/bin/sourcetrail` symlink.
262:To uninstall Sourcetrail run the `/opt/sourcetrail/uninstall.sh` script with `sudo`.
266:Download the `.AppImage` file. Give it permission to execute with `chmod a+x` or via the context menu. To start Sourcetrail double click it or execute it from the Terminal. Sourcetrail creates a folder `~/.config/sourcetrail` at the first run, this is the folder for Sourcetrail settings.
272:The data folder holds certain files that are used by Sourcetrail to run the program. After following the [installation instructions](#installation) the data folder should be located in the following locations on your platform.
276:| Windows | `C:/Users/You/AppData/Local/Coati Software/Sourcetrail` _(used for dynamic data and settings)_ `install_directory/Coati Software/Sourcetrail/data` _(used for static app data)_
```

 `https://appmap.io/docs/reference/guides/using-appmap-diagrams.html`

```text
## Dependency Map
- **Purpose:** The page says it "shows all the code that's relevant to what you're working on and how it's connected."
- **Expand/collapse:** Packages and Web Service endpoints can be expanded and collapsed, but the page gives no detail on the mechanics.
- **Edges:** The page does not describe how connections are drawn.
- **Linking:** You can list a class's functions used by the executed code, explore callers and callees, view SQL queries, and open source code at a specific function's line.
- **Visual design:** Nodes are colored by type (see Flame Graph for the shared palette). The page shows an overview image but describes no further styling.

## Sequence Diagram
- **Layout:** "Function calls are shown as horizontal arrows, ordered from top to bottom as they occurred at runtime."
- **Lifelines:** Each code package is a vertical lane. Inbound HTTP requests appear on the left, and database queries and RPC requests on the right.
- **Expand/collapse:** The `[-]` control collapses a call and its nested events, and `[+]` expands them again. Depth can also be limited so that deeper calls are hidden.
- **Hiding lifelines:** Clicking the "X" on a lifeline label removes it. Hidden lifelines return through the "Filters" control or the "Clear" control.
- **Edges:** Each call is a line from one lifeline to another, and the return value is drawn in the opposite direction.
- **Linking:** Selecting a call shows its details, or you can open the same event in Trace View.
- **Visual design:** Lifeline labels stay pinned at the top while scrolling. Hidden lifelines are excluded from SVG export.

## Trace View
- **Purpose:** It shows "the call tree starting with web service endpoints going through function calls all the way to SQL operations."
- **Navigation:** You can "navigate forward, backward, up, and down through a detailed execution trace."
- **Expand/collapse:** Execution paths can be expanded and collapsed.
- **Edges:** The page does not separately describe edge rendering beyond the call-tree structure.
- **Linking:** You can explore callers and callees, view variable names and values at any point, view SQL queries, and jump to source code.
- **Visual design:** The page includes no specific styling notes.

## Flame Graph
- **Width:** "the width of the event is proportional to how long it takes to execute."
- **Structure:** The bottom layer is the recording name, colored teal. Callers sit below the functions they call, and subsequent calls run left to right.
- **Colors:** Blue marks classes, purple marks database queries, and yellow marks outgoing service calls.
- **Labels:** Each cell shows elapsed time in ms or µs. Hovering reveals names and timing when cells are too small.
- **Zoom:** Clicking an event expands it to full width. You can also zoom with the `+`/`-` controls, the zoom bar, or the mouse wheel.
- **Linking:** "Show in Sequence" or "Show in Trace" opens an event in those views, and "Show in Flame Graph" works in the reverse direction.
```

```mjs
// Benchmark libavoid-js orthogonal routing: N rectangles on a grid, E connectors.
// Usage: node avoid.mjs <pkgsDir>
import { performance } from 'node:perf_hooks';
const pkgs = process.argv[2];
const { AvoidLib } = await import(pkgs + '/node_modules/libavoid-js/dist/index-node.mjs');
await AvoidLib.load(pkgs + '/node_modules/libavoid-js/dist/libavoid.wasm');
const Avoid = AvoidLib.getInstance();

function rng(seed) { let s = seed >>> 0; return () => ((s = (s * 1664525 + 1013904223) >>> 0) / 2 ** 32); }

function run(n, e, incremental) {
  const r = rng(7);
  const router = new Avoid.Router(Avoid.OrthogonalRouting);
  router.setRoutingParameter(Avoid.RoutingParameter.shapeBufferDistance, 6);
  router.setRoutingParameter(Avoid.RoutingParameter.idealNudgingDistance, 6);
  router.setRoutingParameter(Avoid.RoutingParameter.segmentPenalty, 50);
  router.setRoutingOption(Avoid.RoutingOption.nudgeOrthogonalSegmentsConnectedToShapes, true);
  const cols = Math.ceil(Math.sqrt(n * 2));
  const shapes = [];
  for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    const x = (i % cols) * 200, y = Math.floor(i / cols) * 90;
    shapes.push(new Avoid.ShapeRef(router, new Avoid.Rectangle(new Avoid.Point(x, y), new Avoid.Point(x + 140, y + 36))));
  }
  const conns = [];
  for (let k = 0; k < e; k++) {
    const a = shapes[Math.floor(r() * n)], b = shapes[Math.floor(r() * n)];
    if (a === b) continue;
    // classId 0 + no pins => attach to shape centre (ConnEnd(point)) for simplicity
    const ca = new Avoid.ConnEnd(a.position ? a.position() : new Avoid.Point(0, 0));
    conns.push([a, b]);
  }
  // Use point ends at shape centres
  const refs = [];
  const t0 = performance.now();
  for (const [a, b] of conns) {
    const pa = a.position(), pb = b.position();
    refs.push(new Avoid.ConnRef(router, new Avoid.ConnEnd(pa), new Avoid.ConnEnd(pb)));
  }
  router.processTransaction();
  const t1 = performance.now();
  let pts = 0;
  for (const c of refs) { const pl = c.displayRoute(); pts += pl.size(); }
  let t2 = 0;
  if (incremental) {
    // move one shape and reroute (interactive update)
    const s0 = performance.now();
    router.moveShape_delta(shapes[Math.floor(n / 2)], 30, 0);
    router.processTransaction();
    t2 = performance.now() - s0;
  }
  console.log(`libavoid orthogonal: ${String(n).padStart(5)} shapes, ${String(refs.length).padStart(5)} connectors: route ${(t1 - t0).toFixed(0).padStart(6)} ms; move-one-shape reroute ${t2.toFixed(0)} ms; avg ${(pts / refs.length).toFixed(1)} pts/route`);
}
for (const [n, e] of [[24, 60], [100, 150], [300, 450], [500, 750]]) run(n, e, true);

```

```text
The search turned up the paper's abstract and some secondary material, but not the full results section.

- **Main finding:** The abstract reports that slow-in/slow-out pacing outperformed the other tested techniques, though technique differences depending on the type of visual transition were also observed. The paper compared constant speed, slow-in/slow-out, fast-in/fast-out, and an adaptive method (an adaptive technique that slows down the visually complex parts of the animation).
- **Why it works, per the authors' slides:** A slideshare presentation of the paper says the work confirms animation folklore but that the benefit is not for the reason quoted by animators. The slides attribute the advantage to predictability in eye tracking, citing that slow-in/slow-out minimizes risk of losing target in open-loop pursuit and reduces overshooting in closed-loop pursuit. Since these are slide notes rather than the paper itself, treat this as a secondary summary.
- **Practical guidance:** The same slides suggest using slow-in/slow-out when considering different pacings, and otherwise do no harm: constant speed.

The paper's PDF is at cs.au.dk (the Elmqvist group's copy), and the full results section there would give the exact effect sizes and per-transition breakdowns.
```

```text
Sources agree that TypeScript 6.0 deprecates both `baseUrl` and `moduleResolution: node`/`node10`, and that 7.0 is where deprecated options are expected to go away. The results are mostly third-party blogs and a GitHub issue written around the 6.0 release candidate, so I could not confirm the final 6.0 release notes or an official 7.0 removal list.

**Deprecations in 6.0**
- `moduleResolution: node` (node10) and `classic` are deprecated. One source suggests `bundler` for bundled apps and `nodenext` for code run directly by Node.js. The node (aka node10) and classic options for --moduleResolution are now deprecated, and moduleResolution: "bundler"for bundled web apps andmoduleResolution: "nodenext"for modern Node.js packages are the suggested replacements.
- `baseUrl` is deprecated. The usual fix is to move the prefix into your paths entries directly. A Japanese article notes that the warning is TS5101 and that ignoreDeprecations: "6.0" can suppress it temporarily.

**Transition to 7.0**
- 6.0 is described as the last release built on the JavaScript codebase, with TypeScript 7.0 expected to be the native Go-based successor.
- The GitHub issue states that options deprecated in 6.0 will be removed in 7.0.
- Suppression is temporary. One source warns against assuming ignoreDeprecations: "6.0" will still work in 7.0.

**Caveat:** I did not find an official Microsoft changelog or confirmed statement that these specific options are removed in 7.0. Check the TypeScript 6.0 release notes on the TypeScript blog before relying on the removal timing.
```

```text
The ELK documentation supports what you're looking for, with one caveat: I didn't find elkjs-specific docs, so the JavaScript usage rests on the option-key example below.

- **What INCLUDE_CHILDREN does:** The official ELK reference says a node set to this value gets laid out together with all its descendants in one run, until it reaches a descendant set to SEPARATE_CHILDREN. Setting a node's hierarchy handling to INCLUDE_CHILDREN will lay out that node and all of its descendants in a single layout run, until a descendant is encountered which has its hierarchy handling set to SEPARATE_CHILDREN.
- **Why it matters for cross-hierarchy edges:** The same reference notes that including multiple levels of hierarchy in a single layout run may allow cross-hierarchical edges to be laid out properly. The hwtGraph docs add that the option needs to be set to at least two successive levels of hierarchy to have any effect.
- **Where to set it:** An Eclipse forum answer recommends setting the option on the parent node to lay out edges that cross groups. The ELK Layered description in a Sirius commit similarly says cross-hierarchy support is supported when the respective option is activated on the top level.
- **Default behavior:** If the root node is set to INHERIT (or not set at all), the default behavior is SEPARATE_CHILDREN.
- **elkjs usage:** A capellambse-context-diagrams wrapper around elkjs passes `"hierarchyHandling": "INCLUDE_CHILDREN"` as a layout option alongside `"algorithm": "layered"`, which suggests the key is set in the options object on the graph's root node. This is an example from a Python wrapper, not official elkjs documentation.
- **Version note:** ELK 0.7.1 release notes say that ELK Layered now properly interprets hierarchy mode INCLUDE_CHILDREN again, so older versions may behave differently.
```

```text
55:## 3. The map (`domains.yaml`)
57:Schema: see `fixtures/scout-agent.domains.yaml`. Domains are columns, layers are rows (rows come from the file, not hard-coded). Each cell lists path globs and, for data cells, owned tables. `neutral` paths never create edges; `ignore` paths are skipped. Files that match no cell land in an **Unassigned** column.
59:**Tests** are assigned to a domain by its `tests` globs. A test file counts as part of that domain for the rule checker's import rules and the footprint and is listed in the inspector, but it is not drawn in a cell and draws no edges. Tests may write any table: seeding fixture rows is setup, not a product write, so `owns_writes` skips them.
61:**Edges are derived, never declared.** A cross-domain edge exists when a file in domain A imports a file in domain B. Flow down a column is implied and not drawn. The import parser handles `import … from '…'`, `import('…')` and `export … from '…'`. It resolves relative paths by trying the specifier as written, then `.ts`, `.tsx`, `/index.ts`, `/index.tsx`, and maps a `.js` specifier to `.ts`. It ignores bare package and `node:` imports (Scout has none that matter).

159:- **Ghosts:** planned cells are drawn dashed with their step numbers; planned edges are dashed; a ghost that violates an invariant is red.
160:- **Fill-in:** a ghost cell turns solid when a file mapped to it is edited.
161:- **End-of-turn diff:** planned and done is solid; planned and not done stays a ghost; **done but not planned is amber**, which is how the map shows the agent straying from its own plan.
162:- **New versus existing violations:** a violation found on load is drawn red, with a badge on its cell counting the files involved. The key works and Scout is running live at **http://localhost:8787**: real Claude, real web search, real SEC filings.
```

I ran three live research runs through the app: two on Symbotic and one on Veeva. Each took about 70–75 seconds and cost about 2–3 cents (6–7 model calls).

**The first live run exposed a problem, now fixed.** Every search snippet came back empty, so the tools said "the search results came through empty". Claude's newer search tool runs its searches inside code and doesn't cite pages, so there was nothing to extract. Search now uses the standard search tool and asks Claude for a short JSON list of picks, each with a date and a one-sentence summary. Only URLs its searches actually returned are kept. Searches also got faster, from 27 to 9 seconds.

**What the app shows now:**
- **Brief:** real figures and events, e.g. Symbotic's Q3 FY2026 revenue of $720.84M (up 21.7%, ahead of consensus), the ARMS Innovations acquisition, the Stanford Robotics Center partnership, and an angle for the renewal call.
- **Live trail:** while research runs, the planned tools show as dashed waypoints and fill in as each finishes.
- **The leak, visible and real:** the news talking points open with "Talking Points for **Maya Ortiz**". That's the summarizer's shortcut sending her name unredacted to Claude, while the brief written through the gateway shows the `name 1` chip.

**Other fixes from the live runs:**
- Model output was showing raw `#` and `**`; it now renders as formatted text.
- The model was treating `[NAME_1]` as a placeholder the rep forgot to fill in. The gateway now tells it these placeholders stand for real people.
- The company profile now uses the job title you type in, since live enrichment can't find titles.
- That placeholder note briefly broke the offline fakes' canned answers. I caught it from a drop in the proof's call count and fixed it; the offline proof is back to 36 of 212.

**History:** all of this is folded into the "feat: run against live providers" commit. The news summarizer is still the last of 14 commits, the commit before it typechecks with all 24 tests passing, and its proof shows 0 leaks.

**Still open:**
- `DEMO_REPO_SPEC.md` hasn't been committed in the harness repo, because the other session has staged changes there.
- The UI-row map YAML still needs to reach the other session.
- Old Dominion's 10-K has a nearly empty Business section and financial statements; its MD&A is fine.

  **Scope.** I read primary docs and papers, and pulled several PDFs to check the numbers in them directly (van Wijk & Nuij, Heer & Robertson, Elmqvist & Fekete, CodeCity, Cockburn et al.). I wrote no code and changed no files in the repo. Unverified items are flagged at the end.

  ## (a) Ranked references
  
  **1. Sourcetrail, plus its live forks [petermost/Sourcetrail](https://github.com/petermost/Sourcetrail) and [quarkslab/NumbatUI](https://github.com/quarkslab/NumbatUI)** ([docs](https://github.com/CoatiSoftware/Sourcetrail/blob/master/DOCUMENTATION.md))
  - **What it is.** A code explorer whose graph is built around the symbol you've selected, with a code view that stays in sync. The original project was discontinued in 2021 after its Patreon funding fell short.
  - **Steal:**
    - **Bundle nodes** with a count ("N callers"). Clicking one expands it.
    - **Bundled edges** stand for "the edges between the children of these two nodes." Line thickness grows with the count, hovering shows the exact number, and clicking selects all of them. This is edge rollup done properly.
    - A **"Custom Trail" max-depth slider.**
    - **Grouping** by namespace or by file.
    - **Back/forward history** of selections.
  - **Avoid.** The graph is rebuilt around each selected symbol, so there's no stable place to remember (my inference from the docs).
  
  **2. Structurizr / C4** ([implied relationships](https://docs.structurizr.com/dsl/cookbook/implied-relationships/), [navigation](https://docs.structurizr.com/ui/diagrams/navigation))
  - **What it is.** One model with many views. Double-clicking an element opens the next level down.
  - **Steal:**
    - **Implied relationships** are a clean rule for rolling edges up: Person→Container automatically implies Person→System.
    - **`animation` steps** reveal a view step by step.
  - **Avoid:**
    - Levels are separate pages, so you lose context every time you drill down.
    - Only one implied relationship is created per pair, labelled with the first one defined. Multiplicity and severity disappear. Harness needs counts and the worst status on every rolled-up edge.
  
  **3. IcePanel** ([diagramming](https://docs.icepanel.io/features/diagramming), [flows](https://docs.icepanel.io/visual-storytelling/flows))
  - **What it is.** Zoomable C4 views over a shared model.
  - **Steal:**
    - **"Lower connections."** An edge drawn at a deep level is reused at higher levels and kept in sync.
    - **"Expand."** You can show the children of another system inside a bounding area, so cross-scope edges stay visible.
    - **Flows.** Numbered steps play back over the diagram, with alternate (OR) and parallel (AND) paths and "go to flow" jumps across levels. This is the template for the Journeys level and for playing back the agent's plan.
  - **Avoid.** Everything is modelled by hand, so the diagrams drift from the code.
  
  **4. Nx project graph** ([docs](https://nx.dev/features/explore-graph))
  - **What it is.** Composite nodes group projects by folder. The docs call them "essential to navigate a graph of even a moderate size."
  - **Steal:** two separate verbs, **expand in place** and **focus** (re-root on a node), plus a proximity control. Turborepo `devtools` (since 2.7) is a similar local graph explorer.
  - **Avoid.** The docs never say how edges to a collapsed composite are drawn, so there's nothing to learn there.
  
  **5. Windsurf Codemaps (Cognition)** ([blog](https://cognition.com/blog/codemaps))
  - **What it is.** Maps generated per task by a model, with nested sections, "trace guides", a list view and a graph view.
  - **Steal:**
    - Every node links to exact lines of code.
    - A map can be passed into the agent's prompt (`@codemap`).
    - The framing "to understand is to be accountable."
    - Task-scoped maps are a good model for **Journeys**.
  - **Avoid.** Maps are snapshots, and a model sits in the loop. That breaks Harness's "no model calls in hot path" rule, so this belongs only in the cartographer.
  
  **6. Kiali** ([topology](https://v2-24.kiali.io/docs/features/topology))
  - **What it is.** A live service-mesh graph.
  - **Steal:**
    - **Traffic animation.** Dot density shows request rate, speed shows response time, and red diamonds are errors.
    - Health colour on both nodes and edges.
    - **Replay** that can be bookmarked.
    - Double-click opens a detail graph for one node.
    - This is the best existing pattern for showing "the agent is touching this edge right now."
  - **Avoid.** Animating every edge at once. Keep motion for the active path.
  
  **7. Service maps: Datadog, Honeycomb, Jaeger**
  - **Datadog** ([docs](https://docs.datadoghq.com/tracing/services/services_map/)): "Inspect" isolates a node with its callers and callees. Intermediate services that are filtered out collapse automatically. You can group by team or application. Layout runs left to right, from customer-facing to likely root cause.
  - **Honeycomb** ([blog](https://www.honeycomb.io/blog/interating-toward-service-map)): early versions "looked more like a tangle of spaghetti." The team logged layer counts and density to choose the zoom levels at which labels appear and how to bucket edge weights.
  - **Jaeger's deep dependency graph** (via [Logz.io docs](https://docs.logz.io/docs/user-guide/distributed-tracing/navigating-tracing/topology/)): you pick a focal service and see N hops around it.
  - **Steal:** isolate + hops + collapsed intermediaries.
  - **Avoid:** global force-directed layouts.
  
  **8. AppMap** ([diagrams](https://appmap.io/docs/reference/guides/using-appmap-diagrams.html))
  - **What it is.** Four views of recorded runtime behaviour: a dependency map with expandable packages, a sequence diagram (`[+]/[-]` collapse plus a depth limit), a trace view and a flame graph.
  - **Steal:** each view links to the others ("Show in Sequence / Trace / Flame Graph"). A sequence lane is the right drawing for the **module** level of an agent's turn.
  - **Avoid.** It depends on recording real executions.
  
  **9. CodeSee (defunct)** ([map docs](https://docs.codesee.io/docs/explore-your-map), [GitKraken press release](https://www.gitkraken.com/press/gitkraken-acquires-codesee-launches-devex-platform))
  - **What it was.** Maps that start with folders collapsed, a toggle to open each folder, file→file dependency arrows, overlays (hot spots, latest activity, lines of code), and code tours.
  - **What happened.** A LinkedIn notice said commercial operations would end "Thursday, Feb 22" (the year is likely 2024 but unconfirmed). GitKraken acquired it on May 14, 2024 and folded it into its DevEx platform.
  - **Lesson.** A standalone map product struggled. Value comes from sitting inside the workflow, which Harness does.
  - **Avoid.**
    - Overlays replace labels, so you lose your bearings.
    - Layout is dragged by hand.
    - The docs don't explain what happens to edges when a folder is collapsed.
  
  **10. D3 zoomable circle packing, icicle and sunburst (Observable)** ([packing](https://observablehq.com/@d3/zoomable-circle-packing), [icicle](https://observablehq.com/@d3/zoomable-icicle), [sunburst](https://observablehq.com/@d3/zoomable-sunburst))
  - **What it is.** The canonical "zoom into a hierarchy" examples. I checked their source code.
  - **Steal these exact rules:**
    - `d3.interpolateZoom` with a **750 ms** transition; holding Alt slows it to 7,500 ms.
    - Labels are shown only for direct children of the focused node.
    - The sunburst draws only **2 rings** at a time.
    - Icicle labels are hidden when a cell is under **16 px**.
    - Depth is coloured with an HCL ramp.
  - **Avoid.** These show containment only, with no edges, so edges have to be added on top.
  
  **11. Code Canvas (Microsoft Research) and software cartography**
  - **Code Canvas** ([project](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/project/code-canvas/)): an infinite canvas with "smooth semantic zoom," ranging from UML-like boxes down to editable code. It overlays debugger call stacks and search results on a stable layout, with the stated goal of building on spatial memory.
  - **Kuhn et al.** ([arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/1007.4303)) found developers made good use of a map to inspect search results and call graphs. But a layout clustered by topic was "surprising and often confusing."
  - **Lesson.** Harness's domain×layer grid is a meaningful anchor for the layout. Keep it at every level.
  
  **12. Agent-activity and AI code-graph tools, 2025–26**
  - **[JamsusMaximus/codemap](https://github.com/JamsusMaximus/codemap)** ("hotel" view): driven by hooks. Screens glow **yellow on read and green on write**, and agents that are stuck waiting for permission bounce until you notice.
  - **[agent-flow](https://github.com/patoles/agent-flow)**: a node graph of tool calls plus a "file attention heatmap."
  - **[Graphify](https://github.com/Graphify-Labs/graphify)**: tree-sitter parsing, Leiden communities and a force-directed `graph.html`, plus a PreToolUse hook that nudges Claude to query the graph first.
  - **[Understand-Anything](https://github.com/Lum1104/Understand-Anything)**: layer, domain, tour and diff-impact views.

    - Game metaphors that don't encode architecture.
  
  **Also checked:**
  - **CodeCity**: a measured benefit (+24.26% correctness and −12.01% completion time versus Eclipse+Excel, n=41, per the [tech report](https://www.inf.usi.ch/faculty/lanza/PUBS/M/Wett2010a.pdf)). But 3D brings occlusion and navigation costs.
  - **Gource**: lovely history playback (directories as branches, contributors fly to the files they touch), but it isn't navigable. Useful inspiration for a replay "director's cut."
  - **[repo-visualizer](https://githubnext.com/projects/repo-visualization/)**: shows import links only on hover because "there are often too many connections."
  - **DeepWiki**: a wiki plus diagrams generated by a model.
  - **Swimm**: "smart tokens" tied to code, with a "review required" flag when they go stale. A good model for showing that a cartographer label may be out of date.
  - **[Sourcegraph](https://sourcegraph.com/docs/code-navigation/precise-code-navigation)**: no multi-level visual map. Worth stealing its distinction between precise and search-based results, which maps onto Harness's deterministic mapper versus model-labelled cartographer.
  
  ---
  
  ## (b) Interaction patterns and what to combine
  
  1. **Semantic zoom / level of detail.** In Pad++, objects change their rendering with on-screen size ([Bederson](https://cs.umd.edu/~bederson/images/pubs_pdfs/p23-bederson.pdf)). tldraw drops shadows, solidifies strokes and flattens fills when zoomed out, and debounces zoom-dependent rendering above 500 shapes ([perf](https://tldraw.dev/sdk-features/performance)).
  
  2. **Focus+context through degree of interest (DOI).** Furnas defines interest as a-priori importance minus distance from the focus ([CHI '86](https://doi.org/10.1145/22339.22342)). [van Ham & Perer 2009](https://dig.cmu.edu/publications/2009-doigraphs.html) apply this to graphs as "search, show context, expand on demand." [DOITrees](https://idl.uw.edu/papers/doitrees-revisited) give multi-focus layouts within a fixed space. Cockburn et al.'s review warns that geometric **fisheye distortion hurts target acquisition and spatial judgement** ([survey](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2008/01/cockburn-ComputingSurveys09.pdf)). Use DOI to decide *what is visible*, not to distort shapes.
  
  3. **Expand/collapse of compound graphs with edge rollup.**
     - yFiles folding lets a converter add a separate folding edge, merge into an existing one, or exclude it ([MergingFoldingEdgeConverter](https://docs.yworks.com/yfiles-html/api/MergingFoldingEdgeConverter.html)).
     - Cytoscape's expand-collapse plugin produces "meta-edges," optionally grouped by type, with a 1,000 ms default animation ([repo](https://github.com/iVis-at-Bilkent/cytoscape.js-expand-collapse)).
     - Sourcetrail's bundled edges and Structurizr/IcePanel implied relationships are covered above.
     - For layout, ELK's `hierarchyHandling: INCLUDE_CHILDREN` lays out edges that cross hierarchy levels in one pass ([ELK](https://eclipse.dev/elk/reference/options/org-eclipse-elk-hierarchyHandling.html)).
  
  4. **Edge bundling.** Holten's hierarchical edge bundling routes edges along the hierarchy, with bundling strength β (0.85 in his software figures) ([TVCG 2006](https://doi.org/10.1109/TVCG.2006.147)). Force-directed bundling can invent connections that don't exist. [Edge-path bundling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2108.05467) bundles only along real paths.
  
  5. **Camera.**
     - van Wijk & Nuij's optimal zoom/pan path: in their user test, preferred **ρ≈1.42** and **V≈0.90** ([PDF](https://vanwijk.win.tue.nl/zoompan.pdf)).
     - `d3.interpolateZoom` defaults to ρ=√2 and exposes a recommended `duration` you can scale by V ([docs](https://d3js.org/d3-interpolate/zoom)).
     - The paper recommends recomputing the path every frame without stored state, which makes **retargeting mid-flight** trivial. Follow mode needs exactly that. See also Reach & North's "Smooth, Efficient, and Interruptible Zooming and Panning" ([arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/1801.09358)).
  
  6. **Preserving the mental map.** Keeping layouts stable made locating nodes and following paths faster and less error-prone ([Archambault & Purchase, GD 2012](https://cronfa.swan.ac.uk/Record/cronfa13913)). Evidence for comprehension tasks is mixed.
  
  7. **Animated transitions.**
     - Heer & Robertson ([paper](https://idl.uw.edu/papers/animated-transitions)): stage complex changes, keep transitions simple, use slow-in/slow-out, and "make transitions as long as needed, but no longer." Their review recommends about 1 s, and their experiments used 1.25 s.
     - Slow-in/slow-out beat the other pacings tested ([Dragicevic et al.](https://cs.au.dk/~elm/pdf/timedistort.pdf)).
     - **Staggering had negligible or even negative effect** on tracking moving objects ([Chevalier et al.](https://visualcognition.psych.northwestern.edu/publications/ChevalierDragicevicFranconeri2014.pdf)).
     - Use [FLIP](https://aerotwist.com/blog/flip-your-animations/) for DOM layout changes.
  
  8. **Overview and breadcrumbs.** In Hornbæk et al., 80% of users preferred a zoomable interface with an overview, with no accuracy difference ([TOCHI 2002](https://hjemmesider.diku.dk/~kash/papers/TOCHI2002_hornbaek.pdf)). Cockburn's guidance: the overview must reflect changes in the detail view immediately, and users should be able to hide it.
  
  9. **Off-screen indicators.** Halo made tasks 16–33% faster than arrows. Wedge was significantly more accurate than Halo and avoids clutter ([Wedge, CHI '08](https://doi.org/10.1145/1357054.1357179)).
  
  10. **Command palette, history and quick navigation.** Sourcetrail has fuzzy search plus a history stack. Structurizr opens quick navigation with Space.
  
  11. **Follow mode.** Figma Spotlight lets you follow someone and "Stop following" ([help](https://help.figma.com/hc/en-us/articles/360040322673)). Miro has follow and "bring everyone to me." Kumu's focus mode has an in/out degree control and number keys set the depth ([docs](https://docs.kumu.io/guides/focus)).
  
  ### Recommended combination: DOI-driven nested grid
  
  - **Keep one coordinate system at every level.**
    - The domain×layer grid stays as the anchor.
    - Expanding a domain widens its column in place; the other columns compress into thin "spines" that carry their rolled-up badges.
    - Cells open inside the cell. Code opens in a side panel.
    - **Journeys are flow overlays on the System map** (IcePanel- and Codemaps-style numbered steps), not a separate layout. This keeps spatial memory intact, which a cartographic grid supports better than topic-clustered layouts.
  - **Visibility is decided by a DOI function with an entity budget.**
    - Interest = structural importance (planned, violating, agent present, recently edited) minus distance from the user's focus.
    - Expand until the budget is spent. This is "depth is local" stated formally.
    - It should be a pure function of the event log plus the focus, so replay stays a reduction (fits CLAUDE.md).
  - **Edges roll up to the lowest visible ancestor of each endpoint.**
    - Each rolled-up edge carries a count and the worst status.
    - When one end is expanded and the other collapsed, the edge leaves the expanded container through a port, a stub on its boundary.
    - Severity is rolled up by **max, never averaged.** Elmqvist & Fekete's guidelines say aggregates must stay distinguishable from individual items (G4) and must not misrepresent the data (G5) ([PDF](https://cs.au.dk/~elm/pdf/hieragg.pdf)). A red violation three levels down must show as a red edge or badge at System level.
    - Keep the existing rule that a ghost edge gets its own lane.
  - **Activity rolls up the same way.**
    - The agent cursor sits on the deepest *visible* ancestor of the file it's reading.
    - Edits pulse that container.
    - A Wedge marker appears when the agent is off-screen.
    - Kiali-style dots run only along the active edge.
  - **Camera.** Use the van Wijk path (ρ≈√2) and keep it interruptible. In follow mode, move only when the agent's visible ancestor changes at the current level, with some hysteresis. That hysteresis is my recommendation, not something the sources establish.
  - **Navigation chrome.** Breadcrumbs (Journey › Domain › Cell › Module), a hideable minimap, and Cmd-K over domains, files, symbols, plan steps and events.
  
  ---
  
  ## (c) Three visual directions
  
  **1. "Atlas" (cartographic blueprint)**
  - **Mood:** calm and print-like, like a map room.
  - **Techniques:**
    - Nested containers separated by hairlines and one step of elevation per level.
    - An HCL lightness ramp by depth.
    - A theme built from three inputs (base, accent, contrast) in LCH, as Linear does ([post](https://linear.app/now/how-we-redesigned-the-linear-ui)).
    - Orthogonal edges routed through ports, bundled along the hierarchy.
    - Map-style label placement: priority plus collision culling, with 300 ms fades (the [Mapbox `fadeDuration`](https://docs.mapbox.com/mapbox-gl-js/api/map/) default).
    - The agent is the **only** saturated accent. Red and amber are reserved for rules.
  - **Risk:** it can read as static or "enterprise." Liveness then depends on small motion cues.
  
  **2. "Control Room" (live telemetry)**
  - **Mood:** dark mission control, in the spirit of Kiali and Datadog.
  - **Techniques:**
    - Particle flow on active edges (density for frequency, speed for recency).
    - Arc rings around each domain node showing the mix of planned, done, unplanned and violating. The [Grafana node-graph `arc__` fields](https://grafana.com/docs/grafana/latest/panels/visualizations/node-graph) are a model.
    - Soft glow on the focused node.
    - A heat strip along the replay scrubber.
  - **Risks:**
    - It can turn into a lit-up Christmas tree, with glow competing with violation red.
    - Motion sensitivity: needs `prefers-reduced-motion` and the advice to drop animation from high-frequency interactions ([Rauno](https://rauno.me/craft/interaction-design)).
    - GPU cost.
  
  **3. "Strata" (depth-of-field infinite canvas)**
  - **Mood:** the most striking of the three, in the tldraw/Figma vein. You literally fly into a cell.
  - **Techniques:**
    - Parent levels fade to about 10% opacity, with a slight blur, instead of disappearing.
    - Typography changes with zoom: display face for domains, regular UI face for files, monospace for symbols.
    - Icicle or sequence lanes at module level.
    - Camera on the van Wijk path, with staged transitions (camera first, then expansion, then edges).
    - Custom easing curves, and decorative UI motion kept under 500 ms ([Stripe](https://stripe.com/blog/connect-front-end-experience)).
  - **Risks:**
    - The scale range across five levels causes precision and text-rendering problems.
    - Blur is expensive.
    - It's easy to get lost, so breadcrumbs, the minimap and Wedge markers are mandatory.
  
  ---
  
  ## (d) Quantitative guidance
  
  | Topic | Finding |
  |---|---|
  | Node-link vs matrix | Above about **20 nodes**, matrices beat node-link diagrams on most tasks; path-finding is the exception ([Ghoniem et al.](https://hal.archives-ouvertes.fr/hal-00343819)) |
  | Path-finding difficulty | Hard in dense node-link graphs above **50 nodes**, and in sparse ones above **100** (25–175 nodes tested) ([Yoghourdjian et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2008.07944)) |
  | Visible-entity budget | Practical target: about **20–30 detailed nodes in focus** and **≤50 visible entities** per screen |
  | Edge crossings | Reducing crossings is "by far the most important" aesthetic. Bends and symmetry matter less; forcing orthogonal layout had no significant effect (Purchase, GD '97, LNCS 1353). No hard crossing limit was found |
  | Transition length | About **1 s** (Robertson, via Heer & Robertson); experiments used 1.25 s. Decorative UI motion under 500 ms (Stripe) |
  | Reference durations | D3 zoom examples: 750 ms. Mapbox label fades: 300 ms. Cytoscape expand/collapse: 1,000 ms |
  | Camera parameters | ρ 1.42 (SD 0.47), V 0.90 (SD 0.43), n=26 |
  | Off-screen indicators | Halo 16–33% faster than arrows; Wedge more accurate than Halo |
  | Overview / minimap | 80% of users preferred having one |
  | Label rules | Hide labels under 16 px. Label only the children of the focus. Show about 2 levels of hierarchy at once |
  | Scale of real systems | Median Honeycomb team has about 30 services; the largest have hundreds |

  ## Recommended two-tier fact architecture
  
  **Tier 1: syntax facts.** In-process, synchronous and per file. Target ≤5 ms per file, hard cap 20 ms, used by the gate and the live map.
  1. One `oxc-parser.parseSync` per file:
     - The import/export record gives imports and exports, re-exports included, plus type-only flags.
     - One visitor pass collects symbols: top-level functions, classes and methods, exported consts, and members of typed or exported object literals.
     - The same pass collects call sites (enclosing symbol, callee shape), write sites, route registrations, and SQL string literals.
  2. oxc-resolver resolves specifiers (plan below). Syntactic call edges come from import bindings, including namespace imports and barrels (measured above).
  3. The gate keeps using only `imports` and `writes`, so `check()` is unchanged: one function, three call sites.
     - You can add an optional `calls` field to `FactDelta` later. Symbol facts are computed in PostToolUse, which doesn't block.
  4. Files over ~500 KB or minified: use only the import/export record (2.6 ms even at 972 KB).
  5. Python and Go use web-tree-sitter with grammars pinned to the runtime, producing the same schema.
  
  **Tier 2: semantic facts.** Asynchronous, in a worker or child process, never blocking.
  - **TS/JS:** tsgo via `typescript/unstable/sync`, pinned to 7.0.2.
    - Load: after the grid has drawn, resolve all call sites found by Tier 1 in per-file batches.
    - Edit: debounce ~150 ms per file, then `updateSnapshot({fileChanges:{changed}})` and re-resolve that file.
    - Outputs: `calls` edges with `confidence: typed`, plus `implements` edges from class `implements` clauses and objects annotated with an interface type.
    - Fallback: TS 6 LanguageService (ts-morph), about 1–1.5x slower.
  - **Inspector drill-down** ("who calls this?"): LSP call hierarchy on demand.
  - **Python / Go:** pyright (npm, MIT, LSP) and gopls, only if the toolchain is present. SCIP is optional for CI snapshots.
  
  **Data model.** Ids never contain line numbers, so they stay stable across edits that shift code.
  
  | Node kind | Id format |
  |---|---|
  | file | `src/tools/news-summarize.ts` (as today) |
  | symbol | `src/tools/news-summarize.ts#newsSummarize.run`; kind is function / class / method / const / type / property; duplicates get `~2`; anonymous callbacks are `#runAgent.<cb1>`, numbered within their parent |
  | route | `route:POST /api/runs`, params normalized to `{}` |
  | table | `table:runs` |
  | vendor | `vendor:@anthropic-ai/sdk` or `vendor:vendor/news` |
  | entry | `entry:bin/scout`, `entry:script/dev`, `entry:page:/runs/{}` |
  | package | `pkg:@acme/core` |
  
  Edge kinds:
  - `imports` (file→file, with a typeOnly flag)
  - `contains`
  - `calls` (with `{confidence: syntactic | typed | dispatch, count}`)
  - `implements`
  - `handles` (route→symbol)
  - `writes` / `reads` (symbol→table)
  - `uses` (symbol→vendor)
  - `fetches` (UI symbol→route)
  - `starts` (entry→symbol)
  
  Ownership and caching:
  - Edge id is `kind|from|to`. Each edge belongs to the file of its source site, so an update replaces that file's edges (the pattern `Repo.fileChanged` already uses).
  - Per-file records are keyed by `sha1(content)` plus extractor version and cached in `.harness/facts/`.
  
  **Keeping UI state a pure reduction of the event log.** Tier 2 results arrive as events (e.g. `facts_resolved {path, hash, edges}`). The reducer ignores any whose `hash` is not the file's latest. Large baselines can live in content-addressed blobs under `.harness/facts/`, which events reference; replay stays pure because the blobs never change.
  
  **How the levels are built:**
  - **Grid:** the mapper lifts file edges to domains, as today.
  - **Inside a domain:** files grouped by directory, plus that domain's tables, vendors and routes. Rank symbols by Aider-style in-degree / PageRank to choose labels.
  - **Module level:** one file's symbols plus one hop of calls.
  - **Wiring trace:** shortest paths from an entry or route handler to vendor/table sinks over `calls ∪ implements`. Collapse hops within a cell and show interface dispatch as a "via registry" fan-out.
  
  ## "Which symbols did this edit change"
  1. **Inputs.** Old text comes from the `Repo.contents` cache with its cached symbol table, so it isn't reparsed. New text comes from `applyEdit` in the hook or from disk for the watcher. Parse the new text once with oxc.
  2. **Hashes.** For each symbol id, compare:
     - `sigHash`: normalized params, type annotations, modifiers and export flag.
     - `bodyHash`: whitespace-normalized span text.
  3. **Classify** each symbol as added, removed, signature changed, body changed, or renamed (removed plus added with the same `bodyHash`). A span shift with equal hashes is not a change.
  4. **Edge delta.** Diff the file's outgoing call, import and write sets and emit `call_added` / `call_removed`, the same way `edge_added` / `edge_removed` work today.
  5. **Impact.** A signature change marks callers as affected through the reverse index; a body change affects only the symbol itself.
  6. **Turn summary.** `git diff -U0 base -- path` hunks prefilter the symbols whose spans intersect, in both `git show base:path` and the new text; the hashes stay the source of truth.
  
  Measured cost: 1.6–2.4 ms on normal files, 65 ms on the 11.4k-line App.tsx when parsing both sides. Caching the old side halves that, and building the JS AST dominates. For buffers kept open, tree-sitter `getChangedRanges` is an alternative (0.05–1.2 ms).
  
  ## Path-alias and monorepo plan
  1. **Discover:**
     - workspaces from root `package.json` or `pnpm-workspace.yaml`

  2. **Resolve** with oxc-resolver `{ tsconfig: 'auto' }` and `resolveFileSync(file, spec)`.
     - Settings: `conditionNames: ['types','import','module','default']`, `extensionAlias {'.js': ['.ts','.tsx','.js']}`. Symlinks resolve to real repo paths.

  3. **No node_modules installed:** write symlinks under `.harness/ws-modules/<pkg>` and pass that directory as an extra `modules` entry.

     - `.harness/` is an allowed write location.
  4. **Planned files that don't exist yet** (`submit_plan`): oxc-resolver can't see virtual files. Fall back to get-tsconfig `createPathsMatcher`, then the existing `resolvePath` over `exists ∪ planned`.
  5. **Bare imports** that resolve into node_modules become `vendor:<pkg>` nodes.
  6. **Cache:** call `resolver.clearCache()` when a file is created or deleted, or when a package.json or tsconfig changes.
  7. **Deprecations:** TS 6.0 deprecates `baseUrl` and `moduleResolution: node10`, and 7.0 reportedly removes them (third-party sources; unverified). Still support reading `baseUrl` for legacy repos.
  
  ## Routes, writes and entry points (Journeys)
  Adapters are oxc visitor patterns or tree-sitter queries, with a check on what the receiver is bound to so that only real routers match.
  
  - **Routes:**
    - Express / Hono / Fastify / Koa: `X.(get|post|put|patch|delete|all|on|route)('<path>', …)`, where `X` comes from `express()`, `new Hono()` or `Router()`. Apply `app.route` / `basePath` prefixes.
    - Next.js:
      - `app/**/route.ts` exports `GET` / `POST`, and so on.
      - `app/**/page.tsx` files are UI entry points.
      - `pages/api/**` are API routes.
    - Python and Go: FastAPI / Flask decorators; Go `HandleFunc("POST /x")`, chi, gin, echo.
    - Scout's custom `[method, RegExp, handler]` table needs a user-confirmed pattern in `domains.yaml`, which the cartographer can propose.
  - **Writes:**
    - Prisma: `prisma.<model>.(create|createMany|update|updateMany|upsert|delete|deleteMany)` and `$executeRaw`.
    - Drizzle: `db.(insert|update|delete)(ident)`, following `ident` through imports to `pgTable/sqliteTable/mysqlTable('<name>')`.
    - Knex: `knex('<t>').insert/update/del`.
    - TypeORM: `@Entity('<t>')` plus repository `save/insert/update/delete`. This needs types, so it belongs in Tier 2.
    - SQLAlchemy and Django:
      - SQLAlchemy: `session.add(Model(...))`, `insert(Model)`, `update(Model)`, with `__tablename__`.
      - Django: `Model.objects.create/update/bulk_create`.
    - Raw SQL: string or template literals matching `INSERT INTO | UPDATE | DELETE FROM | MERGE INTO <t>`.
    - Keep `owns_writes` on Tier 1 writes only, so it stays deterministic.
  - **Entry points:**
    - `package.json` `bin` and `main`, and the files `scripts` run (e.g. `tsx src/channels/routes.ts`)
    - HTTP routes and UI routes (React Router `path:` entries, Next pages)
    - CLI command registrations, cron and queue handlers
    - Python `__main__`, Go `func main`
  - **Journey** = UI route → `fetch` → API route → wiring trace. Match fetch URLs to route patterns by constant-propagating wrapper arguments; Scout uses ``fetch(`/api${path}`)``. Mark these edges as inferred.
  
  ## Multi-language plan
  - **Python:**
    - Syntax: tree-sitter-python with tags.scm plus import and decorator-route queries; both worked in my test.
    - Module resolution: package roots from `pyproject` (setuptools `where`, poetry `packages`, `src/` layout), `__init__.py`, and relative imports.
    - Syntactic calls through `from x import f` bindings.
    - Tier 2: pyright LSP, or scip-python in batch.
  - **Go:**
    - Syntax: tree-sitter-go. Map import paths to directories using the `go.mod` module prefix (and `go.work`).
    - Because a package is a directory, `pkg.F()` resolves syntactically with high precision. Methods need gopls call hierarchy, or a small `go/packages` + VTA helper when Go is installed. scip-go for batch.
  - **Runtime:** web-tree-sitter (no native builds). Ship grammars from one source, @vscode/tree-sitter-wasm or a self-built CLI matched to the runtime, and pin both together.
  
  ## Risks
  1. **TS 7 API instability.** "No API until 7.1" means the `unstable/*` exports can break. Pin exact versions and hide it behind a `SemanticResolver` interface with the TS 6 fallback.
  2. **oxc is pre-1.0 and ships weekly.** Pin it; the ESTree-shaped AST limits the churn.
  3. **tree-sitter WASM coupling:** a grammar must match its runtime ABI and emscripten build (shown failing above).
  4. **Memory and cold start** for the semantic tier on 5k-file repos (extrapolated, unverified). Keep it out of process, with a heap cap and progress events.
  5. **Dynamic dispatch breaks chains.** Registries, dependency injection, event emitters and string-keyed handlers all do this. Show `dispatch` / `inferred` confidence and never present a trace as complete.
  6. **Gate budget on huge or generated files.** Apply the size cap and ignore list.
  7. **Route detection is framework-specific.** Custom routers need confirmed patterns, and false positives without the receiver-binding check were already seen.
  8. **Event-log size and stale results.** Use content-hash keys and blob references, as described above.
  9. **Toolchains for Python/Go semantics** (venv, Go) are not always present. Fall back to syntax facts.

```text
The search turned up good material on hierarchical edge bundling with D3's `curveBundle`, but nothing on WebGL or force-directed bundling in 2025.

**D3 `curveBundle` (hierarchical edge bundling)**
- The D3 Graph Gallery's basic example shows the standard pattern: a `d3.cluster()` lays out the hierarchy as a circular dendrogram, and links are drawn with `d3.radialLine()` using `d3.curveBundle.beta(0.85)` Once the nodes are positioned, links are done thanks to the radialLine and curveBundle functions.
- Observable's Bostock-style notebook uses the same approach with `d3.lineRadial()` and `d3.curveBundle.beta(0.85)`, and adds hover highlighting of incoming and outgoing edges (shows relationships among classes in a software hierarchy).
- A second Observable notebook colors each edge with a gradient by splitting paths into segments, using `d3.curveBundle` without a beta value (const k = 6; // 2^k colors segments per curve).
- The React Graph Gallery covers the same technique with React rendering the nodes and edges while D3 computes the layout (using d3.js to compute the node position, and React to render the nodes and edges).

**Other options**
- `edgebundleR` is an R htmlwidget that wraps D3 for hierarchical edge bundling. It is version 0.1.4, last published in 2016 (generates interactive circle plots with the nodes around the circumference).

**Gaps**
- No results covered WebGL-based edge bundling or force-directed edge bundling (FDEB), and nothing from 2025 came up. For those, you would need a targeted search, for example on FDEB papers or WebGL libraries such as deck.gl or regl.
```

```javascript
// React Flow stress page: N custom nodes inside 24 group (cell) nodes, ~1.5N edges.
// Exposes window.bench.{zoom, relayout} which return measured frame stats.
import React, { memo, useEffect, useState } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';
import { ReactFlow, ReactFlowProvider, Handle, Position, useReactFlow, useNodesState } from '@xyflow/react';
import '@xyflow/react/dist/style.css';

const params = new URLSearchParams(location.search);
const N = Number(params.get('n') || 500);
const EDGE = params.get('edge') || 'smoothstep';
const VIS = params.get('vis') === '1';

function rng(seed) { let s = seed >>> 0; return () => ((s = (s * 1664525 + 1013904223) >>> 0) / 2 ** 32); }
const r = rng(1);
const COLS = 6, ROWS = 4, CW = 900, CH = 700;
const W = 140, H = 40;

function layout(shift) {
  const nodes = [];
  const perCell = {};
  for (let c = 0; c < COLS; c++) for (let w = 0; w < ROWS; w++) {
    nodes.push({ id: `c${c}_${w}`, type: 'group', position: { x: c * (CW + 60), y: w * (CH + 60) }, style: { width: CW, height: CH }, data: {} });
    perCell[`c${c}_${w}`] = 0;
  }
  const rr = rng(2);
  for (let i = 0; i < N; i++) {
    const cell = `c${Math.floor(rr() * COLS)}_${Math.floor(rr() * ROWS)}`;
    const k = perCell[cell]++;
    const per = Math.floor((CW - 20) / (W + 10));
    const col = (k + shift) % per, row = Math.floor(k / per);
    nodes.push({ id: `f${i}`, type: 'file', parentId: cell, extent: 'parent', position: { x: 10 + col * (W + 10), y: 10 + (row % 14) * (H + 8) }, data: { label: `src/mod${i}/file${i}.ts`, n: i } });
  }
  return nodes;
}
const initialNodes = layout(0);
const edges = [];
for (let k = 0; k < Math.round(N * 1.5); k++) {
  const a = Math.floor(r() * N), b = Math.floor(r() * N);
  if (a !== b) edges.push({ id: `e${k}`, source: `f${a}`, target: `f${b}`, type: EDGE });
}

const FileNode = memo(function FileNode({ data }) {
  const st = data.n % 7;
  return (
    <div style={{ width: W, height: H, border: '1px solid #8899aa', borderRadius: 6, background: st === 0 ? '#fde68a' : '#fff', font: '11px system-ui', display: 'flex', alignItems: 'center', gap: 4, padding: '0 6px', boxSizing: 'border-box' }}>
      <Handle type="target" position={Position.Top} />
      <span style={{ background: '#1f2937', color: '#fff', borderRadius: 8, padding: '0 5px', fontSize: 10 }}>{data.n % 9}</span>
      <span style={{ overflow: 'hidden', textOverflow: 'ellipsis', whiteSpace: 'nowrap' }}>{data.label}</span>
      {st === 3 && <span style={{ width: 8, height: 8, borderRadius: 4, background: '#ef4444' }} />}
      <Handle type="source" position={Position.Bottom} />
    </div>
  );
});
const nodeTypes = { file: FileNode };

function measure(durationMs, step) {
  return new Promise((resolve) => {
    const times = [];
    const t0 = performance.now();
    function frame(t) {
      times.push(t);
      const p = Math.min(1, (t - t0) / durationMs);
      step(p);
      if (p < 1) requestAnimationFrame(frame);
      else {
        const dts = times.slice(1).map((x, i) => x - times[i]).sort((a, b) => a - b);
        resolve({ frames: times.length, fps: +(1000 * (times.length - 1) / (times[times.length - 1] - times[0])).toFixed(1), p50: +dts[Math.floor(dts.length * 0.5)].toFixed(1), p95: +dts[Math.floor(dts.length * 0.95)].toFixed(1), max: +dts[dts.length - 1].toFixed(1) });
      }
    }
    requestAnimationFrame(frame);
  });
}

function Flow() {
  const [nodes, setNodes, onNodesChange] = useNodesState(initialNodes);
  const rf = useReactFlow();
  useEffect(() => {
    const a = initialNodes, b = layout(3);
    window.bench = {
      ready: true,
      count: () => document.querySelectorAll('.react-flow__node').length,
      zoom: () => { rf.setViewport({ x: 0, y: 0, zoom: 0.15 }); return measure(3000, (p) => { const z = 0.15 + 0.85 * Math.sin(p * Math.PI); rf.setViewport({ x: -p * 2000, y: -p * 800, zoom: z }); }); },
      relayout: () => { rf.setViewport({ x: 0, y: 0, zoom: 0.3 }); return measure(2000, (p) => { const e = p < 0.5 ? 2 * p * p : 1 - (-2 * p + 2) ** 2 / 2; setNodes(a.map((n, i) => n.parentId ? { ...n, position: { x: n.position.x + (b[i].position.x - n.position.x) * e, y: n.position.y + (b[i].position.y - n.position.y) * e } } : n)); }); },
    };
  }, []);
  return <ReactFlow nodes={nodes} edges={edges} nodeTypes={nodeTypes} onNodesChange={onNodesChange} onlyRenderVisibleElements={VIS} minZoom={0.05} defaultViewport={{ x: 0, y: 0, zoom: 0.3 }} />;
}

createRoot(document.getElementById('root')).render(<div style={{ width: '100vw', height: '100vh' }}><ReactFlowProvider><Flow /></ReactFlowProvider></div>);

```

```mjs
// Usage: node rf-run.mjs <rfPkgDir> <outDir> <chromiumExecutable>
import { createRequire } from 'node:module';
import { createServer } from 'node:http';
import { readFileSync, writeFileSync, mkdirSync } from 'node:fs';
import { join } from 'node:path';
const [rfDir, outDir, exe] = process.argv.slice(2);
const require = createRequire(rfDir + '/package.json');
const esbuild = require('esbuild');
const { chromium } = require('playwright-core');
mkdirSync(outDir, { recursive: true });
await esbuild.build({
  entryPoints: [new URL('./rf-stress.jsx', import.meta.url).pathname], bundle: true, outdir: outDir, minify: true,
  define: { 'process.env.NODE_ENV': '"production"' }, jsx: 'automatic', nodePaths: [rfDir + '/node_modules'], loader: { '.css': 'css' }, logLevel: 'error',
});
writeFileSync(join(outDir, 'index.html'), '<!doctype html><html><head><link rel="stylesheet" href="rf-stress.css"><style>body{margin:0}</style></head><body><div id="root"></div><script src="rf-stress.js"></script></body></html>');
const server = createServer((req, res) => {
  const p = new URL(req.url, 'http://x').pathname;
  const f = join(outDir, p === '/' ? 'index.html' : p);
  try { const b = readFileSync(f); res.writeHead(200, { 'content-type': f.endsWith('.js') ? 'text/javascript' : f.endsWith('.css') ? 'text/css' : 'text/html' }); res.end(b); } catch { res.writeHead(404); res.end(); }
}).listen(0);
const port = server.address().port;
const browser = await chromium.launch({ executablePath: exe, headless: true, args: ['--enable-gpu-rasterization', '--ignore-gpu-blocklist', '--disable-frame-rate-limit=false'] });
const page = await browser.newPage({ viewport: { width: 1440, height: 900 } });
for (const [n, edge, vis] of [[500, 'smoothstep', 0], [500, 'smoothstep', 1], [500, 'straight', 0], [2000, 'smoothstep', 0], [2000, 'smoothstep', 1]]) {
  const t0 = Date.now();
  await page.goto(`http://localhost:${port}/?n=${n}&edge=${edge}&vis=${vis}`);
  await page.waitForFunction(() => window.bench?.ready, null, { timeout: 120000 });
  await page.waitForTimeout(500);
  const mount = Date.now() - t0;
  const dom = await page.evaluate(() => window.bench.count());
  const zoom = await page.evaluate(() => window.bench.zoom());
  const relayout = await page.evaluate(() => window.bench.relayout());
  console.log(JSON.stringify({ n, edge, onlyRenderVisible: !!vis, mountMs: mount, domNodes: dom, zoom, relayout }));
}
const gpu = await page.evaluate(() => { const c = document.createElement('canvas').getContext('webgl'); const d = c && c.getExtension('WEBGL_debug_renderer_info'); return d ? c.getParameter(d.UNMASKED_RENDERER_WEBGL) : 'n/a'; });
console.log('renderer:', gpu);
await browser.close();
server.close();
```

```text
**G6 v5 Combo summary (based only on the provided page)**

- **Nesting:** A Combo can contain nodes and sub-combos. The example nests `combo1` and `combo2` inside `combo3` via each combo's `combo` field. The page does not state a maximum nesting depth.
- **Collapse/expand:** The `collapse-expand` behavior toggles a Combo on double-click. When collapsed, all nodes inside are hidden, and "all connections will connect to the Combo," so edges from outside nodes are re-routed to it. The page implies the collapsed Combo stays visible as the connection point but does not explicitly say it renders as a node. A `collapsed` style flag also appears in the data example.
- **Animation on collapse:** Not covered.
- **Layouts with Combo support:** Not covered. The page only lists "ComboCombined Layout" and "AntvDagre Layout" in the sidebar without describing their Combo support.
- **Renderers (canvas/SVG/WebGL):** Not covered. The sidebar links to a "renderer" page, but its content is not included here.
- **Related notes:** Dragging a Combo moves its contents, and `dropEffect: 'link'` lets users change a node's Combo membership during a drag. The page advises against using Combos in tree graphs.
```

```text
**Motion 14.0.0** (2 Oct 2026)
- Removed internal APIs that 13.5.1 had restored for compatibility with `framer-motion` 13.0 to 13.4.

**Motion 13.0.0** (5 Aug 2026)
- Removed the optional `@emotion/is-prop-valid` dependency. Prop validation now goes through an explicit `<MotionConfig isValidProp={isPropValid}>`.
- Fixed hardware-accelerated SVG elements not applying their final style when an animation completes.
- Fixed `AnimatePresence` so nodes are marked safe to remove when `propagate` is used with no `motion` children.

**Layout animations, LayoutGroup, layoutId, and React support:** Neither release mentions these. The closest item is the `AnimatePresence` fix in 13.0.0, which concerns exit handling rather than layout. The changelog also doesn't state React version support for either release.
```

Scout is at about the right complexity for the demo. It's already near the upper limit of what reads clearly on a grid in 3 minutes, so I'd point the demo at the complexity it has rather than add more.

**Where it stands** (measured from the code, on the map with the UI row):

| | |
|---|---|
| Grid | 6 domains × 5 layers; 22 of the 30 cells have code |
| Code | 3,671 lines in `src/`, `vendor/` and `scripts/`, plus 1,447 in the web app and 372 in tests; 14 commits |
| External services | 4 live (Claude, web search, web fetch for transcripts, SEC EDGAR), 2 sandboxed (Gmail-style email, HubSpot-style CRM), plus local embeddings and an OpenAI stand-in |
| Data | 6 tables, each with a single owning domain |
| Rules | 3 seeded (DR-1 to DR-3); exactly 1 existing violation |
| Edges between domains | 16 (24 when counted cell to cell) |
| A live research run | about 70 seconds, 6–7 model calls, 2–3 cents |

**Edges that carry the story:**
- **The red edge:** Research tools › Logic → Model gateway › External, from `news-summarize.ts` calling Claude directly. It's a real leak: the app's talking points say "Maya Ortiz" by name while the brief shows a `name 1` chip.
- **The fan-out:** the API routes (Channels › Entry) reach into 4 domains. That's normal for an API layer and reads as "the front door touches everything".
- **The run loop:** Agent loop › Logic → tools, memory, outreach and the gateway, which is the system's backbone.

**One flaw to fix:** four UI pages point back at the shell (Usage, Accounts, Runs and Outreach › UI → Channels › UI), because they import the router from `web/src/app/`. That makes the UI edges look two-way and circular when they should all point outward. Moving `router.tsx` into the neutral `web/src/shared/` removes them, bringing the domain-level edges from 16 to 12 and leaving the UI row as clean outward edges from the shell. It takes about 10 minutes, plus a one-line change to the map YAML.

**How I'd pitch it:**
- **"This is a real production system."** Show the app for 15 seconds: a live run, the trail filling in, real Symbotic numbers. Then cut to the grid: "3,600 lines across 6 domains and 7 external services. You didn't write it, and you know the shape in ten seconds."
- **The red cell is a real data leak, not a lint warning.** Put the app's "Talking Points for Maya Ortiz" next to the brief's `name 1` chip. It's one red edge on the map and one real person's name sent to a model provider.
- **The 10-K fork is genuine, because the shortcut has a real cause.** Through the gateway, Symbotic's actual MD&A loses about 50 figures to `$ [PHONE_22]` tokens. Option A (fix redaction in the gateway) lights a second column, Model gateway › Logic, so the map shows the change leaving the tools column. That's the cross-domain moment the pitch is about. Option B is the red edge.
- **A normal change is a vertical stripe.** The trail renders any new tool on its own, so done right the 10-K tool touches only Research tools › Logic and External: a clean stripe.
- **Memory.** Earnings call transcripts are already served live, so the second-session prompt works against real data.

**What to avoid on stage:**
- **Don't run Scout live during the harness beats.** Seventy seconds of waiting kills the pace. Show finished runs in the app, or start the server with `SCOUT_MODE=offline` for instant runs.
- **Don't add more domains or connectors.** The Build Plan's own test is 5–9 domains with a typical turn lighting 1–3 cells, and Scout already has 22 filled cells. More would make the map harder to read, not more impressive. That also argues against doing the Gmail- and HubSpot-shaped connectors now; the Connections page alone would add the "many integrations" impression at no cost to the map.

**Still with the other session:** the map fixture has no UI row yet. Until it's applied, all 11 web files land in Unassigned.

Want me to do the router fix and update the YAML section in `DEMO_REPO_SPEC.md` to match?

  ## 2. Layout engines (measured timings)
  
  Synthetic repo graph: 6×4 cells, 1.5 edges per file, 140×36 nodes, elkjs 0.12.0, `@dagrejs/dagre` 3.1.1. Times are medians.
  
  | Files | ELK layered `INCLUDE_CHILDREN` orthogonal | ELK flat layered | **ELK per-cell (24 separate runs, total)** | dagre compound | dagre flat |
  |---|---|---|---|---|---|
  | 100 | 220–275 ms | 69–79 ms | **33 ms** | 426–464 ms | 127 ms |
  | 500 | 1.8–2.4 s | 1.2–1.4 s | **~100 ms** | **crashed** ("Not possible to find intersection inside of the rectangle") | 1.9 s |
  | 2000 | 11.5 s | 10.4 s | **~450 ms** | crashed | 44.6 s |
  
  Other measurements:
  - A single expanded cell of 300 files takes 93–201 ms.
  - ELK `rectpacking` on 2000 edgeless nodes takes 309 ms.
  - ELK `stress` takes ~1 s at 100 nodes and 29 s at 500. Don't use it.
  
  **elkjs**
  - 0.12.0 (2026-07-17), licensed EPL-2.0 OR GPL-3.0-or-later ([releases](https://github.com/kieler/elkjs/releases)), 2.8k ★.
  - `elk-worker.min.js` is 1.5 MB raw (~453 kB gz). It runs in a worker via `workerUrl` and is asynchronous ([README](https://github.com/kieler/elkjs)).
  - Options that matter for us ([layered reference](https://eclipse.dev/elk/reference/algorithms/org-eclipse-elk-layered.html)):
    - `hierarchyHandling`
    - `portConstraints` (FIXED_SIDE / FIXED_ORDER)
    - `edgeRouting` ORTHOGONAL
    - `mergeEdges`
    - `considerModelOrder.strategy`
    - `crossingMinimization.forceNodeModelOrder`
    - the interactive set: `cycleBreaking.strategy: INTERACTIVE`, `layering.strategy: INTERACTIVE`, `crossingMinimization.semiInteractive: true`. These reuse the positions of the previous layout.
  - `layerChoiceConstraint` and `positionChoiceConstraint` are only evaluated by external tooling (KLighD), not by ELK itself ([ELK blog](https://eclipse.dev/elk/blog/posts/2023/23-01-09-constraining-the-model.html)).
  
  **dagre**: no ports, no orthogonal routing, and compound mode is unreliable. Avoid it for nested graphs.
  
  **libavoid-js**
  - 0.5.0-beta.5, **LGPL-2.1**, 46 ★, WASM 484 kB (~177 kB gz).
  - **Measured** orthogonal routing with connection pins:
  
  | Shapes / connectors | Route | Reroute after moving one shape |
  |---|---|---|
  | 24 / 59 | 31 ms | 19 ms |
  | 100 / 149 | 158 ms | 269 ms |
  | 200 / 296 | 717 ms | — |
  
  - It scales superlinearly. It is fine for the top-level grid and not for inner levels.
  - Gotchas: in the 0.5 beta the flag is `RouterFlag.OrthogonalRouting.value`. Attaching ends to points inside shapes instead of using pins is 20–100× slower.
  
  **Others**
  - WebCola 3.4.0 was last released in 2019. Good constraint ideas, but stale.
  - `d3-hierarchy` treemap/pack is deterministic and takes milliseconds. Good for file→symbol packing.
  - graphology layouts are force-only.
  
  ## 3. React Flow animation (measured; the key finding)
  
  Headless Chromium doesn't vsync, so read frame times, not fps.
  
  **500 nodes, 750 smoothstep edges, 24 group parents**
  - Camera zoom/pan via `setViewport` every frame: p50 4.5–4.9 ms, p95 7–8.5 ms. That is comfortably 60fps.
  - Animating a relayout with `setNodes` every frame: **p50 37–41 ms (~23 fps)**. Too slow.
  - **FLIP** (commit the new positions once, then `el.animate()` each node's transform with the Web Animations API): the commit takes 27 ms, then **p50 3.6 ms per frame** while it runs. The naive version had one ~240 ms hitch on the first frame.
  
  **2000 nodes**
  - Zoom: p50 18 ms, p95 37 ms.
  - `onlyRenderVisibleElements` brings p50 down to 5.6 ms but spikes to 188 ms while panning.

  - **Renderer:** React Flow 12.12 (pin `~12.12`) as the viewport and DOM node host, with memoized custom nodes.

    - Level 0 keeps the existing deterministic `gridLayout`, with track sizes driven by the size of expanded children.
    - Inner levels use **elkjs layered, one run per expanded container, in a Web Worker**. Do not use one global `INCLUDE_CHILDREN` run.

    - Aggregation itself acts as bundling: collapsed endpoints roll up to the nearest visible ancestor, and stroke width scales with the count.
    - Where an edge crosses a container boundary, give the container side ports (FIXED_SIDE), let ELK route the stub from the inner node to that port, then hand off to the gutter router.

    - Node moves and resizes: FLIP with the Web Animations API.

Measured: ELK per container is 10–25× faster than a hierarchical run and naturally isolates change, which is what preserves the mental map.
  
  ### Architecture sketch
  
  ```
  event log ─(pure reduce)─► UIState ─► derive VisibleTree(expansion set, zoom bucket)
  ```

  **Transition sequence** (a small xstate-style machine, cancellable with `getAnimations().forEach(a => a.finish())`):

  | Risk | Mitigation |

Yes. That framing is better than "add this, watch the gate fire", because it shows the human doing the useful part: spotting the problem, reading the plan on the map, and steering how it gets built before any code exists.

**The natural loop for each beat:**
1. **Notice it in the app.** A bug you can see, or a feature a rep would ask for.
2. **Ask in plain words** in the harness chat.
3. **Review the plan as ghosts on the map.** Which cells it would touch, whether it crosses into another domain, whether an edge goes red.
4. **Steer.** "No, fix it at the source", or answer the A/B question if a rule fires. The agent resubmits and the ghosts move.
5. **Approve and watch it build.** Ghosts fill in, then the result shows up in Scout.
6. **The decision is remembered**, so the next session builds it the same way without asking.

**For Scout, a good beat needs** a request a rep would really make, a shortcut that's tempting but wrong, and a right fix that touches 1–3 cells. Three candidates, each testing a different rule:

**1. Bug: "Revenue shows as 'phone 1' in the company profile."** This is my top pick.
- **Wrong fix A:** format revenue as "$2.2B" in the enrichment adapter. The ghost lands in Research tools › External. It hides the symptom and breaks no rule, so only a human reading the map catches it.
- **Wrong fix B:** have the profile tool call Claude directly, like the news tool does. This draws a red edge (DR-1).
- **Right fix:** tighten the phone pattern in the gateway (Model gateway › Logic), which also fixes every other tool that will ever pass figures through.
- **Why it's strongest:** the review step does the work even when no rule fires. You're steering on judgment, which is what the pitch claims.

**2. Feature: "The brief should say if we've already emailed this person."**
- **Wrong path:** following the README's "Adding a tool" guide, the agent writes an `outreach_history` tool that imports outreach code. Rule DR-3 ("research tools never depend on outreach") turns that edge red before any code exists.
- **Right path:** outreach exposes the history, and the run loop passes it into the brief (Agent loop › Logic plus Outreach › Logic).

**3. Feature: "Let reps mark a contact as do-not-contact from the Outreach page."**
